parts.problemMd:
A square has side length $3 \text{ln} 4$.

Show that the perimeter of the square is $24 \text{ln} 2$.
parts.solutionMd:
The perimeter of a square is four times its side length

$P = 4 \times 3 \text{ln} 4 = 12 \text{ln} 4$

**[M1]**

Write $\text{ln} 4 = \text{ln} 2^{2} = 2 \text{ln} 2$ to reach the required form

**Final answer:** $P = 12 \times 2 \text{ln} 2 = 24 \text{ln} 2$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Uses perimeter $= 4 \times$ side length to obtain $12 \text{ln} 4$.
> 
> **A1**: Converts $\text{ln} 4 = 2 \text{ln} 2$ to reach the printed result $24 \text{ln} 2$. Because the result is given, the working must be shown.

parts.problemMd:
Write the following in the form $a \text{ln} b$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers to be found.

$4 \text{ln} 9 + 2 \text{ln} 81 - 3 \text{ln} 27$
parts.solutionMd:
Write 9, 81 and 27 as powers of 3, then apply the power law $\text{ln} x^{n} = n \text{ln} x$

$4 \text{ln} 9 + 2 \text{ln} 81 - 3 \text{ln} 27 = 4 \text{ln} 3^{2} + 2 \text{ln} 3^{4} - 3 \text{ln} 3^{3}$

**[M1]**

Bring each power down in front of the logarithm

$= 8 \text{ln} 3 + 8 \text{ln} 3 - 9 \text{ln} 3$

**[A1]**

Collect the like terms

$= 7 \text{ln} 3$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writes 9, 81 and 27 as powers of 3 and applies the power law $\text{ln} x^{n} = n \text{ln} x$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct terms $8 \text{ln} 3 + 8 \text{ln} 3 - 9 \text{ln} 3$.
> 
> **A1**: $7 \text{ln} 3$ (that is $a = 7$, $b = 3$).

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$7^{2x-1} = 343$
parts.solutionMd:
Write 343 as a power of 7 so both sides share the base 7

$7^{2x-1} = 7^{3}$

**[M1]**

Equate the indices and solve for $x$

$2 x - 1 = 3$

$x = 2$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Alternative method: you can also take natural logarithms of both sides, giving $( 2 x - 1 ) \text{ln} 7 = \text{ln} 343$. Since $\text{ln} 343 = 3 \text{ln} 7$, this reduces to $2 x - 1 = 3$ as before. Spotting $343 = 7^{3}$ and equating powers is quicker here, but taking logarithms works for any equation of this form, even when the right-hand side is not an exact power of the base.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Reduces the equation to $2 x - 1 = 3$ by any valid method: either by writing $343 = 7^{3}$ and equating powers of 7, or by taking logarithms of both sides.
> 
> **A1**: $x = 2$.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
Use the quotient law $\text{log} \frac{x}{y} = \text{log} x - \text{log} y$, and write 27 and 16 as powers

`4\text{log}\left(\frac{27}{16}\right) = 4\left(\text{log} 27 - \text{log} 16\right) = 4\left(\text{log} 3^{3} - \text{log} 2^{4}\right)`

Apply the power law inside the bracket

Simplify each term

> **M1**: Forms and solves the quadratic $x^{2} - 5 x + 6 = 0$.

> **A1**: $x = 2$ and $x = 3$. Both are valid, since each gives a base that is positive and not equal to 1, and a positive argument $5 x - 6$.

parts.problemMd:
Evaluate

$\text{log}_{2} 8^{2} + 3 \text{log}_{2} 16 - 2 \text{log}_{2} 2^{5}$
parts.solutionMd:
Write each number as a power of 2, using $8 = 2^{3}$ and $16 = 2^{4}$

$\text{log}_{2} 8^{2} + 3 \text{log}_{2} 16 - 2 \text{log}_{2} 2^{5} = \text{log}_{2} 2^{6} + 3 \text{log}_{2} 2^{4} - 2 \text{log}_{2} 2^{5}$

**[M1]**

Evaluate each logarithm and simplify

$= 6 + 12 - 10$

$= 8$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writes the terms as $\text{log}_{2} 2^{6} + 3 \text{log}_{2} 2^{4} - 2 \text{log}_{2} 2^{5}$ (or evaluates each logarithm to $6$, $12$ and $10$).
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $8$.

parts.problemMd:
Evaluate

$3 \text{ln} 2 + 2 \text{ln} 5 - \frac{1}{2} \text{ln} 10000$

giving your answer in the form $\text{ln} p$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the power law to write each term as a single logarithm

$3 \text{ln} 2 + 2 \text{ln} 5 - \frac{1}{2} \text{ln} 10000 = \text{ln} 8 + \text{ln} 25 - \text{ln} 100$

**[M1]**

Combine using the product and quotient laws

`= \text{ln}\left(\dfrac{8 \times 25}{100}\right)`

**[A1]**

Simplify the argument

**Final answer:** $= \text{ln} 2$** so **$p = 2$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Uses the power law to reach $\text{ln} 8 + \text{ln} 25 - \text{ln} 100$ (note $\frac{1}{2} \text{ln} 10000 = \text{ln} 100$).
> 
> **A1**: Correct single logarithm `\text{ln}\left(\dfrac{8 \times 25}{100}\right)`.
> 
> **A1**: $\text{ln} 2$, so $p = 2$.

parts.problemMd:
By writing 5 as $5 \text{ln} e$, show that

$5 \text{ln} 2 + 5$

can be written as $5 \text{ln} 2 e$.
parts.solutionMd:
Write 5 as $5 \text{ln} e$, since $\text{ln} e = 1$

$5 \text{ln} 2 + 5 = 5 \text{ln} 2 + 5 \text{ln} e$

**[M1]**

Factor out the 5

`= 5\left(\text{ln} 2 + \text{ln} e\right)`

**[A1]**

Combine using the product law $\text{ln} 2 + \text{ln} e = \text{ln} 2 e$

**Final answer:** $= 5 \text{ln} 2 e$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writes $5 = 5 \text{ln} e$ to give $5 \text{ln} 2 + 5 \text{ln} e$.
> 
> **A1**: Factors out the 5 to reach `5\left(\text{ln} 2 + \text{ln} e\right)`.
> 
> **A1**: Applies the product law to reach the printed result $5 \text{ln} 2 e$. Because the result is given, the working must be shown.

parts.problemMd:
Evaluate

$4 \text{log}_{3} 729 + 3 \text{log}_{2} 64^{2} - 3 \text{log} 100 + \text{ln} e^{6}$
parts.solutionMd:
Evaluate each logarithm: $\text{log}_{3} 729 = 6$, $\text{log}_{2} 64^{2} = 12$, $\text{log} 100 = 2$ and $\text{ln} e^{6} = 6$

$4 ( 6 ) + 3 ( 12 ) - 3 ( 2 ) + 6 = 24 + 36 - 6 + 6$

**[M1]**

$= 60$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Evaluates all four logarithms correctly ($6$, $12$, $2$ and $6$).
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $60$.

parts.problemMd:
Evaluate

$\frac{1}{2} \text{ln} 196 + \frac{1}{3} \text{ln} 125 + \frac{1}{4} \text{ln} 81 + \frac{1}{5} \text{ln} 32$

giving your answer in the form $\text{ln} q$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the power law to take each coefficient inside as a power, so each term becomes a root

$\frac{1}{2} \text{ln} 196 + \frac{1}{3} \text{ln} 125 + \frac{1}{4} \text{ln} 81 + \frac{1}{5} \text{ln} 32 = \text{ln} 196^{1/2} + \text{ln} 125^{1/3} + \text{ln} 81^{1/4} + \text{ln} 32^{1/5}$

**[M1]**

Evaluate each root

$= \text{ln} 14 + \text{ln} 5 + \text{ln} 3 + \text{ln} 2$

**[A1]**

Combine using the product law

**Final answer:** $= \text{ln} 420$** so **$q = 420$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Uses the power law, for example $\frac{1}{2} \text{ln} 196 = \text{ln} 196^{1/2} = \text{ln} 14$.
> 
> **A1**: All four terms correct: $\text{ln} 14 + \text{ln} 5 + \text{ln} 3 + \text{ln} 2$.
> 
> **A1**: $\text{ln} 420$, so $q = 420$.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$4^{3x+2} = 16^{x+6}$
parts.solutionMd:
Write 16 as a power of 4 so both sides share the base 4

`4^{3x + 2} = \left(4^{2}\right)^{x + 6}`

Multiply the indices on the right-hand side

$4^{3x+2} = 4^{2x+12}$

**[M1]**

Equate the indices and solve

$3 x + 2 = 2 x + 12$

$x = 10$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writes $16 = 4^{2}$ and equates the indices $3 x + 2 = 2 x + 12$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = 10$.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$4^{2x+3} - 8 = 92$

giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Add 8 to both sides

$4^{2x+3} = 100$

**[M1]**

Take natural logarithms of both sides

`\text{ln}\left(4^{2x + 3}\right) = \text{ln} 100`

Bring the exponent down using the power law

$( 2 x + 3 ) \text{ln} 4 = \text{ln} 100$

Divide by $\text{ln} 4$ to make $2 x + 3$ the subject

$2 x + 3 = \frac{\text{ln}100}{\text{ln}4} = 3 . 3219 \dots$

**[A1]**

Solve for $x$, giving the answer correct to 3 significant figures

$x = 0 . 161$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Adds 8 to reach $4^{2x+3} = 100$.
> 
> **A1**: Takes logarithms of both sides and applies the power law to reach $2 x + 3 = \frac{\text{ln}100}{\text{ln}4}$ (or $3 . 32$).
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $x = 0 . 161$ (3 significant figures). Do not round the intermediate value.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the following equations, giving your answers in exact form.

$4 e^{3x-2} = 12$
parts.solutionMd:
Divide both sides by 4

$e^{3x-2} = 3$

Take natural logarithms of both sides, using `\text{ln}\left(e^{3x - 2}\right) = 3x - 2`

$3 x - 2 = \text{ln} 3$

**[M1]**

Make $x$ the subject

$x = \frac{2+\text{ln}3}{3}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Divides by 4 and takes natural logarithms to reach $3 x - 2 = \text{ln} 3$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = \frac{2+\text{ln}3}{3}$.

Recognise a quadratic in $e^{x}$; let $y = e^{x}$

$3 y^{2} - 14 y + 8 = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise and solve for $y$

$( 3 y - 2 ) ( y - 4 ) = 0$

$y = \frac{2}{3}$* or *$y = 4$

**[A1]**

Replace $y$ with $e^{x}$ (both values are positive, so the logarithms are defined)

$e^{x} = \frac{2}{3}$* or *$e^{x} = 4$

Take natural logarithms of both sides

**Final answer:** $x = \text{ln} \frac{2}{3}$** or **$x = \text{ln} 4$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Forms the quadratic $3 y^{2} - 14 y + 8 = 0$ with $y = e^{x}$.
> 
> **A1**: Solves to $y = \frac{2}{3}$ and $y = 4$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = \text{ln} \frac{2}{3}$ and $x = \text{ln} 4$. Both roots are valid because each value of $y$ is positive.

parts.problemMd:
Simplify

$2 \text{ln} 3^{4} + \text{ln} 3^{3} - \text{ln} 9$

giving your answer in the form $a \text{ln} b$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
Apply the power law, writing $9 = 3^{2}$

$2 \text{ln} 3^{4} + \text{ln} 3^{3} - \text{ln} 9 = 8 \text{ln} 3 + 3 \text{ln} 3 - 2 \text{ln} 3$

**[M1]**

Collect the like terms

$= 9 \text{ln} 3$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Applies the power law to each term, including $\text{ln} 9 = 2 \text{ln} 3$.
> 
> **A1**: $9 \text{ln} 3$ (that is $a = 9$, $b = 3$).

parts.problemMd:
Write

`2\text{log}_{a} x + 3\text{log}_{a}\left(x + 1\right) - \text{log}_{a} 4\left(x + 2\right)`

as a single logarithm.
parts.solutionMd:
Apply the power law to the first two terms

$2 \text{log}_{a} x + 3 \text{log}_{a} ( x + 1 ) - \text{log}_{a} 4 ( x + 2 ) = \text{log}_{a} x^{2} + \text{log}_{a} ( x + 1 )^{3} - \text{log}_{a} 4 ( x + 2 )$

**[M1]**

Combine using the product and quotient laws

$= \text{log}_{a} \frac{x^{2}(x+1)^{3}}{4(x+2)}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Applies the power law to give $\text{log}_{a} x^{2}$ and $\text{log}_{a} ( x + 1 )^{3}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct single logarithm $\text{log}_{a} \frac{x^{2}(x+1)^{3}}{4(x+2)}$.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$5^{2x} - 8 \times 5^{x} + 12 = 0$

giving your answers in the form $\text{log}_{a} b$.
parts.solutionMd:
Recognise a quadratic in $5^{x}$; let $y = 5^{x}$

$y^{2} - 8 y + 12 = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise and solve for $y$

$( y - 2 ) ( y - 6 ) = 0$

$y = 2$* or *$y = 6$

**[A1]**

Replace $y$ with $5^{x}$

$5^{x} = 2$* or *$5^{x} = 6$

Take logarithms of both sides to base 5, matching the required form

**Final answer:** $x = \text{log}_{5} 2$** or **$x = \text{log}_{5} 6$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Forms the quadratic $y^{2} - 8 y + 12 = 0$ with $y = 5^{x}$.
> 
> **A1**: Solves to $y = 2$ and $y = 6$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = \text{log}_{5} 2$ and $x = \text{log}_{5} 6$. Accept any correct logarithm of the required form $\text{log}_{a} b$, for example $\text{log}_{25} 4$ and $\text{log}_{25} 36$. A quotient of logarithms such as $\frac{\text{ln}2}{\text{ln}5}$ is not in the required form.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$6 \times 3^{x-1} = 6^{2x}$

giving your answer in the form $\frac{\text{ln}a}{\text{ln}b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
Simplify the left-hand side using $3^{x-1} = \frac{3^{x}}{3}$

$6 \times 3^{x-1} = \frac{6}{3} \times 3^{x} = 2 \times 3^{x}$

**[M1]**

Write the right-hand side with a single base, $6^{2x} = 36^{x}$

$2 \times 3^{x} = 36^{x}$

**[M1]**

Divide both sides by $3^{x}$, using $\frac{36^{x}}{3^{x}} = 12^{x}$

$12^{x} = 2$

**[A1]**

Take logarithms of both sides

$x \text{ln} 12 = \text{ln} 2$

**[M1]**

Make $x$ the subject

$x = \frac{\text{ln}2}{\text{ln}12}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Simplifies the left-hand side to $2 \times 3^{x}$.
> 
> **M1**: Writes $6^{2x} = 36^{x}$.
> 
> **A1**: Reaches $12^{x} = 2$.
> 
> **M1**: Takes logarithms of both sides.
> 
> **A1**: $x = \frac{\text{ln}2}{\text{ln}12}$ (that is $a = 2$, $b = 12$). Accept the equivalent $\text{log}_{12} 2$.

parts.problemMd:
A ship sets sail from a harbour.

After some time, the ship's position is `\left(4\text{ln} 3\right)` km east of the harbour and `\left(3\text{ln} 3\right)` km north of the harbour.

Find the direct distance between the ship and the harbour at this time, giving your answer in the form `\left(p\text{ln} 3\right)` km, where $p$ is an integer to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
The east and north displacements are perpendicular, so use Pythagoras' theorem for the direct distance $d$

$d^{2} = ( 4 \text{ln} 3 )^{2} + ( 3 \text{ln} 3 )^{2}$

**[M1]**

Expand each square, taking out the common factor $( \text{ln} 3 )^{2}$

$d^{2} = 16 ( \text{ln} 3 )^{2} + 9 ( \text{ln} 3 )^{2} = 25 ( \text{ln} 3 )^{2}$

**[A1]**

Take the positive square root

$d = \sqrt{25(\text{ln}3)^{2}} = 5 \text{ln} 3$

**[M1]**

State the distance in the required form

**Final answer:** $d = 5 \text{ln} 3$** km, so **$p = 5$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Applies Pythagoras' theorem: $d^{2} = ( 4 \text{ln} 3 )^{2} + ( 3 \text{ln} 3 )^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Simplifies to $25 ( \text{ln} 3 )^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Takes the positive square root.
> 
> **A1**: $d = 5 \text{ln} 3$ km, so $p = 5$.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

`\text{log}_{3}\left(x + 4\right) = 4 + 2\text{log}_{3} x`

giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Collect the logarithms on one side, then use the power and quotient laws

$\text{log}_{3} ( x + 4 ) - \text{log}_{3} x^{2} = 4$

`\text{log}_{3}\left(\dfrac{x + 4}{x^{2}}\right) = 4`

**[M1]**

Remove the logarithm using $3^{4} = 81$, and rearrange into a quadratic

$\frac{x+4}{x^{2}} = 81  \Rightarrow  81 x^{2} - x - 4 = 0$

**[A1]**

Solve the quadratic and reject the negative root, since $\text{log}_{3} x$ requires $x > 0$

$x = 0 . 228$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Uses the power and quotient laws to reach a single logarithm, `\text{log}_{3}\left(\dfrac{x + 4}{x^{2}}\right) = 4`.
> 
> **A1**: Removes the logarithm and forms the quadratic $81 x^{2} - x - 4 = 0$.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $x = 0 . 228$ (3 significant figures). The negative root is rejected because $\text{log}_{3} x$ requires $x > 0$.

parts.problemMd: Show that $4 - \text{ln} 16$ can be written in the form `4\text{ln}\left(\dfrac{e}{2}\right)`.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the power law to write $\text{ln} 16 = \text{ln} 2^{4} = 4 \text{ln} 2$

$4 - \text{ln} 16 = 4 - 4 \text{ln} 2$

Write 4 as $4 \text{ln} e$, since $\text{ln} e = 1$

$= 4 \text{ln} e - 4 \text{ln} 2$

**[M1]**

Factor out the 4

`= 4\left(\text{ln} e - \text{ln} 2\right)`

**[A1]**

Combine using the quotient law $\text{ln} e - \text{ln} 2 = \text{ln} \frac{e}{2}$

**Final answer:** `= 4\text{ln}\left(\dfrac{e}{2}\right)`** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writes $4 = 4 \text{ln} e$ and $\text{ln} 16 = 4 \text{ln} 2$.
> 
> **A1**: Factors out 4 to reach `4\left(\text{ln} e - \text{ln} 2\right)`.
> 
> **A1**: Uses the quotient law to reach the printed result `4\text{ln}\left(\dfrac{e}{2}\right)`. Because the result is given, the working must be shown.

parts.problemMd:
How many real solutions does the equation have? Justify your answer.

`3\text{log}_{x}\left(x + 1\right) = \text{ln} e^{3}`
parts.solutionMd:
Evaluate the right-hand side using $\text{ln} e^{3} = 3$

$3 \text{log}_{x} ( x + 1 ) = 3$

Divide both sides by 3

$\text{log}_{x} ( x + 1 ) = 1$

**[M1]**

Rewrite in index form: the base $x$ raised to the power 1 gives $x + 1$

$x + 1 = x$

**[M1]**

This requires $1 = 0$, which is impossible, so no value of $x$ satisfies the equation

$\text{No real solutions}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Uses $\text{ln} e^{3} = 3$ to reduce the equation to $\text{log}_{x} ( x + 1 ) = 1$.
> 
> **M1**: Rewrites in index form as $x + 1 = x$.
> 
> **A1**: Concludes there are no real solutions, justified by the contradiction $x + 1 = x$ (equivalently $1 = 0$).

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$2 \times 5^{2x+1} + 21 = 41 \times 5^{x}$

giving your answers in the form $\text{log}_{a} b$, where $a$ and $b$ are rational numbers to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the index law $5^{2x+1} = 5 \times 5^{2x}$ to rewrite the equation in powers of $5^{x}$

$2 \times 5 \times 5^{2x} + 21 = 41 \times 5^{x}$

Let $y = 5^{x}$, so that $5^{2x} = y^{2}$

$2 \times 5 \times y^{2} + 21 = 41 y$

**[M1]**

Rearrange into a quadratic

$10 y^{2} - 41 y + 21 = 0$

**[A1]**

Factorise and solve for $y$

$( 2 y - 7 ) ( 5 y - 3 ) = 0$

$y = \frac{7}{2}$* or *$y = \frac{3}{5}$

**[A1]**

Replace $y$ with $5^{x}$

$5^{x} = \frac{7}{2}$* or *$5^{x} = \frac{3}{5}$

Take logarithms of both sides to base 5, matching the required form

**Final answer:** $x = \text{log}_{5} \frac{7}{2}$** or **$x = \text{log}_{5} \frac{3}{5}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Uses $5^{2x+1} = 5 \times 5^{2x}$ and $y = 5^{x}$ to form an equation in $y$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct quadratic $10 y^{2} - 41 y + 21 = 0$.
> 
> **A1**: Solves to $y = \frac{7}{2}$ and $y = \frac{3}{5}$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = \text{log}_{5} \frac{7}{2}$ and $x = \text{log}_{5} \frac{3}{5}$. Accept any correct logarithm of the required form $\text{log}_{a} b$ with $a$ and $b$ rational, for example $\text{log}_{25} \frac{49}{4}$. A quotient of logarithms such as $\frac{\text{ln}\frac{7}{2}}{\text{ln}5}$ is not in the required form.

parts.problemMd:
Show that

`2\text{log}_{3} x + \text{log}_{3}\left(x^{2} - 1\right) - 2\text{log}_{3}\left(x + 1\right) \equiv \text{log}_{3}\frac{x^{2}\left(x - 1\right)}{\left(x + 1\right)}`
parts.solutionMd:
Apply the power law to the first and third terms

$2 \text{log}_{3} x + \text{log}_{3} ( x^{2} - 1 ) - 2 \text{log}_{3} ( x + 1 ) = \text{log}_{3} x^{2} + \text{log}_{3} ( x^{2} - 1 ) - \text{log}_{3} ( x + 1 )^{2}$

Factorise $x^{2} - 1 = ( x - 1 ) ( x + 1 )$

$= \text{log}_{3} x^{2} + \text{log}_{3} ( x - 1 ) ( x + 1 ) - \text{log}_{3} ( x + 1 )^{2}$

**[M1]**

Combine using the product and quotient laws

$= \text{log}_{3} \frac{x^{2}(x-1)(x+1)}{(x+1)^{2}}$

**[A1]**

Cancel one factor of $( x + 1 )$

**Final answer:** $= \text{log}_{3} \frac{x^{2}(x-1)}{(x+1)}$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Applies the power law and factorises $x^{2} - 1 = ( x - 1 ) ( x + 1 )$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct combined single logarithm $\text{log}_{3} \frac{x^{2}(x-1)(x+1)}{(x+1)^{2}}$.
> 
> **A1**: Cancels to the printed result $\text{log}_{3} \frac{x^{2}(x-1)}{(x+1)}$. Because the result is given, the working must be shown.

parts.problemMd:
Write the following as a single logarithm

`2\text{log}_{p}\left(x + 1\right) + 3\text{log}_{p}\left(x - 1\right) - \text{log}_{p}\left(x^{2} - 1\right)`
parts.solutionMd:
Apply the power law to the first two terms

$2 \text{log}_{p} ( x + 1 ) + 3 \text{log}_{p} ( x - 1 ) - \text{log}_{p} ( x^{2} - 1 ) = \text{log}_{p} ( x + 1 )^{2} + \text{log}_{p} ( x - 1 )^{3} - \text{log}_{p} ( x^{2} - 1 )$

**[M1]**

Combine using the product and quotient laws

$= \text{log}_{p} \frac{(x+1)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}{x^{2}-1}$

Factorise $x^{2} - 1 = ( x - 1 ) ( x + 1 )$ in the denominator

$= \text{log}_{p} \frac{(x+1)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}{(x-1)(x+1)}$

**[A1]**

Cancel the common factors

$= \text{log}_{p} ( x + 1 ) ( x - 1 )^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Applies the power law to give $\text{log}_{p} ( x + 1 )^{2}$ and $\text{log}_{p} ( x - 1 )^{3}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct combined single logarithm over $( x - 1 ) ( x + 1 )$.
> 
> **A1**: Simplifies to $\text{log}_{p} ( x + 1 ) ( x - 1 )^{2}$.

parts.problemMd:
A triangle is drawn inside a circle such that one side of the triangle is the diameter and all three vertices of the triangle lie on the circumference.

The radius of the circle is `\left(3\text{ln} 2\right)` cm.

The two smallest angles in the triangle are $α$ and $β$ respectively, where $β = 2 α$.

Find all three sides of the triangle, giving your answers in the form $a \text{ln} 2$.
parts.solutionMd:
![A triangle inscribed in a circle with one side along the diameter; the vertex on the circumference opposite the diameter is a right angle (the angle in a semicircle); the angles at the two ends of the diameter are marked 2 alpha and alpha, and the radius is 3 ln 2 cm](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/logarithms-and-exponentials/laws-of-logarithms/assets/001-a-triangle-inscribed-in-a-circle-with-one-side-a.png)

The angle in a semicircle is $90 ^{\circ}$, so the vertex opposite the diameter is a right angle; the three angles sum to $180 ^{\circ}$

$90 ^{\circ} + α + 2 α = 180 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Solve for the two smaller angles

$α = 30 ^{\circ} ,  β = 60 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

The diameter is the hypotenuse; its length is twice the radius

$\text{diameter} = 2 \times 3 \text{ln} 2 = 6 \text{ln} 2$

**[B1]**

Use right-angled trigonometry for the side opposite the $30 ^{\circ}$ angle

$6 \text{ln} 2 \times \mathrm{sin} 30 ^{\circ} = 3 \text{ln} 2$

**[M1]**

The side opposite the $60 ^{\circ}$ angle

$6 \text{ln} 2 \times \mathrm{sin} 60 ^{\circ} = 3 \sqrt{3} \text{ln} 2$

State the three sides of the triangle

$6 \text{ln} 2 \, 3 \text{ln} 2 \, 3 \sqrt{3} \text{ln} 2$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Uses the angle in a semicircle ($90 ^{\circ}$) with the angle sum $90 ^{\circ} + α + 2 α = 180 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: $α = 30 ^{\circ}$ and $β = 60 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **B1**: Diameter (hypotenuse) $= 6 \text{ln} 2$.
>

parts.problemMd:
Without using a calculator, show that

$\text{log}_{4} 8 = \text{log}_{9} 27$
parts.solutionMd:
Let $\text{log}_{4} 8 = y$, so $4^{y} = 8$

$4^{y} = 8$

Write both sides in base 2, using $4 = 2^{2}$ and $8 = 2^{3}$

$2^{2y} = 2^{3}$

**[M1]**

Equate the indices

$2 y = 3$

Solve for $y$

$\text{log}_{4} 8 = \frac{3}{2}$

**[A1]**

Repeat for $\text{log}_{9} 27$: let $\text{log}_{9} 27 = z$, so $9^{z} = 27$

$9^{z} = 27$

Write both sides in base 3, using $9 = 3^{2}$ and $27 = 3^{3}$

$3^{2z} = 3^{3}$

Equate the indices and solve

$2 z = 3 \Rightarrow z = \frac{3}{2}$

Both logarithms equal $\frac{3}{2}$, so they are equal

**Final answer:** $\text{log}_{4} 8 = \text{log}_{9} 27 = \frac{3}{2}$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Sets $\text{log}_{4} 8 = y$ and writes $4^{y} = 8$ in base 2 as $2^{2y} = 2^{3}$ (or an equivalent index method).
> 
> **A1**: $\text{log}_{4} 8 = \frac{3}{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Shows $\text{log}_{9} 27 = \frac{3}{2}$ by the same method, so the two are equal. A change-of-base calculator evaluation is not accepted, since the question says "without using a calculator".

parts.problemMd:
The following equations can be used for exponential models.

State whether each one would represent exponential growth or exponential decay.

(i) $y = 3^{-2x}$

(ii) `y = 20 \left(2\right)^{x}`

(iii) $y = 30 a^{-x}$ where $a > 1$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Rewrite with a positive index to reveal the effective base

`y = 3^{-2x} = \left(3^{-2}\right)^{x} = \left(\dfrac{1}{9}\right)^{x}`

The base $\frac{1}{9}$ lies between 0 and 1, so the model decays

**Final answer:** **Exponential decay**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The number being raised to the power $x$ is the base

`y = 20\left(2\right)^{x}`

The base $2$ is greater than 1, so the model grows

**Final answer:** **Exponential growth**

**[B1]**

(iii)

Rewrite with a positive index to reveal the effective base

`y = 30a^{-x} = 30\left(\dfrac{1}{a}\right)^{x}`

Since $a > 1$, the base $\frac{1}{a}$ lies between 0 and 1, so the model decays

**Final answer:** **Exponential decay**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Exponential decay. The effective base $\frac{1}{9}$ lies between 0 and 1.
> 
> **B1**: Exponential growth. The base $2$ is greater than 1.
> 
> **B1**: Exponential decay. Since $a > 1$, the effective base $\frac{1}{a}$ lies between 0 and 1.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the equation $e^{x} + e^{-x} = 0$ has no real solutions.
parts.solutionMd:
*For every real *$x$* both terms are strictly positive, since *$e^{x} > 0$* and *$e^{-x} > 0$

**[B1]**

*Their sum is therefore always positive, so it can never equal zero*

**Final answer:** $e^{x} + e^{-x} > 0$** for all real x**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both terms correctly shown positive: $e^{x} > 0$ and $e^{-x} > 0$ for all real $x$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct conclusion that the sum is always positive, so the equation has no real solution.

parts.problemMd:
Without using a calculator, evaluate $\text{log}_{4}  128$.

Show each stage of your solution carefully.
parts.solutionMd:
Let $y = \text{log}_{4}  128$, so that, by the definition of a logarithm

$4^{y} = 128$

Write both sides as powers of $2$, since $4 = 2^{2}$ and $128 = 2^{7}$

`\left(2^{2}\right)^{y} = 2^{7}`

$2^{2y} = 2^{7}$

**[M1]**

The bases are equal, so the indices must be equal

$2 y = 7$

$\frac{7}{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writing $\text{log}_{4}  128 = y$ as $4^{y} = 128$ and expressing both sides as powers of $2$ to reach $2^{2y} = 2^{7}$. The power law route, $\text{log}_{4} 128 = 7  \text{log}_{4} 2 = 7 \times \frac{1}{2}$, is equally valid.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{7}{2}$ (accept $3 . 5$).

parts.problemMd: Evaluate $\frac{3\text{log}_{6}216-\text{ln}e^{5}+4^{\text{log}_{5}625}}{\text{log}10000}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Evaluate each part: $\text{log}_{6} 216 = 3$, $\text{ln}  e^{5} = 5$, $\text{log}_{5} 625 = 4$ so $4^{\text{log}_{5}625} = 4^{4} = 256$, and $\text{log}  10000 = 4$

$\frac{3(3)-5+256}{4}$

**[M1]**

Simplify the numerator, then divide

$= \frac{260}{4}$

$= 65$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correctly evaluates the component terms ($3  \text{log}_{6} 216 = 9$, $\text{ln}  e^{5} = 5$, $4^{\text{log}_{5}625} = 256$, $\text{log} 10000 = 4$).
> 
> **A1**: $65$.

parts.problemMd: Solve `3^{2\left(x+1\right)} + 3 = 28\left(3^{x}\right)`.
parts.solutionMd:
Rewrite the first term using the index laws, since `3^{2(x+1)} = 3^{2}\cdot 3^{2x} = 9\left(3^{x}\right)^{2}`

`9\left(3^{x}\right)^{2} + 3 = 28\left(3^{x}\right)`

**[B1]**

Substitute $u = 3^{x}$ to form a quadratic, then factorise

$9 u^{2} - 28 u + 3 = 0$

$( 9 u - 1 ) ( u - 3 ) = 0$

$3^{x} = \frac{1}{9}$* or *$3^{x} = 3$

**[M1]**

Write each as a power of 3 and compare exponents

$x = - 2$

**[A1]**

$x = 1$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct rewrite of $3^{2(x+1)}$ as `9\left(3^x\right)^2` (or `9 \cdot 3^{2x}`).
> 
> **M1**: Correct formation and solution of the quadratic in $3^{x}$, reaching $3^{x} = \frac{1}{9}$ and $3^{x} = 3$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = - 2$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = 1$.

parts.problemMd: Find two values of $x$ for which `\text{log}\left(x^{2}\right) = \left(\text{log} \; x\right)^{2}` is true.
parts.solutionMd:
Apply the power law to the left-hand side, since `\text{log}\left(x^{2}\right) = 2\,\text{log} \; x`

`2\,\text{log} \; x = \left(\text{log} \; x\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

Substitute $u = \text{log}  x$ to form a quadratic, then factorise

$u^{2} - 2 u = 0$

$u ( u - 2 ) = 0$

$\text{log}  x = 0$* or *$\text{log}  x = 2$

**[M1]**

Convert each back to $x$ using base 10

$x = 1$

**[A1]**

$x = 100$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of `\text{log}\left(x^2\right) = 2\,\text{log}\,x`.
> 
> **M1**: Correct formation and solution of the quadratic in $\text{log}  x$, reaching $\text{log}  x = 0$ and $\text{log}  x = 2$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = 1$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = 100$.

parts.problemMd:
A particle is travelling with velocity $v  \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds. The velocity of the particle is modelled by $v = 0 . 3 e^{kt}$, where $k$ is a constant.

Write down the initial velocity of the particle.
parts.solutionMd:
The initial velocity is the value of $v$ when $t = 0$

$v = 0 . 3 e^{k(0)} = 0 . 3 e^{0}$

$0 . 3  \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Initial velocity $0 . 3  \text{m s}^{-1}$.

parts.problemMd: Find an expression (in terms of $k$ and $t$) for the acceleration of the particle.
parts.solutionMd:
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so differentiate $v$ with respect to $t$

$a = \frac{dv}{dt} = 0 . 3 \times k \times e^{kt}$

**[M1]**

$a = 0 . 3 k  e^{kt}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct differentiation of $v = 0 . 3 e^{kt}$ with respect to $t$ (multiplying by $k$).
> 
> **A1**: $a = 0 . 3 k  e^{kt}$.

parts.problemMd:
After 12 seconds the velocity of the particle is $0 . 9  \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the value of $k$, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute $v = 0 . 9$ and $t = 12$, then isolate the exponential

$0 . 3 e^{12k} = 0 . 9$

$e^{12k} = 3$

**[M1]**

Take natural logarithms of both sides

$12 k = \text{ln}  3$

**[M1]**

Divide by 12 and evaluate

**Final answer:** $k = 0 . 0916$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct substitution of the values, rearranging to $e^{12k} = 3$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of natural logarithms to reach $12 k = \text{ln}  3$.
> 
> **A1**: An answer which rounds to $k = 0 . 0916$ (3 significant figures).

parts.problemMd: State a problem with the model for large values of $t$.
parts.solutionMd:
With $k > 0$ the exponential grows without limit, so the model gives an ever-increasing velocity

**Final answer:** **The velocity increases without bound, which is unrealistic**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct recognition that the velocity grows without limit (tends to infinity) as $t$ increases, which is not physically realistic.

parts.problemMd: Solve `\left(e^{x} - e^{-x}\right)^{2} = 0`.
parts.solutionMd:
Expand the square, using `e^{x} \cdot e^{-x} = 1` for the middle term

`\left(e^{x}\right)^{2} - 2e^{x}e^{-x} + \left(e^{-x}\right)^{2} = 0`

$e^{2x} - 2 + e^{-2x} = 0$

**[M1]**

Multiply through by $e^{2x}$ to clear the negative power and form a quadratic

$e^{4x} - 2 e^{2x} + 1 = 0$

**[M1]**

Substitute $y = e^{2x}$ and factorise

$( y - 1 )^{2} = 0  \Rightarrow  e^{2x} = 1$

**[M1]**

Take natural logarithms, since $e^{2x} = 1$ gives $2 x = 0$

$x = 0$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A square equals zero only when the thing being squared is zero, so you can go straight from `\left(e^{x}-e^{-x}\right)^{2}=0` to $e^{x} - e^{-x} = 0$, then $e^{2x} = 1$ and $x = 0$, without expanding.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Either correct expansion of the square, using $e^{x} e^{-x} = 1$ to reach $e^{2x} - 2 + e^{-2x} = 0$, or recognising that a square is zero only when the bracket is zero, giving $e^{x} - e^{-x} = 0$.
> 
> **M1**: Reaching an equation in $e^{2x}$ alone: either the quadratic $e^{4x} - 2 e^{2x} + 1 = 0$ (or equivalent) from the expanded form, or $e^{2x} = 1$ from $e^{x} = e^{-x}$ by the shorter route.
> 
> **M1**: Taking logarithms of both sides to solve $e^{2x} = 1$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = 0$.

parts.problemMd: Solve the equation $2 e^{3x} - 11 e^{2x} + 12 e^{x} = 0$, giving answers to 3 significant figures where appropriate.
parts.solutionMd:
Every term has a factor of $e^{x}$, so factorise it out

`e^{x}\left(2e^{2x} - 11e^{x} + 12\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

Since $e^{x} > 0$ for all real $x$, the bracket must be zero; substitute $u = e^{x}$ and factorise

$2 u^{2} - 11 u + 12 = 0$

$( 2 u - 3 ) ( u - 4 ) = 0$

$e^{x} = \frac{3}{2}$* or *$e^{x} = 4$

**[M1]**

Both values are positive, so take natural logarithms of each

**Final answer:** $e^{x} = \frac{3}{2}  \Rightarrow  x = \text{ln}  \frac{3}{2}$** or **$e^{x} = 4  \Rightarrow  x = \text{ln}  4$

**[A1]**

Evaluate each to 3 significant figures

**Final answer:** $x = 0 . 405$** or **$x = 1 . 39$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct factorisation of $e^{x}$ (recognising $e^{x} = 0$ gives no solution).
> 
> **M1**: Correct formation and solution of the quadratic in $e^{x}$, reaching $e^{x} = \frac{3}{2}$ and $e^{x} = 4$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct exact values $x = \text{ln} \frac{3}{2}$ and $x = \text{ln} 4$.
> 
> **A1**: An answer which rounds to $x = 0 . 405$ (3 significant figures).
> 
> **A1**: An answer which rounds to $x = 1 . 39$ (3 significant figures).

parts.problemMd:
State whether the following functions could represent exponential growth or exponential decay.

(i) $\text{f} ( x ) = 5 e^{2x}$

(ii) $\text{f} ( t ) = 100 e^{-t}$

(iii) $\text{f} ( a ) = 20 e^{-ka} ,  k > 0$

(iv) $\text{f} ( t ) = A e^{kt} ,  A ,  k > 0$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The sign of the coefficient of the variable in the exponent decides the behaviour, and here it is $2$, which is positive

$\text{As}  x  \text{increases} ,  5 e^{2x}  \text{increases}$

**Final answer:** **Exponential growth**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The coefficient of $t$ in the exponent is $- 1$, which is negative

$\text{As}  t  \text{increases} ,  100 e^{-t}  \text{decreases}$

**Final answer:** **Exponential decay**

**[B1]**

(iii)

Here $k$ is positive, so the coefficient of $a$ in the exponent, $- k$, is negative

$\text{As}  a  \text{increases} ,  20 e^{-ka}  \text{decreases}$

**Final answer:** **Exponential decay**

**[B1]**

(iv)

Both $A$ and $k$ are positive, so the coefficient of $t$ in the exponent is positive

$\text{As}  t  \text{increases} ,  A e^{kt}  \text{increases}$

**Final answer:** **Exponential growth**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Exponential growth stated for part (i).
> 
> **B1**: Exponential decay stated for part (ii).
> 
> **B1**: Exponential decay stated for part (iii).
> 
> **B1**: Exponential growth stated for part (iv).
> 
> A reason is not required for any of these marks, but a correct classification contradicted by a stated reason does not score. Accept "growth" and "decay" without the word "exponential".

parts.problemMd:
Write the following in the form $e^{kx}$, where $k$ is a constant and $k > 0$.

(i) $e^{3x} \times e^{2x}$

(ii) $5^{x}$

(iii) $2^{x}$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Multiplying powers of the same base means adding the indices

$e^{3x} \times e^{2x} = e^{3x+2x}$

$e^{5x}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Since $\text{ln}$ and $e$ are inverse functions, any positive number $a$ can be written as $a = e^{\text{ln}a}$, so apply that to $5^{x}$

$5^{x} = e^{\text{ln}5^{x}}$

Bring the power down using the law $\text{ln}  a^{n} = n  \text{ln}  a$

$e^{(\text{ln}5)x}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

Use the same identity on $2^{x}$

$2^{x} = e^{\text{ln}2^{x}}$

Bring the power down as before

$e^{(\text{ln}2)x}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $e^{5x}$ for part (i).
> 
> **B1**: $e^{(\text{ln}5)x}$ for part (ii). Accept the equivalent decimal form, for example answers which round to $e^{1.61x}$, and accept $e^{x\text{ln}5}$.
> 
> **B1**: $e^{(\text{ln}2)x}$ for part (iii). Accept answers which round to $e^{0.693x}$, and accept $e^{x\text{ln}2}$.
> 
> Each mark is for the final form only, so no working is required.

parts.problemMd:
Write the following in the form $e^{-kx}$, where $k$ is a constant and $k > 0$.

(i) $\frac{e^{-2x}}{e^{4x}}$

(ii) `\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{x}`

(iii) `\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x}`
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Dividing powers of the same base means subtracting the indices

$\frac{e^{-2x}}{e^{4x}} = e^{-2x-4x}$

$e^{-6x}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Write the reciprocal as a negative index, so that the minus sign is already in place

`\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{x} = 5^{-x}`

Since $\text{ln}$ and $e$ are inverse functions, any positive number $a$ can be written as $a = e^{\text{ln}a}$

$5^{-x} = e^{\text{ln}5^{-x}}$

Bring the power down using the law $\text{ln}  a^{n} = n  \text{ln}  a$

$e^{-(\text{ln}5)x}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

Write the reciprocal as a negative index

`\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x} = 2^{-x}`

Apply the same identity, then bring the power down

$2^{-x} = e^{\text{ln}2^{-x}}$

$e^{-(\text{ln}2)x}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $e^{-6x}$ for part (i).
> 
> **B1**: $e^{-(\text{ln}5)x}$ for part (ii). Accept answers which round to $e^{-1.61x}$, and accept $e^{-x\text{ln}5}$.
> 
> **B1**: $e^{-(\text{ln}2)x}$ for part (iii). Accept answers which round to $e^{-0.693x}$, and accept $e^{-x\text{ln}2}$.
> 
> Each mark is for the final form only, so no working is required. An answer left as $e^{(\text{ln}0.2)x}$ or $e^{(\text{ln}0.5)x}$ is not in the requested form and does not score, because the question specifies $k > 0$.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows a sketch of the graph of $y = e^{-x}$.

On the diagram, add the graph of $y = e^{-2x}$, labelling the point at which the graph intersects the $y$-axis.

Write down the equation of any asymptotes on the graph.

![Sketch of the curve y = e^(-x) on a set of x and y axes, decreasing from the upper left and flattening towards the x-axis on the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/logarithms-and-exponentials/modelling-with-logarithms-and-exponentials/assets/003-sketch-of-the-curve-y-e-x-on-a-set-of-x-and-y-ax.png)
parts.solutionMd:
A change from $e^{-x}$ to $e^{-2x}$ multiplies the $x$ in the exponent by $2$, which is a horizontal stretch of scale factor $\frac{1}{2}$, so the new curve falls away twice as fast

![Two decreasing exponential curves on the same axes, both passing through the point (0, 1) which is labelled, with the steeper curve labelled y = e^(-2x) and the shallower one labelled y = e^(-x), and a dashed horizontal asymptote along y = 0](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/logarithms-and-exponentials/modelling-with-logarithms-and-exponentials/assets/004-two-decreasing-exponential-curves-on-the-same-ax.png)

**[B1]**

Both curves meet the $y$-axis at the same place, because setting $x = 0$ gives $e^{0} = 1$ in each case

$( 0 ,  1 )$

**[B1]**

As $x$ increases, $e^{-2x}$ approaches zero without ever reaching it, and the stretch does not move the horizontal asymptote

$y = 0$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A decreasing curve drawn through the first and second quadrants which is steeper than the given curve and approaches the $x$-axis from above. The two curves must be shown crossing on the $y$-axis.
> 
> **B1**: The intersection with the $y$-axis labelled $( 0 ,  1 )$. Accept the value $1$ marked on the $y$-axis.
> 
> **B1**: $y = 0$ stated as the asymptote. Accept a description such as "the $x$-axis", but the mark is not earned by a dashed line on the diagram alone, since the question asks for an equation.

parts.problemMd:
By taking logarithms (base $e$) of both sides show that the equation

$y = A e^{kx}$

can be written in the form $\text{ln}  y = k x + \text{ln}  A$
parts.solutionMd:
The equation is a product, and taking logarithms is what turns a product into a sum, so apply $\text{ln}$ to both sides

`\text{ln}\;y = \text{ln}\left(Ae^{kx}\right)`

**[B1]**

Split the right-hand side into two terms using the law $\text{log}_{a} x y = \text{log}_{a} x + \text{log}_{a} y$

$\text{ln}  y = \text{ln}  e^{kx} + \text{ln}  A$

**[B1]**

Since $\text{ln}$ and $e$ are inverse functions, $\text{ln}  e^{kx}$ is simply $k x$, which gives the required form

$\text{ln}  y = k x + \text{ln}  A$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Logarithms taken of both sides, giving `\text{ln}\;y = \text{ln}\left(Ae^{kx}\right)` or equivalent.
> 
> **B1**: The right-hand side split into two logarithm terms, giving $\text{ln}  y = \text{ln}  e^{kx} + \text{ln}  A$. Accept the terms in either order.
> 
> **B1**: $\text{ln}  e^{kx}$ simplified to $k x$ to reach the printed result. Because the answer is given, all three steps must be visible, and a bare statement of the final form scores nothing.

parts.problemMd:
The number of rare birds, $B$, in a newly constructed nature reserve at time $t$ years after their release is modelled by the equation

$B = A e^{0.4t}$

where $A$ is a constant. Initially, 24 birds are released into the reserve.

State the value of $A$.
parts.solutionMd:
At the moment of release $t = 0$, and since $e^{0} = 1$ the model gives $B = A$, so $A$ is the initial number of birds

$A = 24$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $A = 24$ stated. This may also be implied by correct use of $24$ in part (b).

parts.problemMd: Find the number of birds in the reserve when $t = 2$.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute $t = 2$ into the model, using the value of $A$ from part (a)

$B = 24 e^{0.4\times2} = 24 e^{0.8}$

**[M1]**

Evaluate, keeping the unrounded value before deciding on the final form

$B = 53 . 413 \dots$

The model counts individual birds, so give the answer as a whole number

$53  \text{birds}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substitution of $t = 2$ into the model, giving $24 e^{0.8}$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: $53$ birds. Accept the unrounded value rounded to 3 significant figures, $53 . 4$, and condone $54$.

parts.problemMd: Find the time taken for the number of birds in the reserve to double.
parts.solutionMd:
Doubling means the population reaches twice its initial value, which is $2 \times 24$

$48 = 24 e^{0.4t}$

Divide both sides by $24$ to isolate the exponential

$2 = e^{0.4t}$

Take natural logarithms of both sides, since the unknown is in the index

$\text{ln}  2 = 0 . 4 t$

**[M1]**

Divide by $0 . 4$ and evaluate

$t = \frac{\text{ln}2}{0.4} = 1 . 7328 \dots$

**Final answer:** $t = 1 . 73  \text{years}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Reduction to $e^{0.4t} = 2$ followed by taking logarithms of both sides. Starting from $48 = 24 e^{0.4t}$ or directly from $2 = e^{0.4t}$ are equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $1 . 73$. Accept the exact forms $\frac{\text{ln}2}{0.4}$ and $2 . 5  \text{ln}  2$, and accept the answer with or without units.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd: Find the acceleration of the rocket when $t = 15$.

parts.problemMd: Find the time taken for the acceleration to reach $100  \text{m s}^{-2}$.

> **M1**: The equation $a = 100$ formed and rearranged to $e^{0.1t} = 10$, or equivalent isolation of the exponential term.

> **A1**: The correct linear logarithmic equation, $0 . 1 t = \text{ln}  10$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: $23 . 0$. The exact form $10  \text{ln}  10$ is accepted and scores this mark in full. A bare $23$ is not accepted, since non-exact answers are required correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.problemMd:
An exponential growth model for the number of bacteria in an experiment is of the form $N = A e^{kt}$

$N$ is the number of bacteria and $t$ is the time in hours since the experiment began.

$A$ and $k$ are constants.

A scientist records the number of bacteria at hourly intervals over a four-hour period.

The results are shown in the table below.

| $t$, hours | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $N$, no. of bacteria | 100 | 210 | 320 | 730 | 1580 |
| $\text{ln}  N$ (3 s.f.) | 4.61 | 5.35 | 5.77 | 6.59 | 7.37 |

Plot the observations on the graph below, plotting $\text{ln}  N$ against $t$.

![Blank plotting grid with t on the horizontal axis from 0 to 5 and ln N on the vertical axis from 0 to 9, ruled in small squares of 0.2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/logarithms-and-exponentials/modelling-with-logarithms-and-exponentials/assets/001-blank-plotting-grid-with-t-on-the-horizontal-axi.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Each column of the table gives one point, with $t$ across and $\text{ln}  N$ up, so plot the five pairs $( 0 ,  4 . 61 )$, $( 1 ,  5 . 35 )$, $( 2 ,  5 . 77 )$, $( 3 ,  6 . 59 )$ and $( 4 ,  7 . 37 )$

![Grid with t from 0 to 5 horizontally and ln N from 0 to 9 vertically, showing five crosses rising steadily from just above 4.6 at t equals 0 to just under 7.4 at t equals 4, with a straight line drawn through the first and last crosses](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/logarithms-and-exponentials/modelling-with-logarithms-and-exponentials/assets/002-grid-with-t-from-0-to-5-horizontally-and-ln-n-fr.png)

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: All five points plotted correctly on the grid, to within half a small square.

parts.problemMd: Using the points $( 0 ,  4 . 61 )$ and $( 4 ,  7 . 37 )$, find an equation for a line of best fit in the form $\text{ln}  N = m t + \text{ln}  c$, where $m$ and $c$ are constants to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
The gradient of the line is the change in $\text{ln}  N$ divided by the change in $t$ between the two given points

$m = \frac{7.37-4.61}{4-0} = \frac{2.76}{4}$

$m = 0 . 69$

**[B1]**

Compare the required form with the equation of a straight line, $y = m x + c$, reading $\text{ln}  N$ in place of $y$ and $t$ in place of $x$

$\text{ln}  N = m t + \text{ln}  c$

The gradient just found is $m$, and one of the given points has $t = 0$, so its $\text{ln}  N$ value is the vertical intercept

$\text{ln}  N = 0 . 69 t + 4 . 61$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The gradient found as $\frac{7.37-4.61}{4-0}$, giving $0 . 69$.
> 
> **B1**: $\text{ln}  N = 0 . 69 t + 4 . 61$. Accept $c = 100$ stated separately alongside the equation.

parts.problemMd: Hence estimate the values of $A$ and $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
The model $N = A e^{kt}$ becomes $\text{ln}  N = k t + \text{ln}  A$ when logarithms are taken, so comparing with part (b) matches $k$ to the gradient

$k = 0 . 69$

**[B1]**

To recover $A$, raise $e$ to the power of each side of the equation in part (b)

$N = e^{0.69t+4.61} = e^{4.61} \times e^{0.69t}$

Comparing this with $N = A e^{kt}$ identifies the constant factor as $A$, so evaluate it

$A = e^{4.61} = 100 . 48 \dots$

$A = 100$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $k = 0 . 69$, obtained by comparing the gradient with the linear form of the model.
> 
> **B1**: $A = 100$. Accept any value in the range $100$ to $101$, since $e^{4.61} = 100 . 5$ and the question asks only for an estimate. Accept $A$ read directly from the table as the value of $N$ at $t = 0$.

parts.problemMd:
In an effort to prevent extinction, scientists released some rare birds into a newly constructed nature reserve.

The population of birds within the reserve is modelled by

$B = 16 e^{0.85t}$

where $B$ is the number of birds $t$ years after being released into the reserve.

State the number of birds the scientists released into the nature reserve.
parts.solutionMd:
The number released is the population at $t = 0$, and since $e^{0} = 1$ the model gives $B = 16$

$16  \text{birds}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $16$ stated. This may also be implied by correct use of $16$ in part (b).

parts.problemMd: According to this model, find the number of birds in the reserve after 3 years.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute $t = 3$ into the model

$B = 16 e^{0.85\times3} = 16 e^{2.55}$

**[M1]**

Evaluate, keeping the unrounded value before rounding

$B = 204 . 91 \dots$

The model counts individual birds, so give the answer as a whole number

$205  \text{birds}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substitution of $t = 3$ into the model, giving $16 e^{2.55}$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: $205$ birds. Accept $204 . 9$ and condone $204$.

parts.problemMd: Find the time taken for the population of birds within the reserve to reach 500.
parts.solutionMd:
Set the population equal to $500$ and divide by $16$ to isolate the exponential

$500 = 16 e^{0.85t}$

$e^{0.85t} = 31 . 25$

Take natural logarithms of both sides, since the unknown is in the index

$0 . 85 t = \text{ln}  31 . 25$

**[M1]**

Divide by $0 . 85$ and evaluate

$t = \frac{\text{ln}31.25}{0.85} = 4 . 0494 \dots$

**Final answer:** $t = 4 . 05  \text{years}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Reduction to $e^{0.85t} = 31 . 25$ followed by taking logarithms of both sides.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $4 . 05$. Accept the exact form $\frac{\text{ln}31.25}{0.85}$, and accept the answer with or without units.

parts.problemMd: Write `\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x}` in the form $e^{kx}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Since $\text{ln}$ and $e$ are inverse functions, any positive number $a$ can be written as $a = e^{\text{ln}a}$

`\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x} = e^{\text{ln}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{x}}`

Bring the power down using the law $\text{ln}  a^{n} = n  \text{ln}  a$, which puts it in the position of $k$

`= e^{\left(\text{ln}\frac{1}{3}\right)x}`

Evaluate the coefficient

**Final answer:** $e^{-1.10x}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $e^{-1.10x}$ for part (a). Accept the exact form `e^{\left(\text{ln}\frac{1}{3}\right)x}` and accept `e^{-\left(\text{ln}\;3\right)x}`. Answers which round to $- 1 . 10$ are accepted for the coefficient.

parts.problemMd:
Write `\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)^{t}` in the form $e^{kt}$.

State whether this would represent exponential growth or exponential decay.
parts.solutionMd:
Apply the same identity to `\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)^{t}`

`\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)^{t} = e^{\text{ln}\left(\frac{2}{7}\right)^{t}} = e^{\left(\text{ln}\frac{2}{7}\right)t}`

Evaluate the coefficient, which is the value of $k$

$k = \text{ln} \frac{2}{7} = - 1 . 2528 \dots$

**Final answer:** $e^{-1.25t}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

The base $\frac{2}{7}$ is less than $1$, so its logarithm is negative, and a negative coefficient of $t$ makes the function fall as $t$ increases

**Final answer:** **Exponential decay**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $e^{-1.25t}$ for part (b). Accept the exact form `e^{\left(\text{ln}\frac{2}{7}\right)t}`. Answers which round to $- 1 . 25$ are accepted.
> 
> **B1**: Exponential decay stated. A correct reason is not required, but the mark is not earned if the stated reason contradicts the answer.

parts.problemMd: Write `\left(\dfrac{7}{10}\right)^{x}` in the form $e^{-kx}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Since $\text{ln}$ and $e$ are inverse functions, write the base as a power of $e$ using $a = e^{\text{ln}a}$, then bring the power down

`\left(\dfrac{7}{10}\right)^{x} = e^{\left(\text{ln}\frac{7}{10}\right)x}`

Evaluate the coefficient, which is negative because $\frac{7}{10}$ is less than $1$

$\text{ln} \frac{7}{10} = - 0 . 35667 \dots$

**Final answer:** $e^{-0.357x}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $e^{-0.357x}$ for part (a). Accept the exact form `e^{\left(\text{ln}\frac{7}{10}\right)x}` and accept `e^{-\left(\text{ln}\frac{10}{7}\right)x}`. Answers which round to $0 . 357$ are accepted for $k$.

parts.problemMd:
Sketch the graph of `y = \left(\dfrac{7}{10}\right)^{x}`.

State the coordinates of the $y$-axis intercept.

Write down the equation of the asymptote.
parts.solutionMd:
Part (a) shows the coefficient of $x$ is negative, so this is exponential decay and the curve falls from left to right, approaching the $x$-axis

![A single decreasing exponential curve on x and y axes, starting high on the left, crossing the y-axis at the labelled point (0, 1), and flattening towards a dashed horizontal asymptote along y = 0 on the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/logarithms-and-exponentials/modelling-with-logarithms-and-exponentials/assets/020-a-single-decreasing-exponential-curve-on-x-and-y.png)

**[B1]**

Substituting $x = 0$ gives `\left(\tfrac{7}{10}\right)^{0} = 1`, which locates the intercept

$( 0 ,  1 )$

As $x$ increases the curve approaches zero without ever reaching it

$y = 0$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A decreasing curve drawn in the first and second quadrants, approaching the $x$-axis from above as $x$ increases and rising steeply as $x$ decreases. The curve must not cross or touch the $x$-axis.
> 
> **B1**: Both $( 0 ,  1 )$ and $y = 0$ given. Accept the intercept written as $y = 1$ and accept the asymptote described as "the $x$-axis". Both are needed for this mark.

parts.problemMd:
By taking logarithms (base $e$) of both sides show that the equation

$y = 5 e^{0.1x}$

can be written as

$\text{ln}  y = 0 . 1 x + \text{ln}  5$
parts.solutionMd:
Taking logarithms turns the product on the right into a sum, so apply $\text{ln}$ to both sides

`\text{ln}\;y = \text{ln}\left(5e^{0.1x}\right)`

Split the right-hand side using the law $\text{log}_{a} x y = \text{log}_{a} x + \text{log}_{a} y$

$\text{ln}  y = \text{ln}  e^{0.1x} + \text{ln}  5$

Since $\text{ln}$ and $e$ are inverse functions, $\text{ln}  e^{0.1x}$ simplifies to $0 . 1 x$, giving the required form

$\text{ln}  y = 0 . 1 x + \text{ln}  5$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The full derivation in part (a), showing logarithms taken of both sides, the right-hand side split into two terms, and $\text{ln}  e^{0.1x}$ simplified to $0 . 1 x$. Because the answer is given, the working must be visible and a bare restatement of the result scores nothing.

parts.problemMd: Given $y = A e^{kx}$ and $\text{ln}  y = 4 . 1 x + \text{ln}  8$, find the values of $A$ and $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
Part (a) shows that $y = A e^{kx}$ always rearranges to the general form

$\text{ln}  y = k x + \text{ln}  A$

Set that alongside the equation given in the question

$\text{ln}  y = 4 . 1 x + \text{ln}  8$

The coefficient of $x$ matches $k$

$k = 4 . 1$

**[B1]**

The constant term matches $\text{ln}  A$

$A = 8$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $k = 4 . 1$.
> 
> **B1**: $A = 8$. An answer of $A = \text{ln}  8$ does not score, since the constant term in the linear form is $\text{ln}  A$, not $A$ itself.

parts.problemMd:
By taking logarithms (base 10) of both sides show that the equation

$y = 2 x^{3.2}$

can be written as

$\text{log}  y = 3 . 2  \text{log}  x + \text{log}  2$
parts.solutionMd:
Taking logarithms turns the product on the right into a sum, so apply $\text{log}$ to both sides

`\text{log}\;y = \text{log}\left(2x^{3.2}\right)`

Split the right-hand side using the law $\text{log}_{a} x y = \text{log}_{a} x + \text{log}_{a} y$

$\text{log}  y = \text{log}  x^{3.2} + \text{log}  2$

Bring the power down using the law $\text{log}_{a} x^{n} = n  \text{log}_{a} x$, which gives the required form

$\text{log}  y = 3 . 2  \text{log}  x + \text{log}  2$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The full derivation in part (a), showing logarithms taken of both sides, the right-hand side split into two terms, and the power brought down to give $3 . 2  \text{log}  x$. Because the answer is given, the working must be visible.

parts.problemMd: Given $y = A x^{b}$ and $\text{log}  y = 1 . 8  \text{log}  x + \text{log}  5$, find the values of $A$ and $b$.
parts.solutionMd:
Part (a) shows that $y = A x^{b}$ always rearranges to the general form

$\text{log}  y = b  \text{log}  x + \text{log}  A$

Set that alongside the equation given in the question

$\text{log}  y = 1 . 8  \text{log}  x + \text{log}  5$

The coefficient of $\text{log}  x$ matches $b$

$b = 1 . 8$

**[B1]**

The constant term matches $\text{log}  A$

$A = 5$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $b = 1 . 8$.
> 
> **B1**: $A = 5$. An answer of $A = \text{log}  5$ does not score, since the constant term in the linear form is $\text{log}  A$, not $A$ itself.

parts.problemMd:
By taking logarithms (base 2) of both sides show that the equation

$y = 3 \times 2^{4x}$

can be written as

$\text{log}_{2}  y = 4 x + \text{log}_{2}  3$
parts.solutionMd:
Taking logarithms turns the product on the right into a sum, so apply $\text{log}_{2}$ to both sides

`\text{log}_{2}\;y = \text{log}_{2}\left(3 \times 2^{4x}\right)`

Split the right-hand side using the law $\text{log}_{a} x y = \text{log}_{a} x + \text{log}_{a} y$

$\text{log}_{2}  y = \text{log}_{2}  2^{4x} + \text{log}_{2}  3$

Working in base 2 makes $\text{log}_{2}  2^{4x}$ simplify to $4 x$, which gives the required form

$\text{log}_{2}  y = 4 x + \text{log}_{2}  3$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The full derivation in part (a), showing logarithms taken of both sides, the right-hand side split into two terms, and $\text{log}_{2}  2^{4x}$ simplified to $4 x$. Because the answer is given, the working must be visible.

parts.problemMd: Given $y = A b^{kx}$ and $\text{log}_{3}  y = 5 x + \text{log}_{3}  7$, find the values of $A$, $b$ and $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
Apply the same process to $y = A b^{kx}$, this time in base 3 to match the equation given

$\text{log}_{3}  y = \text{log}_{3}  A + \text{log}_{3}  b^{kx}$

Bring the power down using the law $\text{log}_{a} x^{n} = n  \text{log}_{a} x$

$\text{log}_{3}  y = \text{log}_{3}  A + k x  \text{log}_{3}  b$

Compare the constant terms with $\text{log}_{3}  y = 5 x + \text{log}_{3}  7$

$A = 7$

**[B1]**

Comparing the terms in $x$ gives $k  \text{log}_{3}  b = 5$. The question is written in base 3, and it is the base $b$ that carries the power of $x$, so take $b = 3$

$b = 3  \text{, so}  \text{log}_{3}  b = \text{log}_{3}  3 = 1$

That leaves $k \times 1 = 5$

$b = 3 ,  k = 5$

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The choice of logarithm base in a question like part (b) is a hint. The equation is written in base 3 precisely so that $\text{log}_{3}  b$ collapses to $1$ when $b = 3$, leaving $k$ visible immediately.
> 
> If you find yourself with two unknowns tangled in a single product such as $k  \text{log}_{3}  b = 5$, look at the base you have been handed before assuming the question is short of information.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $A = 7$.
> 
> **B1**: Both $b = 3$ and $k = 5$. Both values are needed for this mark.

parts.problemMd:
A simple model for the acceleration of a rocket, $A  \text{m s}^{-2}$, is given as

$A = A_{0} e^{0.2t}$

where $t$ is the time in seconds after lift-off and $A_{0}$ is a constant.

State what the constant $A_{0}$ represents.
parts.solutionMd:
At lift-off $t = 0$, and since $e^{0} = 1$ the model reduces to $A = A_{0}$

**Final answer:** $A_{0}$** is the acceleration of the rocket at lift-off**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A statement that $A_{0}$ is the initial acceleration, or the acceleration at lift-off, or the acceleration when $t = 0$. Any of these is sufficient.

parts.problemMd: After 10 seconds, the acceleration is $20  \text{m s}^{-2}$. Find the value of $A_{0}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute the given reading, $A = 20$ when $t = 10$, into the model

$20 = A_{0} e^{0.2\times10} = A_{0} e^{2}$

**[M1]**

Divide by $e^{2}$ to make $A_{0}$ the subject, then evaluate

$A_{0} = \frac{20}{e^{2}} = 2 . 7067 \dots$

**Final answer:** $A_{0} = 2 . 71  \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substitution of $A = 20$ and $t = 10$ into the model, giving $20 = A_{0} e^{2}$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $2 . 71$. Accept the exact form $\frac{20}{e^{2}}$ or $20 e^{-2}$.

parts.problemMd: Find the time taken for the acceleration of the rocket to reach $100  \text{m s}^{-2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Set the acceleration equal to $100$, using the exact value of $A_{0}$ from part (b) so that no rounding is carried forward

$100 = 20 e^{-2} \times e^{0.2t}$

Combine the powers of $e$ and divide by $20$

$e^{0.2t-2} = 5$

Take natural logarithms of both sides

$0 . 2 t - 2 = \text{ln}  5$

**[M1]**

Add $2$ to both sides and divide by $0 . 2$

$t = \frac{2+\text{ln}5}{0.2} = 18 . 047 \dots$

**Final answer:** $t = 18 . 0  \text{s}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The equation $A = 100$ formed using their value of $A_{0}$, rearranged to isolate the exponential, and logarithms taken of both sides.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $18 . 0$. This mark is available whether the exact or the rounded value of $A_{0}$ is carried forward, since both give $18 . 0$ to 3 significant figures. A bare $18$ is not accepted, since non-exact answers are required correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.problemMd:
Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope of the element carbon. Carbon-14 decays exponentially, losing mass as it decays, and is used in carbon dating to estimate the age of objects.

The time it takes the mass of carbon-14 to halve, called its half-life, is approximately 5700 years.

A model for the mass of carbon-14, $m$ g, in an object of age $t$ years is

$m = m_{0} e^{-kt}$

where $m_{0}$ and $k$ are constants.

For an object initially containing 100 g of carbon-14, state the value of $m_{0}$.
parts.solutionMd:
The constant $m_{0}$ is the mass when $t = 0$, since $e^{0} = 1$, and the object initially contains 100 g

$m_{0} = 100$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $m_{0} = 100$.

parts.problemMd: Explain briefly why, if $m_{0} = 100$, then $m$ will equal 50 g when $t = 5700$ years.
parts.solutionMd:
The half-life is defined as the time taken for the mass of carbon-14 to halve

**Final answer:** **Half of the initial 100 g is 50 g**

**[B1]**

The half-life is given as 5700 years, so this halving is reached exactly when $t = 5700$

**Final answer:** **So **$m = 50$** when **$t = 5700$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A statement that half of 100 g is 50 g.
> 
> **B1**: A statement linking the halving to the half-life of 5700 years. Both marks in part (b) are for the explanation, and no calculation is expected.

parts.problemMd: Using the values from part (b), show that the value of $k$ is $1 . 22 \times 10^{-4}$, correct to three significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute the pair of values from part (b) into the model

$50 = 100 e^{-5700k}$

Divide both sides by 100 to isolate the exponential

$\frac{1}{2} = e^{-5700k}$

**[M1]**

Take natural logarithms of both sides, using $\text{ln}  e^{X} = X$

$\text{ln} \frac{1}{2} = - 5700 k$

Divide by $- 5700$ and evaluate, keeping the unrounded value

$k = \frac{-\text{ln}\frac{1}{2}}{5700} = \frac{\text{ln}2}{5700} = 1 . 21605 \dots \times 10^{-4}$

**Final answer:** $k = 1 . 22 \times 10^{-4}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Notice that the 100 g in part (c) cancels at the very first step, leaving $\frac{1}{2} = e^{-5700k}$. That is why a half-life never depends on how much material you started with, and it means you can write down $k = \frac{\text{ln}2}{\text{half-life}}$ directly for any decay question of this type.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substitution of $m = 50$, $m_{0} = 100$ and $t = 5700$ into the model, reduced to $e^{-5700k} = \frac{1}{2}$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Logarithms taken and $k$ obtained as $1 . 22 \times 10^{-4}$. Because the answer is given, the working must be visible. Accept the exact forms $\frac{\text{ln}2}{5700}$ and $\frac{-\text{ln}\frac{1}{2}}{5700}$.

parts.problemMd: A different object currently contains 60 g of carbon-14. Find the mass of carbon-14 that will remain in the object in 2000 years' time.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute the new starting mass and $t = 2000$ into the model, using the unrounded value of $k$

$m = 60 e^{-1.21605\dots\times10^{-4}\times2000}$

Evaluate the index, then the whole expression

$m = 60 e^{-0.24321\dots} = 47 . 046 \dots$

**Final answer:** $m = 47 . 0  \text{g}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substitution of $m_{0} = 60$ and $t = 2000$ into the model using their value of $k$.
>

parts.problemMd:
An exponential growth model for the number of bacteria in an experiment is of the form $N = N_{0} a^{kt}$

$N$ is the number of bacteria and $t$ is the time in hours since the experiment began. $N_{0}$, $a$ and $k$ are constants.

A scientist records the number of bacteria at various points over a six-hour period. The results are shown in the table below.

| $t$, hours | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $N$, no. of bacteria | 100 | 180 | 340 | 620 |
| $\text{log}_{3}  N$ (3 s.f.) | 4.19 | 4.73 | 5.31 | 5.85 |

Plot the observations on the graph below, plotting $\text{log}_{3}  N$ against $t$.

parts.solutionMd:
Each column of the table gives one point, with $t$ across and $\text{log}_{3}  N$ up, so plot the four pairs $( 0 ,  4 . 19 )$, $( 2 ,  4 . 73 )$, $( 4 ,  5 . 31 )$ and $( 6 ,  5 . 85 )$

![Plotting grid with t from 0 to 8 horizontally and log base 3 of N from 0 to 7 vertically, showing four crosses rising steadily from just under 4.2 at t equals 0 to just under 5.9 at t equals 6, with a straight line drawn through them](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/logarithms-and-exponentials/modelling-with-logarithms-and-exponentials/assets/018-plotting-grid-with-t-from-0-to-8-horizontally-an.png)

**[B1]**
