> **M1**: The numerator combined over the common denominator $1 - \text{tan}^{2}  A$ and simplified to $3  \text{tan}  A - \text{tan}^{3}  A$ over that denominator.
> 
> **A1**: The denominator likewise simplified to $1 - 3  \text{tan}^{2}  A$ over $1 - \text{tan}^{2}  A$.
> 
> **A1**: The two fractions divided and the common factor cancelled, giving the correct expression. Multiplying the numerator and denominator of the original nested fraction through by $1 - \text{tan}^{2}  A$ in one step is an equally valid route and earns the same marks.

parts.problemMd:
Hence, or otherwise, solve the equation

$\frac{6\text{tan}x-2\text{tan}^{3}x}{1-3\text{tan}^{2}x} = 2$

for $0 \leq x \leq π$.
parts.solutionMd:
The numerator is twice the numerator in part (a), so the whole left hand side is $2  \text{tan}  3 x$

$2  \text{tan}  3 x = 2   \Rightarrow   \text{tan}  3 x = 1$

**[M1]**

Let $φ = 3 x$, and multiply each part of the interval by $3$ to find the interval for $φ$

$0 \leq φ \leq 3 π$

Take the inverse tangent to find the principal value

$φ = \text{tan}^{-1} ( 1 ) = \frac{π}{4}$

The tangent has period $π$, so add $π$ repeatedly while the values stay in the interval

$φ = \frac{π}{4} + π = \frac{5π}{4}$* and *$φ = \frac{π}{4} + 2 π = \frac{9π}{4}$

**[A1]**

Divide each value by $3$ to return to $x$

$x = \frac{π}{12} ,  \frac{5π}{12} ,  \frac{3π}{4}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The left hand side recognised as $2  \text{tan}  3 x$ using part (a), giving $\text{tan}  3 x = 1$, with the interval for $3 x$ correctly changed to $0 \leq 3 x \leq 3 π$.
> 
> **A1**: At least two correct values of $x$.
> 
> **A1**: All three correct values of $x$, and no others in the interval. The tangent has period $π$, not $2 π$, so a candidate who adds $2 π$ only finds two of the three values and does not earn this mark. Answers must be exact and in terms of $π$; decimals do not earn the accuracy marks, and answers given correctly in degrees are treated as a misread.

parts.problemMd:
Sketch the graph of `y = 2\left(\text{sin} \; x - \text{cos} \; x\right)` for $0 ^{\circ} \leq x \leq 360 ^{\circ}$.

Label any points where the graph intercepts the coordinate axes, and state the coordinates of any maximum and minimum points.
parts.solutionMd:
A sum of a sine and a cosine of the same angle can be modelled as a single sine curve, so expand $R  \text{sin} ( x - α )$ with the compound angle formula $\text{sin} ( A - B ) \equiv \text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  B - \text{cos}  A  \text{sin}  B$, then set it equal to the given function

$2  \text{sin}  x - 2  \text{cos}  x \equiv R  \text{cos}  α  \text{sin}  x - R  \text{sin}  α  \text{cos}  x$

Compare the coefficients of $\text{sin}  x$ and of $\text{cos}  x$ on each side

$R  \text{cos}  α = 2$* and *$R  \text{sin}  α = 2$

**[M1]**

Square and add the two equations, so that $\text{cos}^{2}  α + \text{sin}^{2}  α \equiv 1$ removes $α$

$R^{2} = 2^{2} + 2^{2} = 8   \Rightarrow   R = 2 \sqrt{2}$

**[A1]**

Divide one equation by the other to find $α$

$\text{tan}  α = \frac{2}{2} = 1   \Rightarrow   α = 45 ^{\circ}$

`y = 2\sqrt{2} \; \text{sin}\left(x - 45^{\circ}\right)`

**[A1]**

This is the sine curve stretched to an amplitude of $2 \sqrt{2}$ and translated $45 ^{\circ}$ to the right. It meets the horizontal axis where the sine is zero

$x = 45 ^{\circ}$* and *$x = 225 ^{\circ}$

Substitute $x = 0 ^{\circ}$ and $x = 360 ^{\circ}$ for the two ends of the curve

`y = 2\sqrt{2} \; \text{sin}\left(-45^{\circ}\right) = -2`* and *`y = 2\sqrt{2} \; \text{sin}\left(315^{\circ}\right) = -2`

The maximum and minimum occur where the sine reaches $1$ and $- 1$, a quarter and three quarters of the way through the cycle

$x - 45 ^{\circ} = 90 ^{\circ}   \Rightarrow   x = 135 ^{\circ}$* and *$x - 45 ^{\circ} = 270 ^{\circ}   \Rightarrow   x = 315 ^{\circ}$

Draw one complete cycle with all six points marked

![Graph of y = 2(sin x minus cos x) from x = 0 degrees to x = 360 degrees, a sine shaped curve of amplitude 2 root 2 starting and ending below the horizontal axis, with two labelled crossings of that axis and labelled maximum and minimum points](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/trigonometry/compound-and-double-angle-formulae/assets/003-graph-of-y-2-sin-x-minus-cos-x-from-x-0-degrees-.png)

**[B1 B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The function written in harmonic form and the coefficients compared, giving $R  \text{cos}  α = 2$ and $R  \text{sin}  α = 2$.
> 
> **A1**: $R = 2 \sqrt{2}$. Accept $\sqrt{8}$ provided it is simplified.
> 
> **A1**: $α = 45 ^{\circ}$ and the harmonic form stated. The equivalent form `y = -2\sqrt{2} \; \text{cos}\left(x + 45^{\circ}\right)` is equally acceptable and leads to the same graph.
> 
> **B1**: The correct shape, a single cycle of amplitude $2 \sqrt{2}$ shifted to the right, starting and finishing below the horizontal axis. No part of the curve may go beyond $2 \sqrt{2}$ or $- 2 \sqrt{2}$.
> 
> **B1**: The two crossings of the horizontal axis correctly shown, at $45 ^{\circ}$ and $225 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **B1**: The two ends of the curve correctly shown, at $( 0 ^{\circ} ,  - 2 )$ and $( 360 ^{\circ} ,  - 2 )$. Numbers marked on the axis are accepted in place of full coordinate pairs.
> 
> **B1**: The maximum at `\left(135^{\circ}, \; 2\sqrt{2}\right)` and the minimum at `\left(315^{\circ}, \; -2\sqrt{2}\right)`. Accept $2 . 83$ and $- 2 . 83$ for the exact surds, since the question does not ask for exact values.

parts.problemMd:
Show that

$2 - 2  \text{cot}  2 A  \text{tan}  A \equiv \text{sec}^{2}  A$

for $A \neq \frac{kπ}{2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Start from the left hand side. Use the definition $\text{cot}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{tan}θ}$, then replace $\text{tan}  2 A$ by the double angle formula $\text{tan}  2 A \equiv \frac{2\text{tan}A}{1-\text{tan}^{2}A}$

$2 - 2  \text{cot}  2 A  \text{tan}  A \equiv 2 - 2 \times \frac{1-\text{tan}^{2}A}{2\text{tan}A} \times \text{tan}  A$

**[M1]**

The restriction keeps $\text{tan}  A$ defined and non-zero, so the two factors of $2$ cancel and so does $\text{tan}  A$

`\equiv 2 - \left(1 - \text{tan}^2 \; A\right) \equiv 1 + \text{tan}^2 \; A`

**[M1]**

Finish with the identity $1 + \text{tan}^{2}  A \equiv \text{sec}^{2}  A$

**Final answer:** $2 - 2  \text{cot}  2 A  \text{tan}  A \equiv \text{sec}^{2}  A$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $\text{cot}  2 A$ written as $\frac{1}{\text{tan}2A}$, with the double angle formula for $\text{tan}  2 A$ substituted so that the expression is in $\text{tan}  A$ only. Converting the whole left hand side to sines and cosines instead is an equally valid route and earns this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Both cancellations carried out and the bracket expanded, reaching $1 + \text{tan}^{2}  A$.
> 
> **A1**: The identity $1 + \text{tan}^{2}  A \equiv \text{sec}^{2}  A$ used to reach the printed result. Stating the identity is sufficient. Because the result is given, every line must be correct and the $A$ must be present throughout; abbreviations such as $t$ or $s$ in place of the function names are accepted only if they are defined first. Working from the right hand side back to the left is equally valid.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Show that $\text{sin} ( A - B ) = \text{sin}  A + \text{sin}  B$ does not hold for all values of $A$ and $B$.

(ii) Find values for $A$ and $B$, with $A \neq 0$ and $B \neq 0$, for which the statement does hold.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

One counter-example is enough, so choose two angles whose sines are exact. Take $A = \frac{π}{2}$ and $B = \frac{π}{4}$, and evaluate the left hand side

`\text{sin}(A - B) = \text{sin}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \text{sin} \; \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}`

**[M1]**

Now evaluate the right hand side for the same two angles

$\text{sin}  A + \text{sin}  B = \text{sin}  \frac{π}{2} + \text{sin}  \frac{π}{4} = 1 + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$

The two sides disagree for this choice, so the statement cannot hold for every pair of angles

$\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \neq 1 + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$

**Final answer:** **so **$\text{sin} ( A - B ) = \text{sin}  A + \text{sin}  B$** does not hold for all values of **$A$** and **$B$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Expanding the left hand side gives $\text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  B - \text{cos}  A  \text{sin}  B$, which matches the right hand side when $\text{cos}  A = - 1$, since that makes $\text{sin}  A = 0$ as well. Take $A = π$, with $B = \frac{π}{3}$

`\text{sin}(A - B) = \text{sin}\left(\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \text{sin} \; \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}`

$\text{sin}  A + \text{sin}  B = \text{sin}  π + \text{sin}  \frac{π}{3} = 0 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

Both sides take the same value, so the statement holds for this pair

**Final answer:** $A = π$** and **$B = \frac{π}{3}$

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Sub-part (ii) looks like trial and error, but it is not. Expand the left hand side and compare: $\text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  B - \text{cos}  A  \text{sin}  B$ equals $\text{sin}  A + \text{sin}  B$ whenever $\text{cos}  A = - 1$, because that also forces $\text{sin}  A$ to be zero. So any odd multiple of $π$ for $A$ works with absolutely any $B$ you like. The same argument with $\text{cos}  B = 1$ gives a second family, $B$ any even multiple of $π$, with any $A$.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A pair of values chosen and at least one side evaluated correctly for them. Any counter-example works, so $A = 90 ^{\circ}$ and $B = 30 ^{\circ}$, or any other pair giving different values, earns this mark equally.
> 
> **A1**: Both sides evaluated correctly for the chosen values, shown to be different, with a conclusion that the statement does not hold in general. Simply asserting that the two are unequal, without the numbers, does not earn this mark.
> 
> **B1**: Any pair with $A \neq 0$ and $B \neq 0$ for which the two sides agree, with both sides evaluated to show that they do. Accept any $A$ that is an odd multiple of $π$ paired with any non-zero $B$, or any non-zero $A$ paired with a $B$ that is a non-zero even multiple of $π$. A pair stated without the check does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Use the identities

$\text{sin} ( A \pm B ) \equiv \text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  B \pm \text{cos}  A  \text{sin}  B$

$\text{cos} ( A + B ) \equiv \text{cos}  A  \text{cos}  B - \text{sin}  A  \text{sin}  B$

$\text{cos} ( A - B ) \equiv \text{cos}  A  \text{cos}  B + \text{sin}  A  \text{sin}  B$

to show that

$\text{sin} ( X + Y - Z ) \equiv \text{sin}  X  \text{cos}  Y  \text{cos}  Z + \text{cos}  X  \text{sin}  Y  \text{cos}  Z - \text{cos}  X  \text{cos}  Y  \text{sin}  Z + \text{sin}  X  \text{sin}  Y  \text{sin}  Z$
parts.solutionMd:
The identities take two angles at a time, so group the three into two by treating $X + Y$ as a single angle

`\text{sin}(X + Y - Z) \equiv \text{sin}\left(\left(X + Y\right) - Z\right) \equiv \text{sin}(X + Y) \; \text{cos} \; Z - \text{cos}(X + Y) \; \text{sin} \; Z`

**[M1]**

Now expand $\text{sin} ( X + Y )$ and $\text{cos} ( X + Y )$, each with two angles again

`\equiv \left(\text{sin} \; X \; \text{cos} \; Y + \text{cos} \; X \; \text{sin} \; Y\right)\text{cos} \; Z - \left(\text{cos} \; X \; \text{cos} \; Y - \text{sin} \; X \; \text{sin} \; Y\right)\text{sin} \; Z`

**[M1]**

Multiply out both brackets, taking care with the minus sign in front of the second

**Final answer:** $\text{sin} ( X + Y - Z ) \equiv \text{sin}  X  \text{cos}  Y  \text{cos}  Z + \text{cos}  X  \text{sin}  Y  \text{cos}  Z - \text{cos}  X  \text{cos}  Y  \text{sin}  Z + \text{sin}  X  \text{sin}  Y  \text{sin}  Z$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The three angles grouped into two, with the identity for $\text{sin} ( A - B )$ applied to `\left(X + Y\right) - Z`. Grouping as `X + \left(Y - Z\right)` instead is equally valid and reaches the same four terms.
> 
> **M1**: Both $\text{sin} ( X + Y )$ and $\text{cos} ( X + Y )$ correctly expanded.
> 
> **A1**: Both brackets multiplied out to reach the printed identity, with all four signs correct. The minus sign in front of the second bracket changes both of its signs, so a candidate who expands it as $- \text{cos}  X  \text{cos}  Y  \text{sin}  Z - \text{sin}  X  \text{sin}  Y  \text{sin}  Z$ does not earn this mark. Because the result is given, every line must be correct.

parts.problemMd: Hence show that $\text{sin}  165 ^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}$.
parts.solutionMd:
The angle $165 ^{\circ}$ is not a sum or difference of two standard angles, but it is a combination of three. Choose $X = 180 ^{\circ}$, $Y = 30 ^{\circ}$ and $Z = 45 ^{\circ}$

$X + Y - Z = 180 ^{\circ} + 30 ^{\circ} - 45 ^{\circ} = 165 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Substitute these into part (a)

$\text{sin}  165 ^{\circ} = \text{sin}  180 ^{\circ}  \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ}  \text{cos}  45 ^{\circ} + \text{cos}  180 ^{\circ}  \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ}  \text{cos}  45 ^{\circ} - \text{cos}  180 ^{\circ}  \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ}  \text{sin}  45 ^{\circ} + \text{sin}  180 ^{\circ}  \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ}  \text{sin}  45 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Replace each factor by its exact value, using $\text{sin}  180 ^{\circ} = 0$ and $\text{cos}  180 ^{\circ} = - 1$

`= 0 + (-1)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) - (-1)\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) + 0`

Every term containing $\text{sin}  180 ^{\circ}$ vanishes, leaving two products

$= - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} + \frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}$

**[A1]**

Write the two terms in the order of the printed answer and combine them

**Final answer:** $\text{sin}  165 ^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A valid choice of $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ with $X + Y - Z = 165 ^{\circ}$, using angles whose sines and cosines are exact. Accept any such set, for example $X = 90 ^{\circ}$, $Y = 120 ^{\circ}$, $Z = 45 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **M1**: The chosen values substituted into the identity from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: The exact values put in and the expression reduced to two non-zero terms, giving $\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4} - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}$ or equivalent. The two terms containing $\text{sin}  180 ^{\circ}$ must be seen to vanish rather than simply be dropped.
> 
> **A1**: The printed result reached from correct working. Because the answer is given, every line must be correct. Reading $\text{sin}  165 ^{\circ}$ from a calculator does not earn any of the four marks, since the question says to use part (a).

parts.problemMd:
Show that

$\text{tan}  2 A \equiv \frac{2\text{tan}A}{1-\text{tan}^{2}A}$

State clearly any trigonometric identities you use to show this result.
parts.solutionMd:
The target is a tangent, so start from the identity $\text{tan}  θ \equiv \frac{\text{sin}θ}{\text{cos}θ}$, applied to the angle $2 A$

$\text{tan}  2 A \equiv \frac{\text{sin}2A}{\text{cos}2A}$

**[M1]**

Replace the top with $\text{sin}  2 A \equiv 2  \text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  A$ and the bottom with $\text{cos}  2 A \equiv \text{cos}^{2}  A - \text{sin}^{2}  A$

$\equiv \frac{2\text{sin}A\text{cos}A}{\text{cos}^{2}A-\text{sin}^{2}A}$

**[M1]**

The answer is in tangents, so divide every term in the numerator and the denominator by $\text{cos}^{2}  A$

$\equiv \frac{\frac{2\text{sin}A}{\text{cos}A}}{1-\frac{\text{sin}^{2}A}{\text{cos}^{2}A}}$

**[M1]**

Use $\text{tan}  A \equiv \frac{\text{sin}A}{\text{cos}A}$ once more, in both the numerator and the denominator

**Final answer:** $\text{tan}  2 A \equiv \frac{2\text{tan}A}{1-\text{tan}^{2}A}$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $\text{tan}  2 A$ written as $\frac{\text{sin}2A}{\text{cos}2A}$, with the identity named.
> 
> **M1**: Both double angle formulae substituted and named, $\text{sin}  2 A \equiv 2  \text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  A$ and a correct form of $\text{cos}  2 A$. The form $\text{cos}^{2}  A - \text{sin}^{2}  A$ is the one that works here; the other two forms do not lead anywhere useful.
> 
> **M1**: Numerator and denominator both divided by $\text{cos}^{2}  A$.
> 
> **A1**: The identity $\text{tan}  A \equiv \frac{\text{sin}A}{\text{cos}A}$ used to finish, reaching the printed result. Because the question asks for the identities to be stated, each one must be visible somewhere in the working. Quoting $\text{tan}  2 A$ straight from the formula booklet earns nothing, since the question asks you to show where it comes from. An alternative route through $\text{tan} ( A + A )$ and the compound angle formula for the tangent is equally valid and earns the same marks.

parts.problemMd:
Given that $a  \text{sin}  θ + b  \text{cos}  θ$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants, is to be written in the form $R  \text{sin} ( θ + α )$, find expressions for:

(i) $α$ in terms of $a$ and $b$

(ii) $R$ in terms of $a$ and $b$
parts.solutionMd:
Expand the required form with the compound angle formula $\text{sin} ( A + B ) \equiv \text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  B + \text{cos}  A  \text{sin}  B$, then set it equal to the given expression

$a  \text{sin}  θ + b  \text{cos}  θ \equiv R  \text{cos}  α  \text{sin}  θ + R  \text{sin}  α  \text{cos}  θ$

Compare the coefficients of $\text{sin}  θ$ and of $\text{cos}  θ$ on each side

$R  \text{cos}  α = a$* and *$R  \text{sin}  α = b$

**[M1]**

(i)

Divide the second equation by the first, so that $R$ cancels and $\frac{\text{sin}α}{\text{cos}α} = \text{tan}  α$

$\text{tan}  α = \frac{b}{a}$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse tangent

`\alpha = \text{tan}^{-1}\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)`

**[A1]**

(ii)

Square and add the two equations, so that $\text{cos}^{2}  α + \text{sin}^{2}  α \equiv 1$ removes $α$

`\left(R \; \text{cos} \; \alpha\right)^2 + \left(R \; \text{sin} \; \alpha\right)^2 = R^2\left(\text{cos}^2 \; \alpha + \text{sin}^2 \; \alpha\right) = R^2 = a^2 + b^2`

**[M1]**

Taking the square root leaves a choice of sign

$R = \pm \sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$

**[A1]**

Decide the sign. Since $a$ and $b$ are positive, $\text{tan}  α = \frac{b}{a}$ is positive, so $α$ is acute and $\text{cos}  α$ is positive. Then $R = \frac{a}{\text{cos}α}$ is a positive number divided by a positive number

$R = \sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The compound angle formula applied to $R  \text{sin} ( θ + α )$ and the coefficients compared, giving $R  \text{cos}  α = a$ and $R  \text{sin}  α = b$.
> 
> **M1**: The two equations divided to give $\text{tan}  α = \frac{b}{a}$.
> 
> **A1**: `\alpha = \text{tan}^{-1}\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)`. Accept `\text{arctan}\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)` as an equivalent notation.
> 
> **M1**: The two equations squared and added, with the Pythagorean identity used to reach $R^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: $R = \pm \sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$, or $R = \sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ if the choice of sign is dealt with at the same time.
> 
> **A1**: A correct reason for taking the positive root. Any valid argument earns this, for example that $a$ and $b$ are positive so $α$ is acute and $\text{cos}  α$ is positive, or that $R$ is the amplitude of the curve and so cannot be negative. Writing $R = \sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ with no reason given does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\text{cos}  2 θ = \text{cos}  θ$

for $0 \leq θ < 2 π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Both sides are cosines of different angles, so use the form of the double angle formula written in cosines only, $\text{cos}  2 A \equiv 2  \text{cos}^{2}  A - 1$

$2  \text{cos}^{2}  θ - 1 = \text{cos}  θ$

**[M1]**

Collect everything on one side to give a quadratic in $\text{cos}  θ$

$2  \text{cos}^{2}  θ - \text{cos}  θ - 1 = 0$

Factorise the quadratic

`\left(2 \; \text{cos} \; \theta + 1\right)\left(\text{cos} \; \theta - 1\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

A product is zero when either factor is zero, which gives two equations to solve

$\text{cos}  θ = 1$* or *$\text{cos}  θ = - \frac{1}{2}$

**[A1]**

For the first, the cosine equals $1$ once per period. In this interval that happens only at the left hand end, since $θ = 2 π$ is excluded

$θ = 0$

**[A1]**

For the second, take the inverse cosine, then use the symmetry of the cosine curve about $θ = π$

`\theta = \text{cos}^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}`* and *$θ = 2 π - \frac{2π}{3} = \frac{4π}{3}$

Collect every solution from both factors

$θ = 0 ,  \frac{2π}{3} ,  \frac{4π}{3}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct form of the double angle formula used to write the equation in $\text{cos}  θ$ only. Using $\text{cos}^{2}  θ - \text{sin}^{2}  θ$ and then the Pythagorean identity is equally acceptable.
> 
> **M1**: The quadratic collected on one side and factorised, or solved by the quadratic formula.
> 
> **A1**: Both factors set to zero, giving $\text{cos}  θ = 1$ and $\text{cos}  θ = - \frac{1}{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: At least two correct values of $θ$.
> 
> **A1**: All three correct values, and no others in the interval. The interval is strict at the upper end, so $θ = 2 π$ is not a solution and offering it loses this mark. Answers must be exact and in terms of $π$; decimals do not earn the accuracy marks, and answers given correctly in degrees are treated as a misread.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\text{tan}  2 x = 3  \text{tan}  x$

for $- π \leq x \leq π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Replace the left hand side with the double angle formula $\text{tan}  2 A \equiv \frac{2\text{tan}A}{1-\text{tan}^{2}A}$, then multiply through by the denominator

$\frac{2\text{tan}x}{1-\text{tan}^{2}x} = 3  \text{tan}  x   \Rightarrow   2  \text{tan}  x = 3  \text{tan}  x - 3  \text{tan}^{3}  x$

**[M1]**

Collect everything on one side, then factorise rather than dividing by $\text{tan}  x$

`3 \; \text{tan}^3 \; x - \text{tan} \; x = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \text{tan} \; x\left(3 \; \text{tan}^2 \; x - 1\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

Setting each factor to zero gives three equations, since the bracket has two roots

$\text{tan}  x = 0$* or *$\text{tan}  x = \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

**[A1]**

The tangent is zero at every multiple of $π$, and three of them lie in the interval

$x = - π ,  0 ,  π$

**[A1]**

For the positive root, take the inverse tangent, then subtract the period $π$ to reach the other value in the interval

`x = \text{tan}^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}`* and *$x = \frac{π}{6} - π = - \frac{5π}{6}$

**[A1]**

Do the same for the negative root

`x = \text{tan}^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}`* and *$x = - \frac{π}{6} + π = \frac{5π}{6}$

Collect every solution from all three factors

$x = - π ,  - \frac{5π}{6} ,  - \frac{π}{6} ,  0 ,  \frac{π}{6} ,  \frac{5π}{6} ,  π$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The double angle formula for $\text{tan}  2 x$ substituted and the fraction cleared.
> 
> **M1**: The cubic collected on one side and factorised as `\text{tan} \; x\left(3 \; \text{tan}^2 \; x - 1\right) = 0`. A candidate who divides through by $\text{tan}  x$ loses the whole $\text{tan}  x = 0$ family and does not earn this mark.
> 
> **A1**: All three values of $\text{tan}  x$ found, namely $0$ and $\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. Accept $\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ as an equivalent form.
> 
> **A1**: The family from $\text{tan}  x = 0$, namely $x = - π ,  0 ,  π$. Both endpoints count, since the interval is inclusive.
> 
> **A1**: At least two correct values from the other two families.
> 
> **A1**: All seven correct values, and no others in the interval. Answers must be exact and in terms of $π$; decimals do not earn the accuracy marks, and answers given correctly in degrees are treated as a misread.

parts.problemMd:
Show that

$\text{tan}  2 θ  \text{tan}  θ \equiv \text{sec}  2 θ - 1$
parts.solutionMd:
Start from the left hand side and replace $\text{tan}  2 θ$ with the double angle formula $\text{tan}  2 A \equiv \frac{2\text{tan}A}{1-\text{tan}^{2}A}$, then multiply by $\text{tan}  θ$

$\text{tan}  2 θ  \text{tan}  θ \equiv \frac{2\text{tan}θ}{1-\text{tan}^{2}θ} \times \text{tan}  θ \equiv \frac{2\text{tan}^{2}θ}{1-\text{tan}^{2}θ}$

**[M1]**

Write every tangent in terms of sine and cosine, using $\text{tan}  θ \equiv \frac{\text{sin}θ}{\text{cos}θ}$

$\equiv \frac{\frac{2\text{sin}^{2}θ}{\text{cos}^{2}θ}}{1-\frac{\text{sin}^{2}θ}{\text{cos}^{2}θ}}$

**[M1]**

Multiply the numerator and the denominator by $\text{cos}^{2}  θ$ to clear the inner fractions

$\equiv \frac{2\text{sin}^{2}θ}{\text{cos}^{2}θ-\text{sin}^{2}θ}$

**[A1]**

Now read two double angle formulae backwards. The denominator is $\text{cos}  2 θ$, and rearranging $\text{cos}  2 θ \equiv 1 - 2  \text{sin}^{2}  θ$ makes the numerator $1 - \text{cos}  2 θ$

$\equiv \frac{1-\text{cos}2θ}{\text{cos}2θ}$

**[M1]**

Split the single fraction into two, then use the definition $\text{sec}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$ applied to the angle $2 θ$

$\equiv \frac{1}{\text{cos}2θ} - 1$

**Final answer:** $\text{tan}  2 θ  \text{tan}  θ \equiv \text{sec}  2 θ - 1$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The double angle formula for $\text{tan}  2 θ$ substituted and combined with $\text{tan}  θ$ to give $\frac{2\text{tan}^{2}θ}{1-\text{tan}^{2}θ}$.
> 
> **M1**: Every tangent written in terms of sine and cosine.
> 
> **A1**: The inner fractions cleared, reaching $\frac{2\text{sin}^{2}θ}{\text{cos}^{2}θ-\text{sin}^{2}θ}$.
> 
> **M1**: Both double angle formulae used in reverse, so that the denominator becomes $\text{cos}  2 θ$ and the numerator becomes $1 - \text{cos}  2 θ$. Stating the identities is enough for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: The fraction split and named as $\text{sec}  2 θ - 1$, reaching the printed identity. Working from the right hand side back to the left is equally valid. Because the result is given, every line must be correct and $θ$ must be present throughout; abbreviations such as $s$, $c$ or $t$ in place of the function names are accepted only if they are defined first.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows two right-angled triangles. Angles $A$ and $B$ have been labelled.

![Two right-angled triangles sharing a vertex. The smaller has sides 3 and 4 with hypotenuse 5, and the larger has a vertical side made of two parts of length 3, a horizontal side 8 and hypotenuse 10. Angle A is in the smaller triangle and angle B in the larger, both at the shared vertex](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/trigonometry/compound-and-double-angle-formulae/assets/002-two-right-angled-triangles-sharing-a-vertex-the-.png)

Given that $α = A + B$, find the exact values of $\text{sin}  α$, $\text{cos}  α$ and $\text{tan}  α$.
parts.solutionMd:
For angle $A$, the side of length $4$ is opposite and the side of length $3$ is adjacent, with hypotenuse $5$

$\text{sin}  A = \frac{4}{5}$* and *$\text{cos}  A = \frac{3}{5}$

**[B1]**

For angle $B$, the vertical side is made of two parts, so its length is $3 + 3 = 6$. The side of length $8$ is opposite and this $6$ is adjacent, with hypotenuse $10$

$\text{sin}  B = \frac{8}{10} = \frac{4}{5}$* and *$\text{cos}  B = \frac{6}{10} = \frac{3}{5}$

**[B1]**

To find $\text{sin}  α$, use the compound angle formula $\text{sin} ( A + B ) \equiv \text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  B + \text{cos}  A  \text{sin}  B$

$\text{sin}  α = \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{3}{5} + \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{4}{5} = \frac{12}{25} + \frac{12}{25}$

**[M1]**

Add the two fractions

$\text{sin}  α = \frac{24}{25}$

**[A1]**

To find $\text{cos}  α$, use the compound angle formula $\text{cos} ( A + B ) \equiv \text{cos}  A  \text{cos}  B - \text{sin}  A  \text{sin}  B$

$\text{cos}  α = \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{3}{5} - \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{4}{5} = \frac{9}{25} - \frac{16}{25}$

**[M1]**

Subtract the two fractions. The result is negative, which is correct: adding two angles each larger than $45 ^{\circ}$ gives an obtuse angle

$\text{cos}  α = - \frac{7}{25}$

**[A1]**

Finally, use the identity $\text{tan}  α \equiv \frac{\text{sin}α}{\text{cos}α}$, so the two results above divide

$\text{tan}  α = - \frac{24}{7}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both $\text{sin}  A = \frac{4}{5}$ and $\text{cos}  A = \frac{3}{5}$, read from the smaller triangle.
> 
> **B1**: Both $\text{sin}  B = \frac{4}{5}$ and $\text{cos}  B = \frac{3}{5}$, read from the larger triangle, using the full vertical length of $6$. Accept these left as $\frac{8}{10}$ and $\frac{6}{10}$.
> 
> **M1**: The compound angle formula for $\text{sin} ( A + B )$ used with the values from the diagram.
> 
> **A1**: $\text{sin}  α = \frac{24}{25}$.
> 
> **M1**: The compound angle formula for $\text{cos} ( A + B )$ used with the values from the diagram. Using $\text{cos}  α = \pm \sqrt{1-\text{sin}^{2}α}$ instead earns this mark, but the candidate must then justify choosing the negative root.
> 
> **A1**: $\text{cos}  α = - \frac{7}{25}$. The sign matters; $\frac{7}{25}$ does not earn this mark.
> 
> **B1**: $\text{tan}  α = - \frac{24}{7}$, following from the two results above.

parts.problemMd:
The alternating voltage, $V$, in a domestic electrical circuit, $t$ seconds after it is switched on, is modelled by the function

$V = 115  \text{sin}  ω t + 115 \sqrt{3}  \text{cos}  ω t$

Express

$115  \text{sin}  ω t + 115 \sqrt{3}  \text{cos}  ω t$

in the form

$R  \text{sin} ( ω t + α )$

where $R$ and $α$ are constants to be found, with $R > 0$ and $α$ acute.
parts.solutionMd:
Expand the required form with the compound angle formula $\text{sin} ( A + B ) \equiv \text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  B + \text{cos}  A  \text{sin}  B$, then set it equal to the model

$115  \text{sin}  ω t + 115 \sqrt{3}  \text{cos}  ω t \equiv R  \text{cos}  α  \text{sin}  ω t + R  \text{sin}  α  \text{cos}  ω t$

Compare the coefficients of $\text{sin}  ω t$ and of $\text{cos}  ω t$ on each side

$R  \text{cos}  α = 115$* and *$R  \text{sin}  α = 115 \sqrt{3}$

Square and add the two equations, so that $\text{cos}^{2}  α + \text{sin}^{2}  α \equiv 1$ removes $α$

`R^2 = 115^2 + \left(115\sqrt{3}\right)^2 = 13225 + 39675 = 52900 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; R = 230`

**[B1]**

Divide the second equation by the first, so that $R$ cancels and $\frac{\text{sin}α}{\text{cos}α} = \text{tan}  α$

$\text{tan}  α = \frac{115\sqrt{3}}{115} = \sqrt{3}   \Rightarrow   α = \frac{π}{3}$

**[M1]**

Substitute both constants into the required form

`115 \; \text{sin} \; \omega t + 115\sqrt{3} \; \text{cos} \; \omega t \equiv 230 \; \text{sin}\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $R = 230$. Accept this obtained from `R = \sqrt{115^2 + \left(115\sqrt{3}\right)^2}` or by taking out a factor of $115$ first.
> 
> **M1**: A correct trigonometric method for $α$, such as $\text{tan}  α = \sqrt{3}$.
> 
> **A1**: $α = \frac{π}{3}$ and the form assembled. The question says $α$ is acute, so the exact value is expected; accept $60 ^{\circ}$ only if the rest of the question is then worked in degrees consistently.

parts.problemMd:
In the UK, domestic electricity runs at a frequency, $f$, of 50 Hertz (Hz). The constant $ω$ is given by $ω = 2 π f$.

(i) Find the initial voltage when a domestic appliance, such as a kettle or a television, is switched on.

(ii) Find the time at which the voltage first turns negative.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

First find $ω$ from the frequency

$ω = 2 π f = 2 π \times 50 = 100 π$

The appliance is switched on at $t = 0$, so substitute that into the form from part (a)

`V = 230 \; \text{sin}\left(0 + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 230 \; \text{sin} \; \dfrac{\pi}{3} = 199.185\ldots`

**[M1]**

Round to three significant figures

**Final answer:** $V = 199  \text{volts}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

The voltage turns negative as the sine crosses zero going downwards, which first happens when the angle reaches $π$. The angle starts at $\frac{π}{3}$ when $t = 0$, so it cannot be zero

$100 π t + \frac{π}{3} = π$

**[M1]**

Subtract $\frac{π}{3}$ from both sides, then divide by $100 π$

$100 π t = \frac{2π}{3}   \Rightarrow   t = \frac{2π}{3} \times \frac{1}{100π}$

$t = \frac{1}{150}  \text{seconds}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $ω = 100 π$ found, and $t = 0$ substituted into the model.
> 
> **A1**: An initial voltage which rounds to $199$. Accept the exact form $115 \sqrt{3}$. Substituting into the original model gives $115  \text{sin}  0 + 115 \sqrt{3}  \text{cos}  0$, which reaches the same answer and earns both marks.
> 
> **M1**: The angle set equal to $π$, which is where the sine next crosses zero on the way down. Setting the angle to $0$ does not earn this mark, since the angle already exceeds zero at $t = 0$.
> 
> **A1**: $t = \frac{1}{150}$ seconds. Accept an answer which rounds to $0 . 00667$.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find the period of one cycle of voltage in the UK.

(ii) In the US, the period of one cycle is $\frac{1}{60}$ seconds. Write down the frequency of US domestic electricity.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

One period is one complete turn of the angle, so the angle must increase by $2 π$

$100 π T = 2 π   \Rightarrow   T = \frac{2π}{100π}$

$\text{period} = \frac{1}{50} = 0 . 02  \text{seconds}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Part (i) shows the period is the reciprocal of the frequency, so reverse that

$\text{frequency} = 60  \text{Hz}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A period of $\frac{1}{50}$ seconds, or $0 . 02$ seconds. Accept this found either from $\frac{2π}{ω}$ or directly as $\frac{1}{f}$. An answer of $50$ seconds confuses the period with the frequency and does not earn this mark.
> 
> **B1**: A frequency of $60$ Hz. The command word is "write down", so no working is needed.

parts.problemMd: Show that $5  \text{sin}  θ - 3  \text{cos}  θ$ can be written in the form $R  \text{sin} ( θ - α )$, where $R = \sqrt{34}$ and $α = 0 . 540$ radians correct to three decimal places.
parts.solutionMd:
Expand the required form with the compound angle formula $\text{sin} ( A - B ) \equiv \text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  B - \text{cos}  A  \text{sin}  B$, then set it equal to the given expression

$5  \text{sin}  θ - 3  \text{cos}  θ \equiv R  \text{cos}  α  \text{sin}  θ - R  \text{sin}  α  \text{cos}  θ$

Compare the coefficients of $\text{sin}  θ$ and of $\text{cos}  θ$ on each side

$R  \text{cos}  α = 5$* and *$R  \text{sin}  α = 3$

Square and add the two equations, so that $\text{cos}^{2}  α + \text{sin}^{2}  α \equiv 1$ removes $α$

$R^{2} = 5^{2} + 3^{2} = 34   \Rightarrow   R = \sqrt{34}$

**[B1]**

Divide the second equation by the first, so that $R$ cancels and $\frac{\text{sin}α}{\text{cos}α} = \text{tan}  α$

`\text{tan} \; \alpha = \dfrac{3}{5} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \alpha = \text{tan}^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) = 0.5404195\ldots`

**[M1]**

Round to three decimal places, then substitute both constants into $R  \text{sin} ( θ - α )$

**Final answer:** `5 \; \text{sin} \; \theta - 3 \; \text{cos} \; \theta \equiv \sqrt{34} \; \text{sin}\left(\theta - 0.540\right)`** as required**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $R = \sqrt{34}$. The surd form is needed, since it is the one printed in the question.
> 
> **M1**: A correct trigonometric method for $α$, such as $\text{tan}  α = \frac{3}{5}$, or $\text{sin}  α = \frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}$ using the value of $R$. The minus sign in the expansion of $\text{sin} ( θ - α )$ means the coefficient of $\text{cos}  θ$ is taken as $3$, not $- 3$.
> 
> **B1**: The printed value $α = 0 . 540$ reached, with the unrounded $0 . 5404195 \dots$ seen first. Because the answer is given, going straight to $0 . 540$ loses this mark. An answer in degrees, $30 . 964 ^{\circ}$, is treated as a misread.

parts.problemMd:
Use your result from part (a), and the properties of the sine and cosine functions, to solve the equation

$3  \text{cos}  2 x + 5  \text{sin}  2 x = 0 . 4$

for $0 \leq x \leq 2 π$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Part (a) has a minus sign where this equation has a plus, so put $θ = - 2 x$ into it and use $\text{cos} ( - A ) = \text{cos}  A$ and $\text{sin} ( - A ) = - \text{sin}  A$ on the left hand side

`-5 \; \text{sin} \; 2x - 3 \; \text{cos} \; 2x = \sqrt{34} \; \text{sin}\left(-2x - 0.540\right)`

Apply $\text{sin} ( - A ) = - \text{sin}  A$ to the right hand side as well, then multiply through by $- 1$

`3 \; \text{cos} \; 2x + 5 \; \text{sin} \; 2x = \sqrt{34} \; \text{sin}\left(2x + 0.540\right)`

**[M1]**

The equation becomes a single sine, so divide by $\sqrt{34}$ to isolate it

`\text{sin}\left(2x + 0.540\right) = \dfrac{0.4}{\sqrt{34}} = 0.0685994\ldots`

**[M1]**

Let $φ = 2 x + 0 . 540$, then substitute each end of the interval in turn to find the interval for $φ$

$x = 0   \Rightarrow   φ = 0 + 0 . 540 = 0 . 540$

$x = 2 π   \Rightarrow   φ = 4 π + 0 . 540 = 13 . 106$

$0 . 540 \leq φ \leq 13 . 106$

Take the inverse sine. This principal value is below the interval, so it is not itself a solution, but its partners are

`\varphi = \text{sin}^{-1}\left(0.0685994\ldots\right) = 0.0686534\ldots`

**[A1]**

Use the symmetry $\text{sin}  φ = \text{sin} ( π - φ )$, then add the period $2 π$ repeatedly while the values stay in the interval

$φ = 3 . 072939 \dots ,  6 . 351838 \dots ,  9 . 356124 \dots ,  12 . 635023 \dots$

**[A1]**

Subtract $0 . 5404195 \dots$ from each value and divide by $2$, keeping full precision until the end

**Final answer:** $x = 1 . 27 ,  2 . 91 ,  4 . 41 ,  6 . 05$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Part (a) used with $θ = - 2 x$, together with the odd and even properties of sine and cosine, to reach `3 \; \text{cos} \; 2x + 5 \; \text{sin} \; 2x = \sqrt{34} \; \text{sin}\left(2x + 0.540\right)`. Re-deriving the R form directly for $5  \text{sin}  2 x + 3  \text{cos}  2 x$ reaches the same expression and earns this mark equally.
> 
> **M1**: The equation divided by $\sqrt{34}$ to isolate the sine, with the interval for $2 x + 0 . 540$ correctly found.
> 
> **A1**: A correct principal value, with the recognition that it lies below the interval. Accept answers which round to $0 . 0687$.
> 
> **A1**: At least two correct values of $2 x + 0 . 540$ in the interval.
> 
> **A1**: All four correct values of $x$, and no others in the interval. Accept answers which round to $1 . 27$, $2 . 91$, $4 . 41$ and $6 . 05$. Rounding before the final step can shift the last figure, so full precision should be carried through; answers which round correctly are accepted however the candidate got there.

parts.problemMd: Use an identity for $\text{cos}  2 A$ to derive an identity for $\text{cos}  4 A$, in terms of $\text{cos}  A$.
parts.solutionMd:
Treat $4 A$ as double the angle $2 A$, and use the form of the double angle formula written in cosines only, $\text{cos}  2 θ \equiv 2  \text{cos}^{2}  θ - 1$

$\text{cos}  4 A \equiv 2  \text{cos}^{2}  2 A - 1$

**[M1]**

Apply the same formula again, this time to $\text{cos}  2 A$ itself

`\equiv 2\left(2 \; \text{cos}^2 \; A - 1\right)^2 - 1`

**[M1]**

Expand the square

`\equiv 2\left(4 \; \text{cos}^4 \; A - 4 \; \text{cos}^2 \; A + 1\right) - 1`

**[A1]**

Multiply out the bracket and collect the constants

$\text{cos}  4 A \equiv 8  \text{cos}^{4}  A - 8  \text{cos}^{2}  A + 1$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $\text{cos}  4 A$ written as $2  \text{cos}^{2}  2 A - 1$, or as another correct double angle form of the angle $2 A$.
> 
> **M1**: The double angle formula applied a second time, to replace $\text{cos}  2 A$ by $2  \text{cos}^{2}  A - 1$.
> 
> **A1**: The square correctly expanded, giving $4  \text{cos}^{4}  A - 4  \text{cos}^{2}  A + 1$ inside the bracket. Squaring the bracket as $4  \text{cos}^{4}  A + 1$ loses this mark and the next.
> 
> **A1**: The correct identity, with the constants collected. Routes through $\text{cos}^{2}  2 A - \text{sin}^{2}  2 A$ or $1 - 2  \text{sin}^{2}  2 A$ are equally valid, provided the answer is left in cosines only as the question asks.

parts.problemMd:
Hence, or otherwise, solve the equation

$2  \text{cos}  4 x = 7  \text{sin}^{2}  x - 2$

for $0 \leq x \leq π$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute the identity from part (a) on the left, and use $\text{sin}^{2}  x \equiv 1 - \text{cos}^{2}  x$ on the right, so that the whole equation is in $\text{cos}  x$

`2\left(8 \; \text{cos}^4 \; x - 8 \; \text{cos}^2 \; x + 1\right) = 7\left(1 - \text{cos}^2 \; x\right) - 2`

**[M1]**

Multiply out both sides and collect every term on the left

$16  \text{cos}^{4}  x - 9  \text{cos}^{2}  x - 3 = 0$

**[A1]**

This is a quadratic in $\text{cos}^{2}  x$, so apply the quadratic formula to it

$\text{cos}^{2}  x = \frac{9\pm\sqrt{273}}{32}$

**[M1]**

A square cannot be negative, and $\sqrt{273} > 9$, so the root with the minus sign is rejected. Take the square root of the other

$\text{cos}  x = \pm \sqrt{\frac{9+\sqrt{273}}{32}} = \pm 0 . 893076 \dots$

**[A1]**

Take the inverse cosine of each. Both results lie in the interval, the second by the symmetry of the cosine curve about $x = \frac{π}{2}$

$x = 0 . 466659 \dots$* and *$x = 2 . 674932 \dots$

Round each to three significant figures

**Final answer:** $x = 0 . 467 ,  2 . 67$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Part (a) substituted and the Pythagorean identity used, so that the equation is in $\text{cos}  x$ only.
> 
> **A1**: The correct quartic, $16  \text{cos}^{4}  x - 9  \text{cos}^{2}  x - 3 = 0$, or any correct equivalent.
> 
> **M1**: The equation treated as a quadratic in $\text{cos}^{2}  x$ and solved. Accept the quadratic formula or completing the square; the quartic does not factorise.
> 
> **A1**: The negative root rejected, with a reason, and $\text{cos}  x = \pm 0 . 893$ obtained. A candidate who keeps the negative value of $\text{cos}^{2}  x$ and tries to take its square root does not earn this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Both correct values of $x$, and no others in the interval. Accept answers which round to $0 . 467$ and $2 . 67$. Omitting the solution from the negative value of $\text{cos}  x$ is the most common loss here. Answers given correctly in degrees are treated as a misread.

parts.problemMd: Solve the equation $\text{sec}  θ = 1$ for $0 ^{\circ} \leq θ \leq 360 ^{\circ}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the definition of the secant function to write the equation in terms of cosine

$\text{sec}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ} = 1$

Take the reciprocal of each side

$\text{cos}  θ = 1$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse cosine to find the first value

`\theta = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( 1 \right) = 0°`

**[A1]**

The cosine curve repeats every $360 ^{\circ}$, so add one period to find the next value

$θ = 0 ^{\circ} + 360 ^{\circ} = 360 ^{\circ}$

Both values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$θ = 0 ^{\circ} ,  θ = 360 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $\text{sec}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$ to reach $\text{cos}  θ = 1$. You do not have to write the definition out as a separate line, and reaching $\text{cos}  θ = 1$ by any correct route earns this mark.
> 
> **A1**: The value $θ = 0 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: The value $θ = 360 ^{\circ}$, with no other values inside $0 ^{\circ} \leq θ \leq 360 ^{\circ}$. Both values are needed for this mark. Any values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

`\text{tan} \left( A - 30° \right) = \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{3}`

for $- 180 ^{\circ} \leq A \leq 180 ^{\circ}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute for the whole angle so the equation becomes a standard tangent equation

$\text{Let}  ϕ = A - 30 ^{\circ}$

Find the interval for $ϕ$ by substituting each endpoint of the interval for $A$ into $A - 30 ^{\circ}$

$A = - 180 ^{\circ} \Rightarrow ϕ = - 180 ^{\circ} - 30 ^{\circ} = - 210 ^{\circ}$

$A = 180 ^{\circ} \Rightarrow ϕ = 180 ^{\circ} - 30 ^{\circ} = 150 ^{\circ}$

$- 210 ^{\circ} \leq ϕ \leq 150 ^{\circ}$

Take the inverse tangent to find the principal value

`\phi = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{3} \right) = 30°`

**[M1]**

The tangent curve repeats every $180 ^{\circ}$, so subtract one period to find the other value inside the interval

$ϕ = 30 ^{\circ} - 180 ^{\circ} = - 150 ^{\circ}$

Add $30 ^{\circ}$ to each value of $ϕ$ to return to $A$

$A = 30 ^{\circ} + 30 ^{\circ} = 60 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

$A = - 150 ^{\circ} + 30 ^{\circ} = - 120 ^{\circ}$

Both values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$A = - 120 ^{\circ} ,  A = 60 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct method for a value of $A - 30 ^{\circ}$, which means evaluating `\text{tan}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{3} \right)` to reach $30 ^{\circ}$ or $- 150 ^{\circ}$. Substituting for the angle is not required, and working directly with $A - 30 ^{\circ}$ throughout earns this mark just as well.
> 
> **A1**: The value $A = 60 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: The value $A = - 120 ^{\circ}$, with no other values inside $- 180 ^{\circ} \leq A \leq 180 ^{\circ}$. This mark follows through from your first value, so subtracting $180 ^{\circ}$ from your own value of $A - 30 ^{\circ}$ and then adding $30 ^{\circ}$ is credited. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\frac{1}{\text{sec}x} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2}$

for $- π \leq x \leq π$, giving your answers in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the definition of the secant function to simplify the left hand side

$\frac{1}{\text{sec}x} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{\text{cos}x}} = \text{cos}  x$

So the equation is a cosine equation

$\text{cos}  x = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2}$

**[B1]**

Take the inverse cosine to find the principal value

`x = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2} \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}`

**[M1]**

The cosine curve is symmetrical about the vertical axis, so `\text{cos} \; x = \text{cos} \left( -x \right)` gives the other value

$x = - \frac{π}{4}$

Both values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$x = - \frac{π}{4} ,  x = \frac{π}{4}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Stating or implying that $\text{cos}  x = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2}$. Writing the double reciprocal out first is not required, so going straight to the cosine equation earns this mark. Accept $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ as an equivalent exact form.
> 
> **M1**: A correct method for a value of $x$ in radians, which means taking the inverse cosine of your value.
> 
> **A1**: Both exact values $x = \pm \frac{π}{4}$, with no others inside $- π \leq x \leq π$. The answers must be exact and in terms of $π$ as the question asks, so the decimal pair $\pm 0 . 785$ does not earn this mark. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Express

$8  \text{cos}  θ + 6  \text{sin}  θ$

in the form `R \; \text{cos} \left( \theta - \alpha \right)`, where $R > 0$ and $0 < α < \frac{1}{2} π$.

State the value of $R$ and give the value of $α$ correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Expand `R \; \text{cos} \left( \theta - \alpha \right)` using the `\text{cos} \left( A - B \right)` formula from the formula booklet

`R \; \text{cos} \left( \theta - \alpha \right) = R \; \text{cos} \; \theta \; \text{cos} \; \alpha + R \; \text{sin} \; \theta \; \text{sin} \; \alpha`

Set this equal to the given expression

$8  \text{cos}  θ + 6  \text{sin}  θ = R  \text{cos}  α  \text{cos}  θ + R  \text{sin}  α  \text{sin}  θ$

Compare the coefficients of $\text{cos}  θ$ and of $\text{sin}  θ$

$R  \text{cos}  α = 8$* and *$R  \text{sin}  α = 6$

**[M1]**

Find $R$ by squaring and adding the two equations, since $\text{cos}^{2} α + \text{sin}^{2} α \equiv 1$

$R^{2} = 8^{2} + 6^{2} = 100$

$R = 10$

**[B1]**

Find $α$ by dividing the second equation by the first, since $\frac{\text{sin}α}{\text{cos}α} = \text{tan}  α$

$\text{tan}  α = \frac{6}{8} = \frac{3}{4}$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse tangent

`\alpha = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( \dfrac{3}{4} \right) = 0.6435011 \ldots`

Round to 3 significant figures as the question asks

$R = 10 ,  α = 0 . 644$

**[A1]**

So the expression can be written as

`8 \; \text{cos} \; \theta + 6 \; \text{sin} \; \theta \equiv 10 \; \text{cos} \left( \theta - 0.644 \right)`

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Expanding `R \; \text{cos} \left( \theta - \alpha \right)` correctly and comparing coefficients to reach $R  \text{cos}  α = 8$ and $R  \text{sin}  α = 6$. Both equations are needed. If you go straight to the shortcuts without showing the expansion, this mark is still available provided both $R^{2} = 8^{2} + 6^{2}$ and $\text{tan}  α = \frac{6}{8}$ appear.
> 
> **B1**: $R = 10$. The value of $R$ must be exact. Where $R$ is not a whole number a surd is required, and a decimal is not accepted.
> 
> **M1**: A correct method for $α$, which means $\text{tan}  α = \frac{6}{8}$ or $\frac{3}{4}$, or equivalently `\text{cos}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{8}{10} \right)` or `\text{sin}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{6}{10} \right)` using your own $R$.
> 
> **A1**: $α = 0 . 644$, given to 3 significant figures as the question asks. Accept answers which round to $0 . 644$. An unevaluated `\text{tan}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{3}{4} \right)` earns the method mark but not this one. An answer in degrees `\left( 36.9° \right)` is treated as a misreading of the question.

parts.problemMd:
Show that the equation

$\text{cosec}^{2} x = 2  \text{cosec}  x - 1$

can be expressed in the form

`\left( \text{cosec} \; x - 1 \right)^2 = 0`
parts.solutionMd:
Collect every term on one side to form a quadratic in $\text{cosec}  x$

$\text{cosec}^{2} x - 2  \text{cosec}  x + 1 = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise the quadratic

`\left( \text{cosec} \; x - 1 \right) \left( \text{cosec} \; x - 1 \right) = 0`

Write the repeated factor as a square

**Final answer:** `\left( \text{cosec} \; x - 1 \right)^2 = 0`** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: All terms collected on one side to give the three term quadratic $\text{cosec}^{2} x - 2  \text{cosec}  x + 1 = 0$, or any correct equivalent with everything on one side.
> 
> **A1**: The given squared form reached. Accept the factorised pair `\left( \text{cosec} \; x - 1 \right) \left( \text{cosec} \; x - 1 \right) = 0` followed by the square, or completing the square in place of factorising. Because the answer is printed, every line must be correct and the $x$ must be present throughout.

parts.problemMd:
Hence solve the equation

$\text{cosec}^{2} x = 2  \text{cosec}  x - 1$

for $- 2 π \leq x \leq 2 π$, giving your answers in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use part (a), noting that a square is zero only when the quantity inside it is zero

$\text{cosec}  x - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \text{cosec}  x = 1$

Use the definition of the cosecant function and take reciprocals

$\frac{1}{\text{sin}x} = 1 \Rightarrow \text{sin}  x = 1$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse sine to find the first value

`x = \text{sin}^{-1} \left( 1 \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}`

**[A1]**

The sine equals $1$ only once in each period, so subtract one period of $2 π$ for the other value in the interval

$x = \frac{π}{2} - 2 π = - \frac{3π}{2}$

Both values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$x = - \frac{3π}{2} ,  x = \frac{π}{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The squared form solved to give $\text{cosec}  x = 1$, then $\text{sin}  x = 1$, followed by a correct method for at least one value of $x$ in radians. Reaching $\text{sin}  x = 1$ without going through part (a) is equally acceptable, since the question allows any correct route.
> 
> **A1**: The value $x = \frac{π}{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: The value $x = - \frac{3π}{2}$, with no other values inside $- 2 π \leq x \leq 2 π$. Both answers must be exact and in terms of $π$ as the question asks. Because the sine reaches $1$ only once per period, there is no partner value from the symmetry of the curve, so a candidate who also offers $\frac{π}{2} + π$ or similar loses this mark. Values you give outside the interval are ignored.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\text{cos}  2 θ = \frac{1}{2}$

for $- π \leq θ \leq π$, giving your answers in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute for the double angle so the equation becomes a standard cosine equation

$\text{Let}  u = 2 θ$

Change the interval to match by doubling each part

$- 2 π \leq u \leq 2 π$

Take the inverse cosine to find the principal value

`u = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{2} \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}`

**[M1]**

The cosine curve is symmetrical about the vertical axis, so `\text{cos} \; u = \text{cos} \left( -u \right)` gives a second value

$u = - \frac{π}{3}$

The interval spans two full periods, so add and subtract one period of $2 π$ to find the remaining values

$u = \frac{π}{3} - 2 π = - \frac{5π}{3}$

$u = - \frac{π}{3} + 2 π = \frac{5π}{3}$

**[A1]**

Halve each value of $u$ to return to $θ$

$θ = \pm \frac{π}{6} ,  θ = \pm \frac{5π}{6}$

All four values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$θ = - \frac{5π}{6} ,  - \frac{π}{6} ,  \frac{π}{6} ,  \frac{5π}{6}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Solving as far as `2\theta = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{2} \right)`, working in radians. Substituting for the double angle is not required, and working with $2 θ$ throughout earns this mark just as well.
> 
> **A1**: Any two correct exact values of $θ$, for example $\pm \frac{π}{6}$.
> 
> **A1**: All four correct exact values, with no others inside $- π \leq θ \leq π$. The answers must be exact and in terms of $π$ as the question asks, so the decimal set $\pm 0 . 524$, $\pm 2 . 62$ does not earn this mark. Remember that doubling the interval gives two full periods, so a pair of answers only is not enough. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd: Sketch the graph of $y = \text{sec}  x$ for $- π \leq x \leq π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Start from the cosine curve, since the secant is its reciprocal

$\text{sec}  x = \frac{1}{\text{cos}x}$

The reciprocal is undefined wherever the cosine is zero, which locates the vertical asymptotes

$\text{cos}  x = 0 \Rightarrow x = - \frac{π}{2} ,  x = \frac{π}{2}$

**[B1]**

Find the height of the curve at the middle and at the two ends of the interval, using the fact that the reciprocal of $\pm 1$ is $\pm 1$

$\text{sec}  0 = 1$* and *`\text{sec} \left( \pm \pi \right) = -1`

**[B1]**

Between the asymptotes the cosine is positive and at most $1$, so the reciprocal is at least $1$ and that branch is a U shape with its lowest point at `\left( 0, \; 1 \right)`

Outside the asymptotes the cosine is negative and no less than $- 1$, so each outer branch lies below the axis and reaches $- 1$ at $x = \pm π$

![Graph of y = sec x for x between minus pi and pi, showing a U shaped branch above the x axis with its lowest point at (0, 1), dashed vertical asymptotes at x = minus pi over 2 and x = pi over 2, and two branches below the x axis which rise to the value minus 1 at x = minus pi and x = pi](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/trigonometry/further-trigonometric-equations/assets/001-graph-of-y-sec-x-for-x-between-minus-pi-and-pi-s.png)

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The two asymptotes located at $x = \pm \frac{π}{2}$. Accept them drawn as dashed vertical lines on the sketch or written as equations beside it.
> 
> **B1**: The values $1$ at $x = 0$ and $- 1$ at $x = \pm π$. Accept these marked on the axes or written as the coordinates `\left( 0, \; 1 \right)` and `\left( \pm \pi, \; -1 \right)`.
> 
> **B1**: Correct shape of all three branches, the central one a U lying on or above $y = 1$ and the two outer ones lying on or below $y = - 1$, each curving away towards its asymptote without touching or crossing it. The graph must cover the whole of $- π \leq x \leq π$ with nothing drawn outside it, and the curve must not be drawn with a ruler.

parts.problemMd:
Use your graph to find the set of values of $k$ for which the equation

$\text{sec}  x = k$

has no real roots for $- π \leq x \leq π$.
parts.solutionMd:
The roots of the equation are the values of $x$ where the line $y = k$ crosses the curve $y = \text{sec}  x$, so for no real roots the line must miss the curve completely

![The graph of y = sec x from part (a) with a horizontal line y = k drawn across the gap between the two parts of the curve, passing below the minimum of the central U shaped branch and above the two branches which lie below the x axis, so that the line does not meet the curve anywhere](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/trigonometry/further-trigonometric-equations/assets/002-the-graph-of-y-sec-x-from-part-a-with-a-horizont.png)

Read the two parts of the curve off the graph: the central branch never drops below $1$, and the outer branches never rise above $- 1$

$\text{sec}  x \geq 1$* or *$\text{sec}  x \leq - 1$

So the curve takes no value strictly between $- 1$ and $1$, and a line drawn in that gap misses it

$- 1 < k < 1$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The answer $- 1 < k < 1$. Accept any equivalent form, including `\left| k \right| < 1` and interval notation such as `\left( -1, \; 1 \right)`. The inequalities must be strict: at $k = 1$ the line touches the central branch at `\left( 0, \; 1 \right)` and at $k = - 1$ it touches the outer branches at $x = \pm π$, and each of those is a real root, so $- 1 \leq k \leq 1$ does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\text{cot}^{2} θ - \text{cos}  θ  \text{cosec}^{2} θ = 0$

for $0 < θ < 2 π$, giving your answers in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Write both reciprocal functions in terms of sine and cosine

$\text{cot}^{2} θ = \frac{\text{cos}^{2}θ}{\text{sin}^{2}θ}$* and *$\text{cosec}^{2} θ = \frac{1}{\text{sin}^{2}θ}$

Substitute into the equation

$\frac{\text{cos}^{2}θ}{\text{sin}^{2}θ} - \frac{\text{cos}θ}{\text{sin}^{2}θ} = 0$

Both terms already share the denominator $\text{sin}^{2} θ$, so combine them

$\frac{\text{cos}^{2}θ-\text{cos}θ}{\text{sin}^{2}θ} = 0$

A fraction is zero only when its numerator is zero

$\text{cos}^{2} θ - \text{cos}  θ = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise

`\text{cos} \; \theta \left( \text{cos} \; \theta - 1 \right) = 0`

**[A1]**

Take the first factor and solve

`\text{cos} \; \theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( 0 \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}`

The cosine is zero once every half period, so add $π$ for the next value

$θ = \frac{π}{2} + π = \frac{3π}{2}$

Take the second factor. The cosine equals $1$ at every multiple of its $2 π$ period

$\text{cos}  θ = 1 \Rightarrow θ = 0 ,  2 π$

Check these against the interval, which is strict at both ends, so neither value is allowed

$0 < θ < 2 π \Rightarrow θ \neq 0$* and *$θ \neq 2 π$

Only the values from the first factor survive

$θ = \frac{π}{2} ,  θ = \frac{3π}{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using the definitions of $\text{cot}  θ$ and $\text{cosec}  θ$ to write the equation in terms of sine and cosine, and clearing the denominator to reach an equation in $\text{cos}  θ$ alone. The identity route is equally acceptable: replacing $\text{cot}^{2} θ$ with $\text{cosec}^{2} θ - 1$ and using $1 + \text{cot}^{2} θ \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} θ$ reaches the same equation and earns this mark.
> 
> **A1**: The factorised form `\text{cos} \; \theta \left( \text{cos} \; \theta - 1 \right) = 0`, or the equivalent unfactorised $\text{cos}^{2} θ - \text{cos}  θ = 0$ together with both values of $\text{cos}  θ$.
> 
> **A1**: Both exact values $θ = \frac{π}{2}$ and $θ = \frac{3π}{2}$, and no others inside $0 < θ < 2 π$. The answers must be in terms of $π$ as the question asks. The second factor gives $θ = 0$ and $θ = 2 π$, and both are excluded because the inequalities are strict, so including either loses this mark. It is worth writing that check down rather than simply dropping the factor: you need to show that $\text{cos}  θ = 1$ has no root inside the interval, not just that its principal value sits outside it.

parts.problemMd: Solve the equation $\text{cosec}  2 θ = 2$ for $0 ^{\circ} \leq θ \leq 180 ^{\circ}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the definition of the cosecant function

$\text{cosec}  2 θ = \frac{1}{\text{sin}2θ} = 2$

Take the reciprocal of each side

$\text{sin}  2 θ = \frac{1}{2}$

Substitute for the double angle so this is a standard sine equation

$\text{Let}  ϕ = 2 θ$

Change the interval to match by doubling each part

$0 ^{\circ} \leq ϕ \leq 360 ^{\circ}$

Take the inverse sine to find the principal value

`\phi = \text{sin}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{2} \right) = 30°`

**[M1]**

This is only the principal value, so use the symmetry of the sine curve, `\text{sin} \; \phi = \text{sin} \left( 180° - \phi \right)`, to find the other value in the interval

$ϕ = 180 ^{\circ} - 30 ^{\circ} = 150 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Halve each value of $ϕ$ to return to $θ$

$θ = \frac{30^{\circ}}{2} = 15 ^{\circ}$* and *$θ = \frac{150^{\circ}}{2} = 75 ^{\circ}$

Both values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$θ = 15 ^{\circ} ,  θ = 75 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using $\text{cosec}  2 θ = \frac{1}{\text{sin}2θ}$ to reach $\text{sin}  2 θ = \frac{1}{2}$, then a correct method for one value of $2 θ$. Substituting for the double angle is not required, and working with $2 θ$ throughout earns this mark just as well.
> 
> **M1**: Using the symmetry of the sine curve to obtain the second value of $2 θ$, which is $150 ^{\circ}$. This mark follows through from your first value, so $180 ^{\circ}$ minus your own value is credited.
> 
> **A1**: Both values $θ = 15 ^{\circ}$ and $θ = 75 ^{\circ}$, with no others inside $0 ^{\circ} \leq θ \leq 180 ^{\circ}$. Halving both values of $2 θ$ is essential, and a pair of answers left as $30 ^{\circ}$ and $150 ^{\circ}$ does not earn this mark. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

`\text{tan} \left( 3A - 30° \right) = -\tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{3}`

for $- 120 ^{\circ} \leq A \leq 120 ^{\circ}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute for the whole angle so the equation becomes a standard tangent equation

$\text{Let}  ϕ = 3 A - 30 ^{\circ}$

Find the interval for $ϕ$ by substituting each endpoint of the interval for $A$

`A = -120° \Rightarrow \phi = 3 \left( -120° \right) - 30° = -390°`

`A = 120° \Rightarrow \phi = 3 \left( 120° \right) - 30° = 330°`

$- 390 ^{\circ} \leq ϕ \leq 330 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse tangent to find the principal value

`\phi = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( -\tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{3} \right) = -30°`

The interval is wide enough to hold several periods, so step by the $180 ^{\circ}$ period in both directions and keep every value that lands inside it

$ϕ = - 30 ^{\circ} - 180 ^{\circ} = - 210 ^{\circ}$

$ϕ = - 210 ^{\circ} - 180 ^{\circ} = - 390 ^{\circ}$

$ϕ = - 30 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 150 ^{\circ}$

$ϕ = 150 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 330 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Return to $A$ by adding $30 ^{\circ}$ to each value and dividing by $3$

$A = \frac{-390^{\circ}+30^{\circ}}{3} = - 120 ^{\circ}$* and *$A = \frac{-210^{\circ}+30^{\circ}}{3} = - 60 ^{\circ}$

$A = \frac{-30^{\circ}+30^{\circ}}{3} = 0 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

$A = \frac{150^{\circ}+30^{\circ}}{3} = 60 ^{\circ}$* and *$A = \frac{330^{\circ}+30^{\circ}}{3} = 120 ^{\circ}$

All five values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$A = - 120 ^{\circ} ,  - 60 ^{\circ} ,  0 ^{\circ} ,  60 ^{\circ} ,  120 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Adjusting the interval correctly to $- 390 ^{\circ} \leq 3 A - 30 ^{\circ} \leq 330 ^{\circ}$, or equivalent working that keeps track of the interval for $3 A - 30 ^{\circ}$ throughout. This is the step that decides how many solutions you find, so it is worth writing out.
> 
> **M1**: The principal value `\text{tan}^{-1} \left( -\tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{3} \right) = -30°`, together with use of the $180 ^{\circ}$ period to generate further values of $3 A - 30 ^{\circ}$. At least one further value is needed for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Three correct values of $A$.
> 
> **A1**: All five values $A = - 120 ^{\circ}$, $- 60 ^{\circ}$, $0 ^{\circ}$, $60 ^{\circ}$ and $120 ^{\circ}$, with no others inside $- 120 ^{\circ} \leq A \leq 120 ^{\circ}$. Note that both endpoints of the interval are solutions, so they must be included. Remember to complete both stages of the return to $A$, adding $30 ^{\circ}$ and then dividing by $3$: a set of answers left as values of $3 A - 30 ^{\circ}$ does not earn this mark. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\frac{\text{sin}x}{\text{sec}x} = \frac{1}{4}$

for $- π \leq x \leq π$, giving your answers in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the definition of the secant function to simplify the left hand side

$\frac{\text{sin}x}{\text{sec}x} = \frac{\text{sin}x}{\frac{1}{\text{cos}x}} = \text{sin}  x  \text{cos}  x$

**[M1]**

The product of a sine and a cosine is half of the double angle sine, from $\text{sin}  2 θ \equiv 2  \text{sin}  θ  \text{cos}  θ$

$\text{sin}  x  \text{cos}  x = \frac{1}{2}  \text{sin}  2 x$

Substitute this into the equation and clear the fraction

$\frac{1}{2}  \text{sin}  2 x = \frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow \text{sin}  2 x = \frac{1}{2}$

**[M1]**

Substitute for the double angle so this is a standard sine equation

$\text{Let}  ϕ = 2 x$

Change the interval to match by doubling each part

$- 2 π \leq ϕ \leq 2 π$

Take the inverse sine to find the principal value

`\phi = \text{sin}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{2} \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}`

Use the symmetry of the sine curve, `\text{sin} \; \phi = \text{sin} \left( \pi - \phi \right)`, for the second value

$ϕ = π - \frac{π}{6} = \frac{5π}{6}$

**[A1]**

The interval spans two full periods, so subtract one period of $2 π$ from each value to find the remaining two

$ϕ = \frac{π}{6} - 2 π = - \frac{11π}{6}$

$ϕ = \frac{5π}{6} - 2 π = - \frac{7π}{6}$

Halve each value of $ϕ$ to return to $x$

$x = - \frac{11π}{12} ,  - \frac{7π}{12} ,  \frac{π}{12} ,  \frac{5π}{12}$

All four values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$x = - \frac{11π}{12} ,  - \frac{7π}{12} ,  \frac{π}{12} ,  \frac{5π}{12}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using $\text{sec}  x = \frac{1}{\text{cos}x}$ to reduce the left hand side to $\text{sin}  x  \text{cos}  x$, so that the equation becomes $\text{sin}  x  \text{cos}  x = \frac{1}{4}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $\text{sin}  2 x \equiv 2  \text{sin}  x  \text{cos}  x$ to reach $\text{sin}  2 x = \frac{1}{2}$. The identity does not have to be quoted as a separate line, and using it anywhere in the working earns this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Any two correct exact values of $x$, for example $\frac{π}{12}$ and $\frac{5π}{12}$.
> 
> **A1**: All four correct exact values, with no others inside $- π \leq x \leq π$. The answers must be exact and in terms of $π$ as the question asks, so the decimal set $0 . 262$, $1 . 31$, $- 1 . 83$, $- 2 . 88$ does not earn this mark. Doubling the interval gives two full periods, so a pair of answers only is not enough. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Use the identity

`R \; \text{sin} \left( A + B \right) \equiv R \; \text{cos} \; B \; \text{sin} \; A + R \; \text{sin} \; B \; \text{cos} \; A`

to show that

$3  \text{sin}  θ + 4  \text{cos}  θ$

can be expressed in the form

`5 \; \text{sin} \left( \theta + \alpha \right)`

where

`\alpha = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{4}{3} \right)`
parts.solutionMd:
Apply the given identity with $A = θ$ and $B = α$, then set the result equal to the given expression

$3  \text{sin}  θ + 4  \text{cos}  θ = R  \text{cos}  α  \text{sin}  θ + R  \text{sin}  α  \text{cos}  θ$

**[M1]**

Compare the coefficients of $\text{sin}  θ$ and of $\text{cos}  θ$

$R  \text{cos}  α = 3$* and *$R  \text{sin}  α = 4$

**[A1]**

Find $R$ by squaring and adding the two equations, since $\text{cos}^{2} α + \text{sin}^{2} α \equiv 1$

$R^{2} = 3^{2} + 4^{2} = 25$

$R = 5$

**[M1]**

Find $α$ by dividing the second equation by the first, since $\frac{\text{sin}α}{\text{cos}α} = \text{tan}  α$

`\text{tan} \; \alpha = \dfrac{4}{3} \Rightarrow \alpha = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{4}{3} \right)`

So the expression can be written in the required form

**Final answer:** `3 \; \text{sin} \; \theta + 4 \; \text{cos} \; \theta \equiv 5 \; \text{sin} \left( \theta + \alpha \right), \; \alpha = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{4}{3} \right)`** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using the given identity with $A = θ$ and $B = α$ and equating the result to $3  \text{sin}  θ + 4  \text{cos}  θ$.
> 
> **A1**: Both equations $R  \text{cos}  α = 3$ and $R  \text{sin}  α = 4$. Both are needed.
> 
> **M1**: A correct method for $R$, which means squaring and adding to reach $R^{2} = 3^{2} + 4^{2}$, or an equivalent method such as Pythagoras on a right-angled triangle with shorter sides $3$ and $4$.
> 
> **A1**: $R = 5$ together with $\text{tan}  α = \frac{4}{3}$, giving the printed result. Because the answer is given, every line must be correct. Take care which way up the fraction goes: for the $R  \text{sin}$ form it is the coefficient of $\text{cos}  θ$ over the coefficient of $\text{sin}  θ$, so $\text{tan}  α = \frac{4}{3}$ and not $\frac{3}{4}$.

parts.problemMd:
Hence solve the equation

$3  \text{sin}  θ + 4  \text{cos}  θ = 1$

for $0 \leq θ \leq π$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Use part (a) to replace the left hand side, then divide by $5$

`5 \; \text{sin} \left( \theta + \alpha \right) = 1 \Rightarrow \text{sin} \left( \theta + \alpha \right) = \tfrac{1}{5}`

Evaluate $α$ and keep the unrounded value

`\alpha = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{4}{3} \right) = 0.92729 \ldots`

Substitute for the whole angle so this is a standard sine equation

$\text{Let}  ϕ = θ + α$

Find the interval for $ϕ$ by substituting each endpoint of the interval for $θ$

$θ = 0 \Rightarrow ϕ = 0 + 0 . 92729 \dots = 0 . 92729 \dots$

$θ = π \Rightarrow ϕ = π + 0 . 92729 \dots = 4 . 06888 \dots$

$0 . 92729 \dots \leq ϕ \leq 4 . 06888 \dots$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse sine to find the principal value

`\phi = \text{sin}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{5} \right) = 0.20135 \ldots`

This value is below the lower end of the interval, so it is not a solution. Use the symmetry of the sine curve, `\text{sin} \; \phi = \text{sin} \left( \pi - \phi \right)`, to find the partner value, which does lie inside

$ϕ = π - 0 . 20135 \dots = 2 . 94023 \dots$

**[A1]**

Subtract $α$ to return to $θ$

$θ = 2 . 94023 \dots - 0 . 92729 \dots = 2 . 01293 \dots$

Round to 3 significant figures as the question asks

$θ = 2 . 01$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using part (a) to reach `\text{sin} \left( \theta + \alpha \right) = \tfrac{1}{5}`, with $α$ evaluated, followed by a correct method for a value of $θ + α$. Shifting the interval is the step that decides which values survive, so it is worth writing out. Any correct alternative route is credited, since the question does not force the use of part (a).
> 
> **A1**: The value $θ + α = 2 . 94$, or better. Note that the principal value $0 . 201$ lies outside the shifted interval and so is not itself a solution: reaching $2 . 94$ by the symmetry of the sine curve is what earns this mark.
> 
> **A1**: The single answer $θ = 2 . 01$, correct to 3 significant figures, with no others inside $0 \leq θ \leq π$. Accept answers which round to $2 . 01$. There is only one solution in this interval, so offering a second value inside it loses this mark. Do not round the intermediate values: working with $0 . 93$ and $2 . 94$ throughout gives $2 . 01$ here, but the habit costs accuracy elsewhere. Values you give outside the interval are ignored.

parts.problemMd: State the greatest value of $3  \text{sin}  θ + 4  \text{cos}  θ$ and find the least positive value of $θ$ for which this greatest value occurs. Give your value of $θ$ correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
The sine of any angle is at most $1$, so the greatest value of `5 \; \text{sin} \left( \theta + \alpha \right)` occurs when the sine equals $1$

$\text{Greatest value} = 5$

**[B1]**

Find the angle at which the sine first reaches $1$

`\text{sin} \left( \theta + \alpha \right) = 1 \Rightarrow \theta + \alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{2}`

Subtract $α$ to return to $θ$

$θ = \frac{π}{2} - 0 . 92729 \dots = 0 . 64350 \dots$

Round to 3 significant figures as the question asks

$θ = 0 . 644$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The greatest value $5$. This follows from part (a) with no further calculation, since the greatest value of a sine is $1$. This mark follows through from your own value of $R$.
> 
> **B1**: The value $θ = 0 . 644$, correct to 3 significant figures. Accept answers which round to $0 . 644$. This comes from solving $θ + α = \frac{π}{2}$, and it follows through from your own $α$. An answer in degrees `\left( 36.9° \right)` is treated as a misreading of the question.

parts.problemMd:
Show that the equation

$3  \text{tan}^{2} x = 18 - 2  \text{sec}  x$

can be expressed as

$3  \text{sec}^{2} x + 2  \text{sec}  x - 21 = 0$
parts.solutionMd:
Use the identity $1 + \text{tan}^{2} x \equiv \text{sec}^{2} x$ to write everything in terms of $\text{sec}  x$

$\text{tan}^{2} x \equiv \text{sec}^{2} x - 1$

Substitute into the equation

`3 \left( \text{sec}^2 x - 1 \right) = 18 - 2 \; \text{sec} \; x`

**[M1]**

Expand the bracket and collect every term on one side

$3  \text{sec}^{2} x - 3 = 18 - 2  \text{sec}  x$

**Final answer:** $3  \text{sec}^{2} x + 2  \text{sec}  x - 21 = 0$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $1 + \text{tan}^{2} x \equiv \text{sec}^{2} x$ to replace $\text{tan}^{2} x$. The identity does not have to be quoted as a separate line, and using it anywhere in the working earns this mark.
> 
> **A1**: The printed quadratic reached, with all terms on one side. Because the answer is given, every line must be correct and the $x$ must be present throughout. This part only asks you to reach the quadratic, so there is no need to factorise or solve it here.

parts.problemMd:
Hence solve the equation

$3  \text{tan}^{2} x = 18 - 2  \text{sec}  x$

for $- π \leq x \leq π$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the quadratic from part (a), $3  \text{sec}^{2}  x + 2  \text{sec}  x - 21 = 0$, and factorise it

`\left( 3 \; \text{sec} \; x - 7 \right) \left( \text{sec} \; x + 3 \right) = 0`

Set each factor equal to zero

$\text{sec}  x = \frac{7}{3}$* or *$\text{sec}  x = - 3$

**[M1]**

Use the definition of the secant function to turn each root into a cosine

$\text{cos}  x = \frac{3}{7}$* or *$\text{cos}  x = - \frac{1}{3}$

**[A1]**

Take the inverse cosine of each value, keeping the unrounded results

`x = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( \dfrac{3}{7} \right) = 1.12788 \ldots`

`x = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( -\dfrac{1}{3} \right) = 1.91063 \ldots`

**[A1]**

The cosine curve is symmetrical about the vertical axis, so `\text{cos} \; x = \text{cos} \left( -x \right)` gives a negative partner for each value

$x = - 1 . 12788 \dots$* and *$x = - 1 . 91063 \dots$

Round each of the four values to 3 significant figures as the question asks

$x = - 1 . 91 ,  - 1 . 13 ,  1 . 13 ,  1 . 91$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Solving the three term quadratic from part (a) to obtain at least one value of $\text{sec}  x$. Factorising, the quadratic formula and completing the square are all accepted.
> 
> **A1**: Both values of $\text{cos}  x$, which are $\frac{3}{7}$ and $- \frac{1}{3}$. Reaching only the values of $\text{sec}  x$ is not enough for this mark, since the reciprocal step is needed before the inverse cosine.
> 
> **A1**: Two correct values of $x$, for example $1 . 13$ and $1 . 91$.
> 
> **A1**: All four values $x = \pm 1 . 13$ and $\pm 1 . 91$, correct to 3 significant figures, with no others inside $- π \leq x \leq π$. Accept answers which round to these. This mark follows through from your own values, so the negative of each of your positive answers is credited. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\text{cos}  2 θ = \text{cos}  θ - 1$

for $- π \leq θ \leq π$, giving your answers in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
The right hand side is written in $\text{cos}  θ$, so choose the form of the double angle identity that is also in cosine only

$\text{cos}  2 θ \equiv 2  \text{cos}^{2} θ - 1$

Substitute it into the equation

$2  \text{cos}^{2} θ - 1 = \text{cos}  θ - 1$

**[M1]**

The $- 1$ on each side cancels, leaving only two terms

$2  \text{cos}^{2} θ - \text{cos}  θ = 0$

**[A1]**

Factorise, taking out the common factor of $\text{cos}  θ$

`\text{cos} \; \theta \left( 2 \; \text{cos} \; \theta - 1 \right) = 0`

Set each factor equal to zero

$\text{cos}  θ = 0$* or *$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{1}{2}$

**[M1]**

Take the first value and use the inverse cosine to find the principal value

`\theta = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( 0 \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}`

Use the symmetry of the cosine curve, `\text{cos} \; \theta = \text{cos} \left( -\theta \right)`, for its partner

$θ = - \frac{π}{2}$

**[A1]**

Take the second value and find its principal value the same way

`\theta = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{2} \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}`

Apply the same symmetry for its partner

$θ = - \frac{π}{3}$

All four values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$θ = - \frac{π}{2} ,  - \frac{π}{3} ,  \frac{π}{3} ,  \frac{π}{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using a correct form of the double angle identity for $\text{cos}  2 θ$ to produce an equation in one trigonometric function. Choosing $2  \text{cos}^{2} θ - 1$ is the efficient route because the right hand side is already in cosine, but $1 - 2  \text{sin}^{2} θ$ or $\text{cos}^{2} θ - \text{sin}^{2} θ$ followed by $\text{sin}^{2} θ \equiv 1 - \text{cos}^{2} θ$ reaches the same place and earns this mark.
> 
> **A1**: The two term quadratic $2  \text{cos}^{2} θ - \text{cos}  θ = 0$, or any correct equivalent with all terms on one side.
> 
> **M1**: Factorising and solving to obtain at least one value of $\text{cos}  θ$. Do not divide through by $\text{cos}  θ$: that loses the whole $\text{cos}  θ = 0$ branch and with it half the answers.
> 
> **A1**: Any two correct exact values of $θ$.
> 
> **A1**: All four correct exact values, with no others inside $- π \leq θ \leq π$. The answers must be exact and in terms of $π$ as the question asks. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd: Sketch the graph of $y = \text{cot}^{2} θ$ for $- 2 π \leq θ \leq 2 π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Start from the cotangent curve, since squaring it gives the required graph

$\text{cot}  θ = \frac{\text{cos}θ}{\text{sin}θ}$

The cotangent is undefined wherever the sine is zero, and squaring does not change that, so these are the vertical asymptotes

$\text{sin}  θ = 0 \Rightarrow θ = - 2 π ,  - π ,  0 ,  π ,  2 π$

**[B1]**

The graph meets the axis wherever the cotangent is zero, which is where the cosine is zero

$\text{cot}  θ = 0 \Rightarrow θ = - \frac{3π}{2} ,  - \frac{π}{2} ,  \frac{π}{2} ,  \frac{3π}{2}$

**[B1]**

Squaring makes every value positive, so the curve never drops below the axis and each of those four points is a minimum where it just touches
