![Graph of y = cot squared theta for theta between minus 2 pi and 2 pi, showing four U shaped branches all lying on or above the horizontal axis, each touching the axis at its lowest point, with the touch points at theta = minus 3 pi over 2, minus pi over 2, pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2, and dashed vertical asymptotes at theta = minus 2 pi, minus pi, 0, pi and 2 pi](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/trigonometry/further-trigonometric-equations/assets/004-graph-of-y-cot-squared-theta-for-theta-between-m.png)

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: All five asymptotes located at $θ = - 2 π$, $- π$, $0$, $π$ and $2 π$. Accept them drawn as dashed vertical lines on the sketch or written as equations beside it.
> 
> **B1**: The four points where the curve meets the axis, at $θ = \pm \frac{π}{2}$ and $\pm \frac{3π}{2}$. Accept these marked on the axis or given as coordinates.
> 
> **B1**: Correct shape of all four branches, each a U lying entirely on or above the horizontal axis and touching it at its lowest point, curving away towards its asymptotes without touching them. Because the function is squared, no part of the curve may go below the axis. The graph must cover the whole of $- 2 π \leq θ \leq 2 π$ with nothing drawn outside it.

parts.problemMd:
By drawing suitable horizontal lines on your sketch, show how the number of real roots of the equation

$\text{cot}^{2} θ = k$

for $- 2 π \leq θ \leq 2 π$, where $k$ is a constant, can be $0$, $4$ or $8$.
parts.solutionMd:
The roots of the equation are the values of $θ$ where the horizontal line $y = k$ meets the curve $y = \text{cot}^{2} θ$, so counting roots means counting intersections

![The graph of y = cot squared theta from part (a) with three horizontal lines drawn across it: one below the axis labelled k less than 0 which misses the curve completely, one along the axis labelled k = 0 which touches each of the four branches at its lowest point with the four contacts marked by crosses, and one above the axis labelled k greater than 0 which cuts every branch twice with the eight crossings marked by crosses](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/trigonometry/further-trigonometric-equations/assets/005-the-graph-of-y-cot-squared-theta-from-part-a-wit.png)

**[B1]**

Take each case in turn, starting with a line below the axis, where the curve never reaches

$k < 0 \Rightarrow \text{no intersections, so} 0 \text{real roots}$

A line along the axis is tangent to each branch at its lowest point, touching it once rather than cutting it twice

$k = 0 \Rightarrow 4 \text{intersections, so} 4 \text{real roots}$

Any line above the axis cuts each of the four branches twice

$k > 0 \Rightarrow 8 \text{intersections, so} 8 \text{real roots}$

$k < 0 \text{gives} 0 \text{roots} ,  k = 0 \text{gives} 4 \text{roots} ,  k > 0 \text{gives} 8 \text{roots}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Three horizontal lines drawn on the sketch in the three distinct positions, one below the axis, one along the axis and one above it, together with the idea that a root corresponds to an intersection of $y = k$ with the curve. Marking the intersections with crosses or dots is the clearest way to show the counting.
> 
> **B1**: All three cases correctly matched to their number of roots: $0$ roots when $k < 0$, $4$ when $k = 0$ and $8$ when $k > 0$. All three are needed for this mark. The case $k = 0$ is the one to watch: the line lies along the axis and touches each branch at its minimum instead of cutting it, so each branch contributes one root rather than two, giving $4$ and not $8$.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\text{cot}^{2} θ = \text{sec}^{2} θ - 1$

for $0 ^{\circ} \leq θ \leq 360 ^{\circ}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the identity $\text{sec}^{2} θ \equiv 1 + \text{tan}^{2} θ$ on the right hand side, where the two $1$s cancel

`\text{sec}^2 \theta - 1 = \left( 1 + \text{tan}^2 \theta \right) - 1 = \text{tan}^2 \theta`

Write the left hand side in terms of $\text{tan}  θ$ as well

$\text{cot}^{2} θ = \frac{1}{\text{tan}^{2}θ}$

So the equation becomes a single equation in $\text{tan}  θ$

$\frac{1}{\text{tan}^{2}θ} = \text{tan}^{2} θ \Rightarrow \text{tan}^{4} θ = 1$

**[M1]**

Take the square root of each side

$\text{tan}^{2} θ = \pm 1$

A square cannot be negative, so discard $\text{tan}^{2} θ = - 1$ and keep the positive root

$\text{tan}^{2} θ = 1 \Rightarrow \text{tan}  θ = \pm 1$

**[A1]**

Take the inverse tangent of each value

`\text{tan}^{-1} \left( 1 \right) = 45°`* and *`\text{tan}^{-1} \left( -1 \right) = -45°`

The value $- 45 ^{\circ}$ lies outside the interval, so add the $180 ^{\circ}$ period to each value until every solution inside the interval is found. Start from $45 ^{\circ}$

$θ = 45 ^{\circ}$

$θ = 45 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 225 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

Now bring $- 45 ^{\circ}$ into the interval and continue

$θ = - 45 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 135 ^{\circ}$

$θ = 135 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 315 ^{\circ}$

All four values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$θ = 45 ^{\circ} ,  135 ^{\circ} ,  225 ^{\circ} ,  315 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using $\text{sec}^{2} θ \equiv 1 + \text{tan}^{2} θ$ together with $\text{cot}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{tan}θ}$ to reduce the equation to one trigonometric function, reaching $\text{tan}^{4} θ = 1$ or an equivalent such as $\text{cot}^{2} θ = \text{tan}^{2} θ$. Working in sines and cosines throughout reaches the same place and earns this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $\text{tan}  θ = \pm 1$. Both signs are needed. The step $\text{tan}^{2} θ = \pm 1$ should be resolved by rejecting $- 1$, since a square cannot be negative; writing that reason down is worth the moment it takes, because it explains why only two values of $\text{tan}  θ$ survive from a fourth power equation.
> 
> **A1**: Any two correct values of $θ$.
> 
> **A1**: All four values $θ = 45 ^{\circ}$, $135 ^{\circ}$, $225 ^{\circ}$ and $315 ^{\circ}$, with no others inside $0 ^{\circ} \leq θ \leq 360 ^{\circ}$. Note that `\text{tan}^{-1} \left( -1 \right) = -45°` is outside the interval and is not itself a solution, so the period must be added to bring its partners into range. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd: Solve the equation $\text{sec}^{2} 2 x = 1 + \text{tan}  2 x$ for $0 ^{\circ} \leq x \leq 180 ^{\circ}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the identity $\text{sec}^{2} θ \equiv 1 + \text{tan}^{2} θ$ on the left hand side

$1 + \text{tan}^{2} 2 x = 1 + \text{tan}  2 x$

**[M1]**

The $1$ on each side cancels, so collect the remaining terms and factorise

$\text{tan}^{2} 2 x - \text{tan}  2 x = 0$

`\text{tan} \; 2x \left( \text{tan} \; 2x - 1 \right) = 0`

**[A1]**

Set each factor equal to zero

$\text{tan}  2 x = 0$* or *$\text{tan}  2 x = 1$

Substitute for the double angle and change the interval to match by doubling each part

$\text{Let}  ϕ = 2 x ,$* so *$0 ^{\circ} \leq ϕ \leq 360 ^{\circ}$

Take the first factor, where the tangent is zero at every multiple of its $180 ^{\circ}$ period

$ϕ = 0 ^{\circ} ,  180 ^{\circ} ,  360 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Take the second factor and use the inverse tangent, then add the period

`\phi = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( 1 \right) = 45°`

Add the $180 ^{\circ}$ period for the next value inside the interval

$ϕ = 45 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 225 ^{\circ}$

Halve every value of $ϕ$ to return to $x$

$x = 0 ^{\circ} ,  90 ^{\circ} ,  180 ^{\circ}$* and *$x = 22 . 5 ^{\circ} ,  112 . 5 ^{\circ}$

All five values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$x = 0 ^{\circ} ,  22 . 5 ^{\circ} ,  90 ^{\circ} ,  112 . 5 ^{\circ} ,  180 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $\text{sec}^{2} 2 x \equiv 1 + \text{tan}^{2} 2 x$. The identity does not have to be quoted separately, and using it anywhere earns this mark.
> 
> **A1**: The factorised form `\text{tan} \; 2x \left( \text{tan} \; 2x - 1 \right) = 0`, or the equivalent $\text{tan}^{2} 2 x - \text{tan}  2 x = 0$ together with both values of $\text{tan}  2 x$.
> 
> **M1**: A correct method for values of $2 x$ from either factor, working in degrees.
> 
> **A1**: All five values $x = 0 ^{\circ}$, $22 . 5 ^{\circ}$, $90 ^{\circ}$, $112 . 5 ^{\circ}$ and $180 ^{\circ}$, with no others inside $0 ^{\circ} \leq x \leq 180 ^{\circ}$. Note that both ends of the interval are solutions, so leaving out $0 ^{\circ}$ or $180 ^{\circ}$ loses this mark. Do not divide the equation through by $\text{tan}  2 x$: that removes the $\text{tan}  2 x = 0$ factor and with it three of the five answers. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Given that

`\text{sin} \left( 2A - B \right) = \tfrac{1}{4} \left( \sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2} \right)`

where $3 A = 4 B$ and $60 ^{\circ} < B < A < 300 ^{\circ}$, find the value of $A$ and the value of $B$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the linear relation to write $B$ in terms of $A$

$3 A = 4 B \Rightarrow B = \frac{3}{4} A$

Substitute into the angle so the equation involves $A$ only

$2 A - B = 2 A - \frac{3}{4} A = \frac{5A}{4}$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse sine of the given exact value

`\text{sin}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{4} \left( \sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2} \right) \right) = 75°`

Change the interval to match. Since $60 ^{\circ} < A < 300 ^{\circ}$, multiply through by $\frac{5}{4}$

$75 ^{\circ} < \frac{5A}{4} < 375 ^{\circ}$

Use the symmetry of the sine curve, `\text{sin} \; \phi = \text{sin} \left( 180° - \phi \right)`, to find the values inside that interval

$\frac{5A}{4} = 75 ^{\circ}$* or *$\frac{5A}{4} = 105 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Solve each for $A$, then test it against the condition

$\frac{5A}{4} = 75 ^{\circ} \Rightarrow A = 60 ^{\circ}$

This one fails the condition $60 ^{\circ} < A$, because the inequality is strict, so reject it and take the other value

$\frac{5A}{4} = 105 ^{\circ} \Rightarrow A = 84 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

Find $B$ from the linear relation

`B = \tfrac{3}{4} \left( 84° \right) = 63°`

Check the condition holds, since $60 ^{\circ} < 63 ^{\circ} < 84 ^{\circ} < 300 ^{\circ}$

$A = 84 ^{\circ} ,  B = 63 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using $3 A = 4 B$ to eliminate one variable, reaching an equation in a single variable such as `\text{sin} \left( \tfrac{5A}{4} \right) = \tfrac{1}{4} \left( \sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2} \right)`. Eliminating $A$ instead of $B$ is equally acceptable.
> 
> **M1**: Evaluating the inverse sine to reach $75 ^{\circ}$, together with use of the symmetry of the sine curve to obtain the second value $105 ^{\circ}$. Both are needed for this mark, since the first one is the value that gets rejected.
> 
> **A1**: $A = 84 ^{\circ}$, having rejected $A = 60 ^{\circ}$. The rejection matters: $\frac{5A}{4} = 75 ^{\circ}$ gives $A = 60 ^{\circ}$, which fails the strict inequality $60 ^{\circ} < A$, so it is not a solution. Simply not mentioning it is weaker than writing the rejection down.
> 
> **A1**: $B = 63 ^{\circ}$, with the pair checked against $60 ^{\circ} < B < A < 300 ^{\circ}$. This mark follows through from your own value of $A$.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\frac{\text{cos}x}{\text{cosec}x} - \text{cot}  x = 0$

for $- 2 π \leq x \leq 2 π$, giving your answers in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the definitions of the cosecant and cotangent functions to write everything in sines and cosines

$\frac{\text{cos}x}{\text{cosec}x} = \text{cos}  x  \text{sin}  x$* and *$\text{cot}  x = \frac{\text{cos}x}{\text{sin}x}$

**[M1]**

Substitute both into the equation and take out the common factor of $\text{cos}  x$

`\text{cos} \; x \; \text{sin} \; x - \dfrac{\text{cos} \; x}{\text{sin} \; x} = \text{cos} \; x \left( \text{sin} \; x - \dfrac{1}{\text{sin} \; x} \right) = 0`

Combine the bracket over the common denominator $\text{sin}  x$

`\text{cos} \; x \left( \dfrac{\text{sin}^2 x - 1}{\text{sin} \; x} \right) = 0`

Use $\text{sin}^{2} x - 1 \equiv - \text{cos}^{2} x$, which collapses the whole expression

$\frac{-\text{cos}^{3}x}{\text{sin}x} = 0$

**[A1]**

A fraction is zero only when its numerator is zero, so the single condition is

$\text{cos}^{3} x = 0 \Rightarrow \text{cos}  x = 0$

Take the inverse cosine for the first value, then use the $2 π$ period and the symmetry of the curve

`x = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( 0 \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}`

Use the symmetry of the cosine curve, `\text{cos} \; x = \text{cos} \left( -x \right)`, for its partner

$x = - \frac{π}{2}$

**[A1]**

The interval reaches $\pm 2 π$, so the cosine is zero twice more

$x = \frac{3π}{2}$* and *$x = - \frac{3π}{2}$

All four values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$x = - \frac{3π}{2} ,  - \frac{π}{2} ,  \frac{π}{2} ,  \frac{3π}{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using $\text{cosec}  x = \frac{1}{\text{sin}x}$ and $\text{cot}  x = \frac{\text{cos}x}{\text{sin}x}$ to write the equation in sines and cosines only.
> 
> **A1**: Reducing to a single condition in one function, which means reaching $\text{cos}^{3} x = 0$ or the equivalent factorised form `\text{cos} \; x \left( \text{sin}^2 x - 1 \right) = 0`. Taking the factorised route and splitting into the two cases $\text{cos}  x = 0$ and $\text{sin}  x = \pm 1$ is equally valid and earns this mark. Note if you do that these two cases have exactly the same solutions, because the sine is $\pm 1$ precisely where the cosine is zero, so they must not be counted twice.
> 
> **A1**: Any two correct exact values of $x$.
> 
> **A1**: All four correct exact values, with no others inside $- 2 π \leq x \leq 2 π$. The answers must be exact and in terms of $π$ as the question asks. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd: Show that $6  \text{cos}  θ - 8  \text{sin}  θ$ can be expressed in the form `R \; \text{cos} \left( \theta + \alpha \right)`, where $R > 0$ and $α$ is an acute angle measured in radians.
parts.solutionMd:
Expand `R \; \text{cos} \left( \theta + \alpha \right)` using the `\text{cos} \left( A + B \right)` formula from the formula booklet, then equate it to the given expression

$6  \text{cos}  θ - 8  \text{sin}  θ = R  \text{cos}  α  \text{cos}  θ - R  \text{sin}  α  \text{sin}  θ$

Compare the coefficients of $\text{cos}  θ$ and of $\text{sin}  θ$

$R  \text{cos}  α = 6$* and *$R  \text{sin}  α = 8$

**[M1]**

Find $R$ by squaring and adding, since $\text{cos}^{2} α + \text{sin}^{2} α \equiv 1$

$R^{2} = 6^{2} + 8^{2} = 100 \Rightarrow R = 10$

**[A1]**

Find $α$ by dividing the second equation by the first

`\text{tan} \; \alpha = \dfrac{8}{6} \Rightarrow \alpha = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right) = 0.92729 \ldots`

This is acute, as required, so the expression can be written as

`6 \; \text{cos} \; \theta - 8 \; \text{sin} \; \theta \equiv 10 \; \text{cos} \left( \theta + 0.927 \right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Expanding `R \; \text{cos} \left( \theta + \alpha \right)` correctly and comparing coefficients to reach $R  \text{cos}  α = 6$ and $R  \text{sin}  α = 8$. Note the minus sign in the expansion of `\text{cos} \left( A + B \right)`, which is what makes the coefficient of $\text{sin}  θ$ come out as $+ 8$ rather than $- 8$.
> 
> **A1**: $R = 10$. The value of $R$ must be exact; where it is not a whole number a surd is required and a decimal is not accepted.
> 
> **A1**: $α = 0 . 927$, with the answer confirmed as acute. An unevaluated `\text{tan}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{4}{3} \right)` is not enough here, since the question asks for an angle in radians.

parts.problemMd:
Hence solve the equation

$3  \text{cos}  θ - 4  \text{sin}  θ - 2 = 0$

for $0 \leq θ \leq 2 π$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
The expression here is exactly half of the one in part (a), so halve that result

`3 \; \text{cos} \; \theta - 4 \; \text{sin} \; \theta = \tfrac{1}{2} \left( 6 \; \text{cos} \; \theta - 8 \; \text{sin} \; \theta \right) = 5 \; \text{cos} \left( \theta + 0.92729 \ldots \right)`

**[M1]**

Substitute into the equation and rearrange

`5 \; \text{cos} \left( \theta + \alpha \right) = 2 \Rightarrow \text{cos} \left( \theta + \alpha \right) = \tfrac{2}{5}`

Substitute for the whole angle

$\text{Let}  ϕ = θ + α$

Find the interval for $ϕ$ by substituting each endpoint of the interval for $θ$ into $θ + α$

$θ = 0 \Rightarrow ϕ = 0 + 0 . 92729 \dots = 0 . 92729 \dots$

$θ = 2 π \Rightarrow ϕ = 2 π + 0 . 92729 \dots = 7 . 21048 \dots$

$0 . 92729 \dots \leq ϕ \leq 7 . 21048 \dots$

Take the inverse cosine for the principal value

`\phi = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{2}{5} \right) = 1.15927 \ldots`

Use the symmetry of the cosine curve about $2 π$ for the second value inside the shifted interval

$ϕ = 2 π - 1 . 15927 \dots = 5 . 12390 \dots$

**[A1]**

Subtract $α$ from each value to return to $θ$

$θ = 1 . 15927 \dots - 0 . 92729 \dots = 0 . 23198 \dots$

$θ = 5 . 12390 \dots - 0 . 92729 \dots = 4 . 19661 \dots$

Round each to 3 significant figures as the question asks

$θ = 0 . 232 ,  θ = 4 . 20$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Recognising that $3  \text{cos}  θ - 4  \text{sin}  θ$ is half of the expression in part (a), and so using `5 \; \text{cos} \left( \theta + \alpha \right)` with the same $α$. Working the $R$ form out again from scratch for the halved expression is equally acceptable and reaches the same place, since the question allows any correct route.
> 
> **A1**: A correct second value of $θ + α$, which is $5 . 12$ or better. Shifting the interval is what shows this value belongs and the negative partner does not.
> 
> **A1**: Both answers $θ = 0 . 232$ and $4 . 20$, correct to 3 significant figures, with no others inside $0 \leq θ \leq 2 π$. Accept answers which round to these. Do not round the intermediate values. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd: State the least value of $6  \text{cos}  θ - 8  \text{sin}  θ$ and find the least positive value of $θ$ for which this least value occurs. Give your value of $θ$ correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
The cosine of any angle is at least $- 1$, so the least value of `10 \; \text{cos} \left( \theta + \alpha \right)` occurs when the cosine equals $- 1$

$\text{Least value} = - 10$

**[B1]**

Find the angle at which the cosine first reaches $- 1$

`\text{cos} \left( \theta + \alpha \right) = -1 \Rightarrow \theta + \alpha = \pi`

Subtract $α$ to return to $θ$

$θ = π - 0 . 92729 \dots = 2 . 21429 \dots$

Round to 3 significant figures as the question asks

$θ = 2 . 21$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The least value $- 10$. This follows from part (a) with no further calculation, since the least value of a cosine is $- 1$. This mark follows through from your own value of $R$.
> 
> **B1**: The value $θ = 2 . 21$, correct to 3 significant figures, from solving $θ + α = π$. Accept answers which round to $2 . 21$, and this mark follows through from your own $α$. Note this is the least positive value: the cosine also equals $- 1$ at $θ + α = 3 π$, but that gives a larger $θ$. An answer in degrees `\left( 126.9° \right)` is treated as a misreading of the question.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$2  \text{cot}^{2} x = 8 - \text{cosec}  x$

for $- π \leq x \leq π$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures where appropriate.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the identity $1 + \text{cot}^{2} x \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x$ to write the left hand side in terms of $\text{cosec}  x$

$\text{cot}^{2} x \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x - 1$

Substitute and collect every term on one side

`2 \left( \text{cosec}^2 x - 1 \right) = 8 - \text{cosec} \; x`

$2  \text{cosec}^{2} x + \text{cosec}  x - 10 = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise the quadratic and set each factor to zero

`\left( 2 \; \text{cosec} \; x + 5 \right) \left( \text{cosec} \; x - 2 \right) = 0`

$\text{cosec}  x = - \frac{5}{2}$* or *$\text{cosec}  x = 2$

Take reciprocals to turn each root into a sine

$\text{sin}  x = - \frac{2}{5}$* or *$\text{sin}  x = \frac{1}{2}$

**[A1]**

Take the second value first, since it gives exact answers. Use the inverse sine, then the symmetry `\text{sin} \; x = \text{sin} \left( \pi - x \right)`

`x = \text{sin}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{2} \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}`

Apply the symmetry for the second value

$x = π - \frac{π}{6} = \frac{5π}{6}$

**[A1]**

Now take the negative value, where the inverse sine gives a negative principal value

`x = \text{sin}^{-1} \left( -\tfrac{2}{5} \right) = -0.41151 \ldots`

Use the same symmetry, measuring from $- π$ this time, for the other negative solution

$x = - π + 0 . 41151 \dots = - 2 . 73007 \dots$

Give the exact answers exactly and round the other two to 3 significant figures

$x = - 2 . 73 ,  - 0 . 412 ,  \frac{π}{6} ,  \frac{5π}{6}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $1 + \text{cot}^{2} x \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x$ to form the three term quadratic $2  \text{cosec}^{2} x + \text{cosec}  x - 10 = 0$, or a correct equivalent with all terms on one side.
> 
> **A1**: Both values of $\text{sin}  x$, which are $\frac{1}{2}$ and $- \frac{2}{5}$. Factorising, the formula and completing the square are all accepted for solving the quadratic. Stopping at the values of $\text{cosec}  x$ is not enough, since the reciprocal step is needed next.
> 
> **A1**: Both exact values $x = \frac{π}{6}$ and $\frac{5π}{6}$. These come from $\text{sin}  x = \frac{1}{2}$ and should be left exact, since they are standard values.
> 
> **A1**: Both remaining values $x = - 0 . 412$ and $- 2 . 73$, correct to 3 significant figures, with no others inside $- π \leq x \leq π$. Accept answers which round to these. Note that $\text{sin}  x = - \frac{2}{5}$ has both its solutions in the negative half of the interval, so the second one is found by measuring from $- π$ rather than from $π$. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$8  \text{cos}^{4} θ - 5  \text{cos}  2 θ - 2 = 0$

for $0 \leq θ \leq π$, giving your answers in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
The rest of the equation is in $\text{cos}  θ$, so choose the double angle form that is also in cosine only

$\text{cos}  2 θ \equiv 2  \text{cos}^{2} θ - 1$

Substitute it in

`8 \; \text{cos}^4 \theta - 5 \left( 2 \; \text{cos}^2 \theta - 1 \right) - 2 = 0`

**[M1]**

Expand and collect, which leaves a quadratic in $\text{cos}^{2} θ$

$8  \text{cos}^{4} θ - 10  \text{cos}^{2} θ + 3 = 0$

**[A1]**

Factorise, treating $\text{cos}^{2} θ$ as the variable

`\left( 4 \; \text{cos}^2 \theta - 3 \right) \left( 2 \; \text{cos}^2 \theta - 1 \right) = 0`

$\text{cos}^{2} θ = \frac{3}{4}$* or *$\text{cos}^{2} θ = \frac{1}{2}$

Take the square root of each, keeping both signs

$\text{cos}  θ = \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$* or *$\text{cos}  θ = \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

**[M1]**

Take the first pair. On $0 \leq θ \leq π$ the cosine takes each value once, and the negative value gives $π$ minus the first

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow θ = \frac{π}{6}$

$\text{cos}  θ = - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow θ = π - \frac{π}{6} = \frac{5π}{6}$

**[A1]**

Take the second pair the same way

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow θ = \frac{π}{4}$

$\text{cos}  θ = - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow θ = π - \frac{π}{4} = \frac{3π}{4}$

All four values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$θ = \frac{π}{6} ,  \frac{π}{4} ,  \frac{3π}{4} ,  \frac{5π}{6}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using a correct form of the double angle identity for $\text{cos}  2 θ$ to produce an equation in $\text{cos}  θ$ alone. Choosing $2  \text{cos}^{2} θ - 1$ is the efficient route because the rest of the equation is already in cosine.
> 
> **A1**: The quadratic $8  \text{cos}^{4} θ - 10  \text{cos}^{2} θ + 3 = 0$, or a correct equivalent with all terms on one side.
> 
> **M1**: Solving to obtain at least one value of $\text{cos}^{2} θ$ and taking the square root to reach a value of $\text{cos}  θ$. Treating $\text{cos}^{2} θ$ as a single variable is the clearest way in; a substitution such as $u = \text{cos}^{2} θ$ is fine. Both square roots are needed, since dropping the negative ones loses half the answers.
> 
> **A1**: Any two correct exact values of $θ$.
> 
> **A1**: All four correct exact values, with no others inside $0 \leq θ \leq π$. The answers must be exact and in terms of $π$ as the question asks. Accept $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ as an equivalent form of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ along the way. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Find the set of values of the constant $k$ for which the equation

$\text{cosec}  θ = k$

for $- π \leq θ \leq 2 π$, has

(i) no real roots,

(ii) exactly 1 real root,

(iii) exactly 2 real roots,

(iv) exactly 4 real roots.
parts.solutionMd:
The roots are the values of $θ$ where the line $y = k$ meets the curve $y = \text{cosec}  θ$, so counting roots means counting intersections

Sketch the curve over the interval, using the sine curve underneath as a guide. The asymptotes sit where $\text{sin}  θ = 0$

$\text{sin}  θ = 0 \Rightarrow θ = - π ,  0 ,  π ,  2 π$

Note the interval is not symmetric, so it holds three branches: two below the axis, each with a highest point of $- 1$, and only one above the axis, with a lowest point of $1$

![Graph of y = cosec theta for theta between minus pi and 2 pi, showing three branches with dashed vertical asymptotes at theta = minus pi, 0, pi and 2 pi. One branch lies above the horizontal axis on 0 to pi with its lowest point at (pi over 2, 1). Two branches lie below the axis, on minus pi to 0 and on pi to 2 pi, each with a highest point of minus 1 at theta = minus pi over 2 and theta = 3 pi over 2. A horizontal line y = k is drawn below the value minus 1, cutting each of the two lower branches twice at four marked points](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/trigonometry/further-trigonometric-equations/assets/003-graph-of-y-cosec-theta-for-theta-between-minus-p.png)

(i)

A line between the two turning values misses the curve completely, since the curve takes no value strictly between $- 1$ and $1$

$- 1 < k < 1$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Raising the line to $1$ makes it touch the single upper branch at its lowest point, and there is only one such branch in this interval

$k = 1$

**[B1]**

(iii)

There are two ways to get exactly two roots. Lowering the line to $- 1$ makes it touch each of the two lower branches once, and raising it above $1$ makes it cut the single upper branch twice

**Final answer:** $k = - 1$** or **$k > 1$

**[B1]**

(iv)

Taking the line below $- 1$ makes it cut both lower branches twice each

$k < - 1$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: (i) $- 1 < k < 1$. Accept any equivalent form, including `\left| k \right| < 1` and interval notation such as `\left( -1, \; 1 \right)`. The inequalities must be strict, since $k = \pm 1$ each give roots.
> 
> **B1**: (ii) $k = 1$ only. The interval contains just one branch above the axis, so the line $y = 1$ touches the curve exactly once.
> 
> **B1**: (iii) Both $k = - 1$ and $k > 1$ are needed for this mark. These are two different situations giving the same count: at $k = - 1$ the line is tangent to each of the two lower branches, giving one root from each; for $k > 1$ the line cuts the single upper branch twice. Finding only one of the two loses this mark.
> 
> **B1**: (iv) $k < - 1$. Each of the two lower branches is cut twice, giving four roots in total. It is worth noticing why there is no value of $k$ giving 3 roots: the branches come in a pair below the axis and singly above, so the counts jump from 2 to 4.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\text{cot}^{2} θ = 15 - 6  \text{cosec}  θ$

for $- 180 ^{\circ} \leq θ \leq 180 ^{\circ}$, giving your answers correct to 1 decimal place where appropriate.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the identity $1 + \text{cot}^{2} θ \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} θ$ to write the left hand side in terms of $\text{cosec}  θ$

$\text{cot}^{2} θ \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} θ - 1$

Substitute and collect every term on one side

$\text{cosec}^{2} θ - 1 = 15 - 6  \text{cosec}  θ$

$\text{cosec}^{2} θ + 6  \text{cosec}  θ - 16 = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise the quadratic and set each factor to zero

`\left( \text{cosec} \; \theta + 8 \right) \left( \text{cosec} \; \theta - 2 \right) = 0`

$\text{cosec}  θ = - 8$* or *$\text{cosec}  θ = 2$

Take reciprocals to turn each root into a sine

$\text{sin}  θ = - \frac{1}{8}$* or *$\text{sin}  θ = \frac{1}{2}$

**[A1]**

Take the second value, which gives exact answers. Use the inverse sine, then the symmetry `\text{sin} \; \theta = \text{sin} \left( 180° - \theta \right)`

`\theta = \text{sin}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{2} \right) = 30°`

Apply the symmetry for the second value

$θ = 180 ^{\circ} - 30 ^{\circ} = 150 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

Now take the negative value

`\theta = \text{sin}^{-1} \left( -\tfrac{1}{8} \right) = -7.18075 \ldots°`

Apply the same symmetry, measuring from $- 180 ^{\circ}$ this time

$θ = - 180 ^{\circ} + 7 . 18075 \dots ^{\circ} = - 172 . 81924 \dots ^{\circ}$

Give the exact answers exactly and round the other two to 1 decimal place

$θ = - 172 . 8 ^{\circ} ,  - 7 . 2 ^{\circ} ,  30 ^{\circ} ,  150 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $1 + \text{cot}^{2} θ \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} θ$ to form the three term quadratic $\text{cosec}^{2} θ + 6  \text{cosec}  θ - 16 = 0$, or a correct equivalent with all terms on one side.
> 
> **A1**: Both values of $\text{sin}  θ$, which are $\frac{1}{2}$ and $- \frac{1}{8}$. Factorising, the formula and completing the square are all accepted. Stopping at the values of $\text{cosec}  θ$ is not enough.
> 
> **A1**: Both values $θ = 30 ^{\circ}$ and $150 ^{\circ}$, from $\text{sin}  θ = \frac{1}{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Both values $θ = - 7 . 2 ^{\circ}$ and $- 172 . 8 ^{\circ}$, correct to 1 decimal place, with no others inside $- 180 ^{\circ} \leq θ \leq 180 ^{\circ}$. Accept answers which round to these. Because $\text{sin}  θ = - \frac{1}{8}$ is only just negative, both of its solutions lie near the ends of the negative half of the interval, so the second is found by measuring from $- 180 ^{\circ}$. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\text{sin}^{3} 3 θ - \text{sin}  3 θ  \text{cos}^{2} 3 θ = 0$

for $0 ^{\circ} \leq θ < 180 ^{\circ}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Take out the common factor of $\text{sin}  3 θ$

`\text{sin} \; 3\theta \left( \text{sin}^2 3\theta - \text{cos}^2 3\theta \right) = 0`

**[M1]**

Set each factor to zero

$\text{sin}  3 θ = 0$* or *$\text{sin}^{2} 3 θ - \text{cos}^{2} 3 θ = 0$

Take the second factor and divide every term by $\text{cos}^{2} 3 θ$, which is safe here because the sine and cosine are never both zero

$\frac{\text{sin}^{2}3θ}{\text{cos}^{2}3θ} - \frac{\text{cos}^{2}3θ}{\text{cos}^{2}3θ} = 0$

Use $\frac{\text{sin}3θ}{\text{cos}3θ} = \text{tan}  3 θ$ on the first term

$\text{tan}^{2} 3 θ - 1 = 0$

Rearrange to isolate the tangent

$\text{tan}^{2} 3 θ = 1$

Substitute for the tripled angle and change the interval to match by tripling each part

$\text{Let}  ϕ = 3 θ ,$* so *$0 ^{\circ} \leq ϕ < 540 ^{\circ}$

Take the first factor. The sine is zero at every multiple of $180 ^{\circ}$

$ϕ = 0 ^{\circ} ,  180 ^{\circ} ,  360 ^{\circ}$

$\text{(not} 540 ^{\circ} \text{, since the interval is strict)}$

**[M1]**

Take the second factor, where the square root gives two values of the tangent

$\text{tan}  ϕ = 1$* or *$\text{tan}  ϕ = - 1$

Take the positive value. The inverse tangent gives the first solution, and the tangent has period $180 ^{\circ}$

`\phi = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( 1 \right) = 45°`

Add the period, and then add it again, staying inside the interval

$ϕ = 45 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 225 ^{\circ}$

$ϕ = 225 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 405 ^{\circ}$

Now take the negative value. Here the inverse tangent is negative, so add the period to bring it into the interval

`\text{tan}^{-1} \left( -1 \right) = -45° \text{ (outside the interval)}`

$ϕ = - 45 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 135 ^{\circ}$

Add the period twice more, as before

$ϕ = 135 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 315 ^{\circ}$

$ϕ = 315 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 495 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

Divide every value of $ϕ$ by $3$ to return to $θ$

$θ = 0 ^{\circ} ,  60 ^{\circ} ,  120 ^{\circ}$* and *$θ = 15 ^{\circ} ,  75 ^{\circ} ,  135 ^{\circ}$* and *$θ = 45 ^{\circ} ,  105 ^{\circ} ,  165 ^{\circ}$

All nine values lie inside the interval, so give them together in order

$θ = 0 ^{\circ} ,  15 ^{\circ} ,  45 ^{\circ} ,  60 ^{\circ} ,  75 ^{\circ} ,  105 ^{\circ} ,  120 ^{\circ} ,  135 ^{\circ} ,  165 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Factorising to `\text{sin} \; 3\theta \left( \text{sin}^2 3\theta - \text{cos}^2 3\theta \right) = 0`. Do not divide the equation through by $\text{sin}  3 θ$: that removes the first factor and loses three of the nine answers.
> 
> **M1**: A correct method for values of $3 θ$ from either factor, with the interval tripled to $0 ^{\circ} \leq 3 θ < 540 ^{\circ}$. Getting that interval right is what makes the full answer set reachable. The bracket may be handled as $\text{tan}^{2} 3 θ = 1$, or by recognising $\text{sin}^{2} 3 θ - \text{cos}^{2} 3 θ \equiv - \text{cos}  6 θ$ and solving $\text{cos}  6 θ = 0$; both are correct and reach the same six values.
> 
> **A1**: At least four correct values of $θ$.
> 
> **A1**: All nine correct values, with no others inside $0 ^{\circ} \leq θ < 180 ^{\circ}$. Note the interval is strict at the top, so $θ = 180 ^{\circ}$ is excluded, but it is inclusive at the bottom, so $θ = 0 ^{\circ}$ must be given. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$5  \text{sin}  θ + 2  \text{cos}  θ = 3$

for $- π \leq θ \leq π$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Write the left hand side in the single form `R \; \text{sin} \left( \theta + \alpha \right)`, expanding with the `\text{sin} \left( A + B \right)` formula and comparing coefficients

$R  \text{cos}  α = 5$* and *$R  \text{sin}  α = 2$

Square and add for $R$, keeping it exact

$R^{2} = 5^{2} + 2^{2} = 29 \Rightarrow R = \sqrt{29}$

Find $α$ by dividing the second equation by the first, since $\frac{\text{sin}α}{\text{cos}α} = \text{tan}  α$

$\text{tan}  α = \frac{2}{5} \Rightarrow α = 0 . 38050 \dots$

**[M1]**

So the equation becomes a single sine equation

`\sqrt{29} \; \text{sin} \left( \theta + \alpha \right) = 3 \Rightarrow \text{sin} \left( \theta + \alpha \right) = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{29}}`

Substitute for the whole angle

$\text{Let}  ϕ = θ + α$

Find the interval for $ϕ$ by substituting each endpoint of the interval for $θ$ into $θ + α$

$θ = - π \Rightarrow ϕ = - π + 0 . 38050 \dots = - 2 . 76108 \dots$

$θ = π \Rightarrow ϕ = π + 0 . 38050 \dots = 3 . 52210 \dots$

$- 2 . 76108 \dots \leq ϕ \leq 3 . 52210 \dots$

Take the inverse sine for the principal value

`\phi = \text{sin}^{-1} \left( \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{29}} \right) = 0.59087 \ldots`

**[A1]**

Use the symmetry of the sine curve, `\text{sin} \; \phi = \text{sin} \left( \pi - \phi \right)`, for the second value, which also lies inside the shifted interval

$ϕ = π - 0 . 59087 \dots = 2 . 55072 \dots$

Subtract $α$ from each value to return to $θ$

$θ = 0 . 59087 \dots - 0 . 38050 \dots = 0 . 21036 \dots$

**[A1]**

$θ = 2 . 55072 \dots - 0 . 38050 \dots = 2 . 17021 \dots$

Round each to 3 significant figures as the question asks

$θ = 0 . 210 ,  θ = 2 . 17$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Reaching the single form, which means an exact $R = \sqrt{29}$ together with a correct method for $α$ such as $\text{tan}  α = \frac{2}{5}$. The value of $R$ must be exact here; a decimal such as $5 . 39$ used in the working is not accepted.
> 
> **A1**: A correct value of $θ + α$, which is $0 . 591$ or better.
> 
> **A1**: One correct value of $θ$, which is $0 . 210$.
> 
> **A1**: Both answers $θ = 0 . 210$ and $2 . 17$, with no others inside $- π \leq θ \leq π$. Accept answers which round to these. Do not round the intermediate values, and in particular do not replace $\sqrt{29}$ by $5 . 39$ partway through. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd: State the greatest value of $5  \text{sin}  θ + 2  \text{cos}  θ$ and the second positive value of $θ$ for which it occurs. Give your value of $θ$ correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
The sine of any angle is at most $1$, so the greatest value is $R$ itself, and $R$ is exact

$\text{Greatest value} = \sqrt{29}$

**[B1]**

It occurs when the sine equals $1$, which happens once per period. Find the first such angle, then add a full period for the second

`\text{sin} \left( \theta + \alpha \right) = 1 \Rightarrow \theta + \alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{2}`* or *$\frac{π}{2} + 2 π$

Subtract $α$ from the second of these to get the second positive value

$θ = \frac{5π}{2} - 0 . 38050 \dots = 7 . 47347 \dots$

Round to 3 significant figures as the question asks

$θ = 7 . 47$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The greatest value $\sqrt{29}$, which follows from part (a) with no further calculation. Give it as an exact surd: the question's accuracy instruction applies only to $θ$, so there is nothing here to round, and CIE requires an exact $R$ in any case. Accept an exact equivalent. This mark follows through from your own value of $R$.
> 
> **B1**: The value $θ = 7 . 47$, correct to 3 significant figures. Accept answers which round to $7 . 47$, and this mark follows through from your own $α$. The second positive value is wanted, so a full period of $2 π$ must be added to the first: the first positive value is $1 . 19$, which does not earn this mark. Note this lies outside the interval used in part (a), which is fine, because part (b) sets no interval.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$3  \text{sec}^{4} θ + 16 = 16 + 16  \text{tan}^{2} θ$

for $- π \leq θ \leq π$, giving your answers in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Factorise the right hand side, then use the identity $1 + \text{tan}^{2} θ \equiv \text{sec}^{2} θ$ on the bracket

`16 + 16 \; \text{tan}^2 \theta = 16 \left( 1 + \text{tan}^2 \theta \right) = 16 \; \text{sec}^2 \theta`

**[M1]**

The equation is now entirely in $\text{sec}  θ$, so collect every term on one side

$3  \text{sec}^{4} θ + 16 = 16  \text{sec}^{2} θ$

$3  \text{sec}^{4} θ - 16  \text{sec}^{2} θ + 16 = 0$

Factorise, treating $\text{sec}^{2} θ$ as the variable

`\left( 3 \; \text{sec}^2 \theta - 4 \right) \left( \text{sec}^2 \theta - 4 \right) = 0`

$\text{sec}^{2} θ = \frac{4}{3}$* or *$\text{sec}^{2} θ = 4$

**[A1]**

Take the square root of each, then reciprocate to reach the cosine

$\text{sec}  θ = \pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \Rightarrow \text{cos}  θ = \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$\text{sec}  θ = \pm 2 \Rightarrow \text{cos}  θ = \pm \frac{1}{2}$

**[M1]**

Solve the first pair. On $- π \leq θ \leq π$ each value of the cosine is taken twice, symmetrically about zero

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow θ = \pm \frac{π}{6}$

$\text{cos}  θ = - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow θ = \pm \frac{5π}{6}$

Solve the second pair the same way

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow θ = \pm \frac{π}{3}$

$\text{cos}  θ = - \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow θ = \pm \frac{2π}{3}$

All eight values lie inside the interval, so give them together

$θ = \pm \frac{π}{6} ,  \pm \frac{π}{3} ,  \pm \frac{2π}{3} ,  \pm \frac{5π}{6}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Reducing the equation to one in $\text{sec}  θ$ alone. Either route earns this mark and both meet at the same quadratic. Factorising the right hand side as `16 \left( 1 + \text{tan}^2 \theta \right) = 16 \; \text{sec}^2 \theta` gives $3  \text{sec}^{4} θ + 16 = 16  \text{sec}^{2} θ$. Subtracting $16$ from each side first is equally valid and gives $3  \text{sec}^{4} θ = 16  \text{tan}^{2} θ$, which becomes the same equation once $\text{tan}^{2} θ = \text{sec}^{2} θ - 1$ is used.
> 
> **A1**: Both values of $\text{sec}^{2} θ$, which are $\frac{4}{3}$ and $4$. Factorising, the formula and completing the square are all accepted on the quadratic in $\text{sec}^{2} θ$.
> 
> **M1**: Taking square roots and reciprocating to reach values of $\text{cos}  θ$. Both signs of each square root are needed, since dropping the negatives loses half the answers.
> 
> **A1**: All eight exact values, with no others inside $- π \leq θ \leq π$. The answers must be exact and in terms of $π$ as the question asks. Accept $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$ as equivalent forms along the way. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Given that

`\text{cos} \left( A - B \right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}`

and

`\text{tan} \left( \tfrac{1}{2}A - B \right) = \sqrt{3}`

where $0 \leq 2 B < A \leq 360 ^{\circ}$, find the possible values of $A$ and $B$.
parts.solutionMd:
Before solving anything, use the given condition to find the interval each of the two given angles must lie in. Since $2 B < A$, halving gives $B < \frac{1}{2} A$, so both angles are positive

$A - B > 0$* and *$\frac{1}{2} A - B > 0$

Since $A \leq 360 ^{\circ}$ and $B \geq 0$, each angle is bounded above as well

$0 < A - B \leq 360 ^{\circ}$* and *$0 < \frac{1}{2} A - B \leq 180 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Solve the first condition inside its interval, taking the inverse cosine for the first value

`A - B = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) = 150°`

Use the symmetry of the cosine curve, `\text{cos} \; \phi = \text{cos} \left( 360° - \phi \right)`, for the second value

$A - B = 360 ^{\circ} - 150 ^{\circ} = 210 ^{\circ}$

Now solve the second condition inside its interval, taking the inverse tangent

`\tfrac{1}{2}A - B = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( \sqrt{3} \right) = 60°`

The tangent has period $180 ^{\circ}$, so the next value would be $240 ^{\circ}$, which is outside the interval. This is therefore the only solution of the second condition

**[M1]**

Rearrange that single equation to give $A$ in terms of $B$

$\frac{1}{2} A = 60 ^{\circ} + B \Rightarrow A = 120 ^{\circ} + 2 B$

Substitute into the first condition, where the $2 B$ and the $- B$ combine

`\left( 120° + 2B \right) - B = 150°`* or *$210 ^{\circ}$

$120 ^{\circ} + B = 150 ^{\circ}$* or *$210 ^{\circ}$

Solve for each value of $B$

$B = 30 ^{\circ}$* or *$B = 90 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

Find the matching value of $A$ for each

`B = 30° \Rightarrow A = 120° + 2 \left( 30° \right) = 180°`

`B = 90° \Rightarrow A = 120° + 2 \left( 90° \right) = 300°`

Both pairs satisfy the given condition, since $0 \leq 60 ^{\circ} < 180 ^{\circ}$ and $0 \leq 180 ^{\circ} < 300 ^{\circ}$

**Final answer:** $A = 180 ^{\circ} ,  B = 30 ^{\circ}$** or **$A = 300 ^{\circ} ,  B = 90 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using the given condition $0 \leq 2 B < A \leq 360 ^{\circ}$ to establish an interval for each of the two given angles, reaching $0 < A - B \leq 360 ^{\circ}$ and $0 < \frac{1}{2} A - B \leq 180 ^{\circ}$. Doing this first is what makes the rest of the question straightforward, because it settles how many values each condition can supply before any solving begins.
> 
> **M1**: Correct values from both given conditions inside those intervals, which means $A - B = 150 ^{\circ}$ or $210 ^{\circ}$ from the cosine, and $\frac{1}{2} A - B = 60 ^{\circ}$ from the tangent. Values from only one condition are not enough.
> 
> **A1**: Both values of $B$, which are $30 ^{\circ}$ and $90 ^{\circ}$, from substituting $A = 120 ^{\circ} + 2 B$ into the first condition.
> 
> **A1**: Both correct pairs, with no others. Note that the tangent condition supplies only one value: its next value, $60 ^{\circ} + 180 ^{\circ} = 240 ^{\circ}$, lies outside $0 < \frac{1}{2} A - B \leq 180 ^{\circ}$. Establishing that interval at the start is much safer than generating $240 ^{\circ}$ and then having to notice later that it makes $A$ negative. Note also that $B$ appears in the condition as $2 B$, so it is $2 B < A$ that must hold, not $B < A$.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\text{cosec}^{2} x - 2  \frac{\text{cosec}x}{\text{sec}x} = 9$

for $0 \leq x \leq 2 π$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Simplify the quotient using the definitions of the two reciprocal functions

$\frac{\text{cosec}x}{\text{sec}x} = \frac{1/\text{sin}x}{1/\text{cos}x} = \frac{\text{cos}x}{\text{sin}x} = \text{cot}  x$

**[M1]**

Substitute that in, then use $1 + \text{cot}^{2} x \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x$ to write the whole equation in $\text{cot}  x$

$\text{cosec}^{2} x - 2  \text{cot}  x = 9$

$1 + \text{cot}^{2} x - 2  \text{cot}  x = 9$

**[A1]**

Collect every term on one side and factorise

$\text{cot}^{2} x - 2  \text{cot}  x - 8 = 0$

`\left( \text{cot} \; x - 4 \right) \left( \text{cot} \; x + 2 \right) = 0`

Set each factor to zero, then take reciprocals to reach the tangent

$\text{cot}  x = 4 \Rightarrow \text{tan}  x = \frac{1}{4}$* or *$\text{cot}  x = - 2 \Rightarrow \text{tan}  x = - \frac{1}{2}$

**[M1]**

Take the first root. The inverse tangent gives a value inside the interval, and the tangent has period $π$

`x = \text{tan}^{-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{4} \right) = 0.24497 \ldots`

Add the period for the second value

$x = 0 . 24497 \dots + π = 3 . 38657 \dots$

**[A1]**

Take the second root. Here the inverse tangent is negative, so it lies outside the interval; add the period to bring it in, then add it again

`\text{tan}^{-1} \left( -\tfrac{1}{2} \right) = -0.46364 \ldots \text{ (outside the interval)}`

$x = - 0 . 46364 \dots + π = 2 . 67794 \dots$

Add the period again for the fourth value

$x = 2 . 67794 \dots + π = 5 . 81953 \dots$

Round each of the four values to 3 significant figures as the question asks

$x = 0 . 245 ,  2 . 68 ,  3 . 39 ,  5 . 82$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Recognising that $\frac{\text{cosec}x}{\text{sec}x} = \text{cot}  x$, or equivalently rewriting the whole equation in sines and cosines. This is the step that makes the question tractable.
> 
> **A1**: Correct use of $1 + \text{cot}^{2} x \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x$ to reach an equation in $\text{cot}  x$ alone, such as $1 + \text{cot}^{2} x - 2  \text{cot}  x = 9$.
> 
> **M1**: Solving the three term quadratic to obtain at least one value of $\text{cot}  x$, and reciprocating to a value of $\text{tan}  x$. Factorising, the formula and completing the square are all accepted.
> 
> **A1**: Two correct values of $x$.
> 
> **A1**: All four values $x = 0 . 245$, $2 . 68$, $3 . 39$ and $5 . 82$, correct to 3 significant figures, with no others inside $0 \leq x \leq 2 π$. Accept answers which round to these. Remember the tangent has period $π$, not $2 π$, so each root of the quadratic gives two solutions in this interval; and the principal value from $\text{tan}  x = - \frac{1}{2}$ is negative, so it must be shifted into the interval rather than reported or discarded. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$8  \text{sin}^{4} 2 θ = 2 - 5  \text{cos}  4 θ$

for $- \frac{1}{2} π \leq θ \leq \frac{1}{2} π$, giving your answers in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
The left hand side is in $\text{sin}  2 θ$, so treat $4 θ$ as double $2 θ$ and choose the double angle form written in sine only

$\text{cos}  4 θ \equiv 1 - 2  \text{sin}^{2} 2 θ$

Substitute it in

`8 \; \text{sin}^4 2\theta = 2 - 5 \left( 1 - 2 \; \text{sin}^2 2\theta \right)`

**[M1]**

Expand the bracket and collect every term on one side

$8  \text{sin}^{4} 2 θ = - 3 + 10  \text{sin}^{2} 2 θ$

$8  \text{sin}^{4} 2 θ - 10  \text{sin}^{2} 2 θ + 3 = 0$

**[A1]**

Factorise, treating $\text{sin}^{2} 2 θ$ as the variable

`\left( 4 \; \text{sin}^2 2\theta - 3 \right) \left( 2 \; \text{sin}^2 2\theta - 1 \right) = 0`

$\text{sin}^{2} 2 θ = \frac{3}{4}$* or *$\text{sin}^{2} 2 θ = \frac{1}{2}$

Take the square root of each, keeping both signs, which gives four values in all

$\text{sin}  2 θ = \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$* or *$\text{sin}  2 θ = \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

**[M1]**

Substitute for the double angle and change the interval to match by doubling each part

$\text{Let}  ϕ = 2 θ ,$* so *$- π \leq ϕ \leq π$

Take the first value, $\text{sin}  ϕ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, and use the inverse sine for the first solution

`\phi = \text{sin}^{-1} \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}`

Use the symmetry `\text{sin} \; \phi = \text{sin} \left( \pi - \phi \right)` for the second solution

$ϕ = π - \frac{π}{3} = \frac{2π}{3}$

The sine is an odd function, so $\text{sin}  ϕ = - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is solved by the negatives of those two values

$ϕ = - \frac{π}{3}$

$ϕ = - \frac{2π}{3}$

**[A1]**

Now take $\text{sin}  ϕ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and work the same way

`\phi = \text{sin}^{-1} \left( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}`

$ϕ = π - \frac{π}{4} = \frac{3π}{4}$

The odd symmetry again gives the solutions of $\text{sin}  ϕ = - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$ϕ = - \frac{π}{4}$

$ϕ = - \frac{3π}{4}$

Halve every value of $ϕ$ to return to $θ$

$θ = \pm \frac{π}{6} ,  \pm \frac{π}{3}$* and *$θ = \pm \frac{π}{8} ,  \pm \frac{3π}{8}$

All eight values lie inside the interval, so give them together in order

$θ = \pm \frac{π}{8} ,  \pm \frac{π}{6} ,  \pm \frac{π}{3} ,  \pm \frac{3π}{8}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using a correct double angle form for $\text{cos}  4 θ$ in terms of $\text{sin}  2 θ$ to produce an equation in one function. Choosing $1 - 2  \text{sin}^{2} 2 θ$ is the efficient route because the left hand side is already in sine; the other forms will work but leave more to tidy up.
> 
> **A1**: The quadratic $8  \text{sin}^{4} 2 θ - 10  \text{sin}^{2} 2 θ + 3 = 0$, or a correct equivalent with all terms on one side.
> 
> **M1**: Solving to obtain at least one value of $\text{sin}^{2} 2 θ$ and taking the square root to reach a value of $\text{sin}  2 θ$. Both square roots of both values are needed for the full answer set, giving four values of $\text{sin}  2 θ$ in all.
> 
> **A1**: At least four correct values of $θ$.
> 
> **A1**: All eight correct exact values, with no others inside $- \frac{1}{2} π \leq θ \leq \frac{1}{2} π$. The answers must be exact and in terms of $π$ as the question asks. Two things multiply the count here: doubling the interval gives a full $2 π$ of range in $ϕ$, and the quadratic supplies four values of $\text{sin}  2 θ$ rather than two. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Given that $x = - 2$ is a root of the equation

$x^{3} + 12 x^{2} + 44 x + 48 = 0$

solve the equation by factorisation.
parts.solutionMd:
Since $x = - 2$ is a root, `\left( x + 2 \right)` is a factor, so divide the cubic by it

`x^3 + 12x^2 + 44x + 48 = \left( x + 2 \right) \left( x^2 + 10x + 24 \right)`

**[M1 A1]**

Factorise the quadratic quotient

`x^2 + 10x + 24 = \left( x + 4 \right) \left( x + 6 \right)`

So the cubic factorises completely

`\left( x + 2 \right) \left( x + 4 \right) \left( x + 6 \right) = 0`

**[M1]**

Set each factor to zero

$x = - 6 ,  x = - 4 ,  x = - 2$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Dividing the cubic by `\left( x + 2 \right)`, by long division, synthetic division or by comparing coefficients. Can be implied.
> 
> **A1**: The correct quotient $x^{2} + 10 x + 24$.
> 
> **M1**: Factorising or otherwise solving the quadratic quotient. The formula and completing the square are equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1**: All three roots $x = - 6$, $- 4$ and $- 2$. The given root $x = - 2$ must appear in the final answer, since the question asks you to solve the equation rather than just find the other two roots.

parts.problemMd:
Hence solve the equation

`\text{sec} \; \theta \left( \text{sec}^2 \theta + 44 \right) + 12 \left( \text{tan}^2 \theta + 5 \right) = 0`

for $0 ^{\circ} \leq θ \leq 180 ^{\circ}$, giving your answers correct to 1 decimal place where appropriate.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the identity $1 + \text{tan}^{2} θ \equiv \text{sec}^{2} θ$ to replace $\text{tan}^{2} θ$

$\text{tan}^{2} θ \equiv \text{sec}^{2} θ - 1$

Substitute, then expand both brackets

`\text{sec} \; \theta \left( \text{sec}^2 \theta + 44 \right) + 12 \left( \text{sec}^2 \theta - 1 + 5 \right) = 0`

$\text{sec}^{3} θ + 44  \text{sec}  θ + 12  \text{sec}^{2} θ + 48 = 0$

**[M1]**

Write it in descending powers, which is exactly the cubic from part (a) with $x = \text{sec}  θ$

$\text{sec}^{3} θ + 12  \text{sec}^{2} θ + 44  \text{sec}  θ + 48 = 0$

**[A1]**

So the roots carry straight over from part (a)

$\text{sec}  θ = - 6 ,  - 4 ,  - 2$

Take reciprocals to reach the cosine

$\text{cos}  θ = - \frac{1}{6} ,  - \frac{1}{4} ,  - \frac{1}{2}$

**[M1]**

Every value is negative with modulus at most $1$, so each gives exactly one angle in the interval. Take the inverse cosine of each

`\theta = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( -\tfrac{1}{6} \right) = 99.59406 \ldots°`

`\theta = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( -\tfrac{1}{4} \right) = 104.47751 \ldots°`

`\theta = \text{cos}^{-1} \left( -\tfrac{1}{2} \right) = 120°`

Give the exact answer exactly and round the other two to 1 decimal place

$θ = 99 . 6 ^{\circ} ,  104 . 5 ^{\circ} ,  120 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $1 + \text{tan}^{2} θ \equiv \text{sec}^{2} θ$ and expansion of both brackets, so that the equation is written in $\text{sec}  θ$ alone.
> 
> **A1**: Reaching the cubic $\text{sec}^{3} θ + 12  \text{sec}^{2} θ + 44  \text{sec}  θ + 48 = 0$, recognisably the same as part (a) with $x = \text{sec}  θ$. Note the $+ 48$ comes from `12 \left( -1 + 5 \right) = 48`, so the constants must be combined carefully.
> 
> **M1**: Using the roots from part (a) to obtain values of $\text{sec}  θ$, and reciprocating to values of $\text{cos}  θ$. Re-solving the cubic from scratch is acceptable but wastes the work already done in (a).
> 
> **A1**: All three values $θ = 99 . 6 ^{\circ}$, $104 . 5 ^{\circ}$ and $120 ^{\circ}$, with no others inside $0 ^{\circ} \leq θ \leq 180 ^{\circ}$. Accept answers which round to these, and give $120 ^{\circ}$ exactly. Note that no root is rejected here: all three values of $\text{cos}  θ$ are negative with modulus at most $1$, so each gives exactly one angle in the interval. Values you give outside the interval are ignored, but an extra value inside it loses this mark.

parts.problemMd: Sketch the graph of $y = \text{cosec}  x$, for $- 180 ^{\circ} \leq x \leq 180 ^{\circ}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the definition $\text{cosec}  x = \frac{1}{\text{sin}x}$

$\text{cosec}  x = \frac{1}{\text{sin}x}$

There is an asymptote wherever $\text{sin}  x = 0$, since the fraction is undefined there

$x = - 180 ^{\circ} , x = 0 ^{\circ} , x = 180 ^{\circ}$

The turning points sit where the sine curve peaks

$\text{sin}  90 ^{\circ} = 1 \Rightarrow \text{cosec}  90 ^{\circ} = 1$

`\text{sin} \; \left(- 90^{\circ}\right) = - 1 \Rightarrow \text{cosec} \; \left(- 90^{\circ}\right) = - 1`

One over a shrinking value grows without limit, so each branch sweeps away towards its asymptotes

![Graph of y = cosec x for x between -180 and 180 degrees, showing a U-shaped branch above the x-axis with its minimum at (90, 1) and an upside-down branch below the x-axis with its maximum at (-90, -1), with dashed vertical asymptotes at x = -180, x = 0 and x = 180, and a faint y = sin x curve drawn as a guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/trigonometry/reciprocal-trigonometric-functions/assets/001-graph-of-y-cosec-x-for-x-between-180-and-180-deg.png)

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both branches drawn with the correct shape, the branch for $0 ^{\circ} < x < 180 ^{\circ}$ lying above the line $y = 1$ with its lowest point at `\left(90^{\circ} , 1\right)`, and the branch for $- 180 ^{\circ} < x < 0 ^{\circ}$ lying below the line $y = - 1$ with its highest point at `\left(- 90^{\circ} , - 1\right)`. No incorrect curvature, and neither branch may touch or cross the $x$-axis.
> 
> **B1**: All three asymptotes shown at $x = - 180 ^{\circ}$, $x = 0 ^{\circ}$ and $x = 180 ^{\circ}$, with each branch approaching them without reaching them. Accept dashed vertical lines on the sketch, or the three equations written alongside it. Work outside $- 180 ^{\circ} \leq x \leq 180 ^{\circ}$ is ignored.

parts.problemMd: Solve the equation $\text{cot}  x = 3$ for $- π \leq x \leq π$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the definition $\text{cot}  x = \frac{1}{\text{tan}x}$

$\frac{1}{\text{tan}x} = 3$

Rearrange to make $\text{tan}  x$ the subject

$\text{tan}  x = \frac{1}{3}$

Take the inverse tangent, keeping the unrounded value

`x = \text{tan}^{- 1} \left(\frac{1}{3}\right) = 0 . 32175 \ldots`

**[M1 A1]**

Find the other solution by subtracting the period

$x = 0 . 32175 \dots - π = - 2 . 81984 \dots$

Round each value to 3 significant figures

**Final answer:** $x = 0 . 322$** or **$x = - 2 . 82$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $\text{cot}  x = \frac{1}{\text{tan}x}$ to reach $\text{tan}  x = \frac{1}{3}$, followed by a correct method for at least one value of $x$. Any valid route to $\text{tan}  x = \frac{1}{3}$ earns this, including writing $\text{cot}  x$ as $\frac{\text{cos}x}{\text{sin}x}$ first.
> 
> **A1**: One correct value, which is $0 . 322$. Accept answers which round to $0 . 322$, and accept a more accurate value provided it is correct.
> 
> **A1**: The second value $- 2 . 82$, with no other values inside $- π \leq x \leq π$. Values given outside the interval are ignored. Answers given in degrees, $18 . 4 ^{\circ}$ and $- 161 . 6 ^{\circ}$, are treated as a misreading of the question, so the method marks still stand but this accuracy mark is not earned.

parts.problemMd:
Sketch the graph of $y = \text{sec}  θ$, for $- π \leq θ \leq π$.

Label any points of intersection with the coordinate axes and state the equations of any asymptotes.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the definition $\text{sec}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$

$\text{sec}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$

There is an asymptote wherever $\text{cos}  θ = 0$, since the fraction is undefined there

$θ = - \frac{π}{2} , θ = \frac{π}{2}$

**[B1]**

To find where the curve meets the vertical axis, substitute $θ = 0$

$\text{sec}  0 = \frac{1}{\text{cos}0} = \frac{1}{1} = 1$

A fraction with numerator $1$ is never zero, so the curve misses the horizontal axis

**Final answer:** **The curve meets the y-axis at (0, 1) and does not cross the theta-axis**

**[B1]**

Between the asymptotes $\text{cos}  θ$ is positive and at most $1$

$\text{sec}  θ \geq 1$* for *$- \frac{π}{2} < θ < \frac{π}{2}$

Outside them it is negative, reaching $- 1$ at each end of the interval

`\text{sec} \; \left(\pm \pi\right) = \frac{1}{- 1} = - 1`

![Graph of y = sec theta for theta between -pi and pi, showing a U-shaped central branch above the horizontal axis with its lowest point labelled (0, 1), and two outer branches below the horizontal axis rising to the marked endpoints (-pi, -1) and (pi, -1), with dashed vertical asymptotes at theta = -pi over 2 and theta = pi over 2, and a faint y = cos theta curve drawn as a guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/trigonometry/reciprocal-trigonometric-functions/assets/004-graph-of-y-sec-theta-for-theta-between-pi-and-pi.png)

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both asymptotes stated as equations, $θ = - \frac{π}{2}$ and $θ = \frac{π}{2}$. Accept $x = \pm \frac{π}{2}$ or the decimal equivalents. Dashed lines drawn on the sketch without the equations do not earn this mark, since the question asks for the equations.
> 
> **B1**: The intersection with the vertical axis given as `\left(0 , 1\right)`, and a statement that there is no intersection with the horizontal axis. Accept the value $1$ marked on the vertical axis in place of the coordinate pair.
> 
> **B1**: The central branch drawn correctly for $- \frac{π}{2} < θ < \frac{π}{2}$, lying on or above $y = 1$, symmetrical about the vertical axis, with its lowest point at `\left(0 , 1\right)` and rising towards both asymptotes.
> 
> **B1**: Both outer branches drawn correctly, lying on or below $y = - 1$ and reaching $- 1$ at $θ = - π$ and $θ = π$. No incorrect curvature, and no part of the graph may be drawn in the region between $y = - 1$ and $y = 1$. Work outside $- π \leq θ \leq π$ is ignored.

parts.problemMd:
Starting with the identity

$\text{sin}^{2} x + \text{cos}^{2} x \equiv 1$

show that

(i) $1 + \text{cot}^{2} x \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x$

(ii) $\text{tan}^{2} x + 1 \equiv \text{sec}^{2} x$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Divide every term by $\text{sin}^{2} x$, so the first term becomes $1$

$\frac{\text{sin}^{2}x}{\text{sin}^{2}x} + \frac{\text{cos}^{2}x}{\text{sin}^{2}x} \equiv \frac{1}{\text{sin}^{2}x}$

**[M1]**

Cancel the first term

$1 + \frac{\text{cos}^{2}x}{\text{sin}^{2}x} \equiv \frac{1}{\text{sin}^{2}x}$

Use the definitions $\text{cot}  x = \frac{\text{cos}x}{\text{sin}x}$ and $\text{cosec}  x = \frac{1}{\text{sin}x}$, each squared

`1 + \left(\frac{\text{cos} \; x}{\text{sin} \; x}\right)^{2} \equiv \left(\frac{1}{\text{sin} \; x}\right)^{2}`

**Final answer:** $1 + \text{cot}^{2} x \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x$** as required**

**[A1]**

(ii)

This time divide every term by $\text{cos}^{2} x$

$\frac{\text{sin}^{2}x}{\text{cos}^{2}x} + \frac{\text{cos}^{2}x}{\text{cos}^{2}x} \equiv \frac{1}{\text{cos}^{2}x}$

**[M1]**

Cancel the second term

$\frac{\text{sin}^{2}x}{\text{cos}^{2}x} + 1 \equiv \frac{1}{\text{cos}^{2}x}$

Use the definitions $\text{tan}  x = \frac{\text{sin}x}{\text{cos}x}$ and $\text{sec}  x = \frac{1}{\text{cos}x}$, each squared

`\left(\frac{\text{sin} \; x}{\text{cos} \; x}\right)^{2} + 1 \equiv \left(\frac{1}{\text{cos} \; x}\right)^{2}`

**Final answer:** $\text{tan}^{2} x + 1 \equiv \text{sec}^{2} x$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Every term of $\text{sin}^{2} x + \text{cos}^{2} x \equiv 1$ divided by $\text{sin}^{2} x$. All three terms must be divided, not just two.
> 
> **A1**: The result $1 + \text{cot}^{2} x \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x$ reached, with a concluding statement. Accept reaching $\frac{\text{cos}^{2}x}{\text{sin}^{2}x}$ as $\frac{1}{\text{tan}^{2}x}$ and then $\text{cot}^{2} x$. Because the answer is given, every line must be correct, and the $x$ must be present throughout. Abbreviations such as $s$, $c$ or $t$ in place of the function names are accepted only if they are defined first.
> 
> **M1**: Every term of $\text{sin}^{2} x + \text{cos}^{2} x \equiv 1$ divided by $\text{cos}^{2} x$. All three terms must be divided.
> 
> **A1**: The result $\text{tan}^{2} x + 1 \equiv \text{sec}^{2} x$ reached, with a concluding statement, and every line correct with the $x$ present. A candidate who works instead from the first result, replacing $\text{cot}^{2} x$ and $\text{cosec}^{2} x$ by $\frac{1}{\text{tan}^{2}x}$ and $\frac{1}{\text{sin}^{2}x}$ and rearranging, earns both marks for this identity provided the argument is complete.

parts.problemMd:
Show that

$\text{sec}^{2} θ \text{sin}  θ \equiv \text{tan}  θ \text{sec}  θ$
parts.solutionMd:
Start from the left hand side and use the definition $\text{sec}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$

$\text{sec}^{2} θ \text{sin}  θ \equiv \frac{1}{\text{cos}^{2}θ} \times \text{sin}  θ \equiv \frac{\text{sin}θ}{\text{cos}^{2}θ}$

**[M1]**

Split the fraction into two factors to match the right hand side

$\frac{\text{sin}θ}{\text{cos}^{2}θ} \equiv \frac{\text{sin}θ}{\text{cos}θ} \times \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$

**[M1]**

Use the definitions $\text{tan}  θ = \frac{\text{sin}θ}{\text{cos}θ}$ and $\text{sec}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$

$\equiv \text{tan}  θ \times \text{sec}  θ$

**Final answer:** $\text{sec}^{2} θ \text{sin}  θ \equiv \text{tan}  θ \text{sec}  θ$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $\text{sec}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$ to write the left hand side as $\frac{\text{sin}θ}{\text{cos}^{2}θ}$. Starting instead from the right hand side and writing $\text{tan}  θ \text{sec}  θ$ as $\frac{\text{sin}θ}{\text{cos}θ} \times \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$ earns this mark equally.
> 
> **M1**: The single fraction separated into the product $\frac{\text{sin}θ}{\text{cos}θ} \times \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$, or the equivalent step in the other direction.
> 
> **A1**: The identity completed correctly. Because the result is given, every line must be correct and the $θ$ must be present throughout. Abbreviations such as $s$, $c$ or $t$ in place of the function names are accepted only if they are defined first, and missing brackets do not earn this mark. Working on both sides at once is accepted provided the two sides are brought to the same expression and a concluding statement is written.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\text{cosec}^{2} x - 2 \text{cosec}  x - 8 = 0$

for $0 ^{\circ} \leq x \leq 360 ^{\circ}$, giving your answers correct to 1 decimal place where appropriate.
parts.solutionMd:
This is a quadratic in $\text{cosec}  x$, so factorise it as one

`\left(\text{cosec} \; x - 4\right) \left(\text{cosec} \; x + 2\right) = 0`

Set each factor to zero

$\text{cosec}  x = 4$* or *$\text{cosec}  x = - 2$

Use the definition $\text{cosec}  x = \frac{1}{\text{sin}x}$

$\text{sin}  x = \frac{1}{4}$* or *$\text{sin}  x = - \frac{1}{2}$

Take the inverse sine of the first value, keeping the unrounded value

`x = \text{sin}^{- 1} \left(\frac{1}{4}\right) = 14 . 4775 \ldots^{\circ}`

**[M1]**

Use the symmetry of the sine curve for the other solution from this branch

$x = 180 ^{\circ} - 14 . 4775 \dots ^{\circ} = 165 . 5224 \dots ^{\circ}$

Now take the inverse sine of the second value

`x = \text{sin}^{- 1} \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right) = - 30^{\circ}`

This is not within the interval, so use the symmetry and the period to find two alternative solutions

`x = 180^{\circ} - \left(- 30^{\circ}\right) = 210^{\circ}`

$x = - 30 ^{\circ} + 360 ^{\circ} = 330 ^{\circ}$

Round the two non-exact values to 1 decimal place

$x = 14 . 5 ^{\circ} , 165 . 5 ^{\circ} , 210 ^{\circ} , 330 ^{\circ}$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The equation treated as a quadratic in $\text{cosec}  x$ and solved, followed by a correct method leading to at least one value of $x$. Accept factorising, the quadratic formula or completing the square. A candidate who first replaces $\text{cosec}  x$ by $\frac{1}{\text{sin}x}$ and forms the quadratic $8 \text{sin}^{2} x + 2 \text{sin}  x - 1 = 0$ earns this mark equally.
> 
> **A1**: One correct value of $x$. Accept answers which round to $14 . 5 ^{\circ}$, and accept a more accurate value provided it is correct. Answers under-rounded to $14 ^{\circ}$ or $166 ^{\circ}$ do not earn a mark.
> 
> **A1**: The three remaining values $165 . 5 ^{\circ}$, $210 ^{\circ}$ and $330 ^{\circ}$, with no other values inside $0 ^{\circ} \leq x \leq 360 ^{\circ}$. Values given outside the interval are ignored. Answers given in radians are treated as a misreading of the question, so at most two of the three marks are available.

parts.problemMd:
Show that

$\text{cot}  x \text{cosec}  x \text{sec}  x \equiv 1 + \text{cot}^{2} x$
parts.solutionMd:
Start from the left hand side and write each function in terms of sine and cosine

$\text{cot}  x \text{cosec}  x \text{sec}  x \equiv \frac{\text{cos}x}{\text{sin}x} \times \frac{1}{\text{sin}x} \times \frac{1}{\text{cos}x}$

**[M1]**

Multiply the three fractions and cancel $\text{cos}  x$

$\equiv \frac{\text{cos}x}{\text{sin}^{2}x\text{cos}x} \equiv \frac{1}{\text{sin}^{2}x} \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x$

**[M1]**

Finish with the identity $1 + \text{cot}^{2} x \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x$, read in the other direction

$\equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x \equiv 1 + \text{cot}^{2} x$

**Final answer:** $\text{cot}  x \text{cosec}  x \text{sec}  x \equiv 1 + \text{cot}^{2} x$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: All three functions on the left hand side written in terms of sine and cosine. Accept $\text{cot}  x$ written as $\frac{1}{\text{tan}x}$ provided the work is then completed correctly.
> 
> **M1**: The product simplified to $\frac{1}{\text{sin}^{2}x}$ or to $\text{cosec}^{2} x$. A candidate using $\frac{1}{\text{tan}x}$ reaches this by way of $\text{tan}  x \text{cos}  x \equiv \text{sin}  x$, which earns the mark equally.
> 
> **A1**: The identity $1 + \text{cot}^{2} x \equiv \text{cosec}^{2} x$ used to complete the argument, with the result reached. Starting from the right hand side and replacing $1 + \text{cot}^{2} x$ by $\text{cosec}^{2} x$ first is equally valid. Because the result is given, every line must be correct and the $x$ must be present throughout. Abbreviations such as $s$, $c$ or $t$ in place of the function names are accepted only if they are defined first.

parts.problemMd:
Solve the equation

$\text{sec}  θ \text{tan}  θ - \text{sec}  θ = 0$

for $0 \leq θ \leq 2 π$, giving your answers in an exact form.
parts.solutionMd:
Factorise rather than divide, so that no solution is lost

`\text{sec} \; \theta \left(\text{tan} \; \theta - 1\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

Set each factor to zero

$\text{sec}  θ = 0$* or *$\text{tan}  θ - 1 = 0$

A fraction with numerator $1$ is never zero, so the first branch gives no solutions

$\text{tan}  θ = 1$

**[A1]**

Take the inverse tangent

`\theta = \text{tan}^{- 1} \left(1\right) = \frac{\pi}{4}`

**[A1]**

Find the other solution by adding the period

$θ = \frac{π}{4} + π = \frac{5π}{4}$

$θ = \frac{π}{4} , θ = \frac{5π}{4}$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is tempting to divide both sides by $\text{sec}  θ$ at the start, and here that happens to be safe, because $\text{sec}  θ$ can never equal zero. Get into the habit of factorising anyway. With a shared factor such as $\text{sin}  θ$ or $\text{tan}  θ$, which can be zero, dividing throws away solutions and the mark scheme will not credit it.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The equation factorised to `\text{sec} \; \theta \left(\text{tan} \; \theta - 1\right) = 0`, with an attempt to solve at least one factor. Dividing both sides by $\text{sec}  θ$ earns this mark equally, since $\text{sec}  θ$ is never zero. Rewriting the whole equation in terms of $\text{sin}  θ$ and $\text{cos}  θ$ is also accepted.
> 
> **A1**: $\text{tan}  θ = 1$ obtained. You are not required to state or justify that $\text{sec}  θ = 0$ gives no solutions, and simply leaving that branch aside is not penalised.
> 
> **A1**: The value $\frac{π}{4}$, or any exact equivalent such as $\frac{1}{4} π$.
> 
> **A1**: The value $\frac{5π}{4}$, or any exact equivalent, with no other values inside $0 \leq θ \leq 2 π$. Values given outside the interval are ignored. Because the question asks for an exact form, decimal answers such as $0 . 785$ and $3 . 93$, or answers in degrees, do not earn the two accuracy marks for the values.

parts.problemMd: Sketch the graph of $y = 2 \text{sec}  2 x$ for $- π \leq x \leq π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the definition $\text{sec}  2 x = \frac{1}{\text{cos}2x}$

$y = 2 \text{sec}  2 x = \frac{2}{\text{cos}2x}$

Read the curve as a horizontal stretch of scale factor $\frac{1}{2}$ and a vertical stretch of scale factor $2$

There is an asymptote wherever $\text{cos}  2 x = 0$

$x = - \frac{3π}{4} , x = - \frac{π}{4} , x = \frac{π}{4} , x = \frac{3π}{4}$

Find the turning points, where $\text{cos}  2 x$ reaches $\pm 1$

$\text{cos}  0 = 1 \Rightarrow y = 2$* at *$x = 0$

`\text{cos} \; \left(\pm \pi\right) = - 1 \Rightarrow y = - 2`* at *$x = \pm \frac{π}{2}$

The interval is closed, so check the two ends as well

`\text{cos} \; \left(\pm 2 \pi\right) = 1 \Rightarrow y = 2`* at *$x = \pm π$

![Graph of y = 2 sec 2x for x between -pi and pi, showing a U-shaped branch above the horizontal axis with its minimum labelled (0, 2), two inverted branches below the axis with maximum points labelled (-pi over 2, -2) and (pi over 2, -2), and two part branches rising from the endpoints (-pi, 2) and (pi, 2), with dashed vertical asymptotes at x = -3pi over 4, -pi over 4, pi over 4 and 3pi over 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/trigonometry/reciprocal-trigonometric-functions/assets/002-graph-of-y-2-sec-2x-for-x-between-pi-and-pi-show.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct secant shape throughout, with each branch curving away from the horizontal axis towards its asymptotes and no branch touching or crossing them. No incorrect curvature, and the curve must not be drawn with a ruler.
> 
> **B1**: The minimum of the central branch at `\left(0 , 2\right)` and the maximum of each lower branch at `\left(- \frac{\pi}{2} , - 2\right)` and `\left(\frac{\pi}{2} , - 2\right)`, correctly placed. Accept the values marked on the axes rather than written as coordinate pairs.
> 
> **B1**: The graph drawn across the whole of $- π \leq x \leq π$, including the part branches that reach the endpoints `\left(- \pi , 2\right)` and `\left(\pi , 2\right)`, and nothing drawn outside the interval. The asymptotes need not be drawn as lines or stated as equations, but the curve must behave correctly at each of them.

parts.problemMd: By sketching a suitable straight line on your diagram, show that the equation $2 \text{sec}  2 x = 4$ has four solutions in this interval.
parts.solutionMd:
Solutions occur where the curve has height $4$, so add that horizontal line

$y = 4$

The line misses the two branches below the axis and cuts the three above it

![The graph of y = 2 sec 2x for x between -pi and pi with the horizontal line y = 4 drawn across it, crossing the central branch twice and each of the two end branches once, with all four points of intersection marked by crosses](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-2/trigonometry/reciprocal-trigonometric-functions/assets/003-the-graph-of-y-2-sec-2x-for-x-between-pi-and-pi-.png)

**[B1]**

Count the crossings to answer the question

**Final answer:** **The line meets the curve four times, so the equation has four solutions in this interval**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The horizontal line $y = 4$ drawn on the diagram. It must be recognisably straight and horizontal, and placed above the minimum point of the central branch.
> 
> **B1**: All four points of intersection identified and the conclusion stated. Mark the intersections with dots or crosses, or say in words that the roots are at the points of intersection. Because the number of solutions is given in the question, the concluding statement is needed as well as the marked points.

parts.problemMd:
Use the definitions of the secant, cosecant and cotangent functions to show that

$\text{sec}  θ \text{cot}  θ \equiv \text{cosec}  θ$
parts.solutionMd:
Write each function on the left in terms of sine and cosine

$\text{sec}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$* and *$\text{cot}  θ = \frac{\text{cos}θ}{\text{sin}θ}$

Multiply the two together and cancel $\text{cos}  θ$

$\text{sec}  θ \text{cot}  θ \equiv \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ} \times \frac{\text{cos}θ}{\text{sin}θ} \equiv \frac{1}{\text{sin}θ}$

**[M1]**

Recognise the remaining fraction as the cosecant

$\equiv \frac{1}{\text{sin}θ} \equiv \text{cosec}  θ$

**Final answer:** $\text{sec}  θ \text{cot}  θ \equiv \text{cosec}  θ$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Both $\text{sec}  θ$ and $\text{cot}  θ$ written in terms of sine and cosine and multiplied together. Accept $\text{cot}  θ$ written first as $\frac{1}{\text{tan}θ}$ and then converted.
> 
> **A1**: The product simplified to $\frac{1}{\text{sin}θ}$ and identified as $\text{cosec}  θ$, completing the identity. Because the result is given, every line must be correct and the $θ$ must be present throughout. Abbreviations such as $s$ or $c$ in place of the function names are accepted only if they are defined first.

parts.problemMd:
Hence solve the equation

$\text{sec}  θ \text{cot}  θ = - 2$

for $0 \leq θ \leq 2 π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use part (a) to replace the left hand side with a single function

$\text{cosec}  θ = - 2$

Use the definition $\text{cosec}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{sin}θ}$

$\text{sin}  θ = - \frac{1}{2}$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse sine to find the principal value

`\theta = \text{sin}^{- 1} \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right) = - \frac{\pi}{6}`

This is not within the interval, so use the symmetry of the sine curve to find an alternative solution

`\theta = \pi - \left(- \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{7 \pi}{6}`

**[A1]**

Find another solution by adding the period

$θ = - \frac{π}{6} + 2 π = \frac{11π}{6}$

$θ = \frac{7π}{6} , θ = \frac{11π}{6}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Part (a) used to reduce the equation to $\text{cosec}  θ = - 2$, then $\text{sin}  θ = - \frac{1}{2}$ obtained, followed by a correct method for at least one value of $θ$. Ignoring part (a) and working directly from $\frac{1}{\text{cos}θ} \times \frac{\text{cos}θ}{\text{sin}θ} = - 2$ earns this mark equally.
> 
> **A1**: One correct value, which is $\frac{7π}{6}$. Because the question does not ask for an exact answer, the decimal equivalent $3 . 67$ is equally acceptable, as is any exact equivalent such as $\frac{7}{6} π$.
> 
> **A1**: The second value $\frac{11π}{6}$, or $5 . 76$, with no other values inside $0 \leq θ \leq 2 π$. Values given outside the interval are ignored. Answers given in degrees are treated as a misreading of the question.

parts.problemMd:
Show that the equation

$3 - \text{sec}  θ = \frac{2}{\text{sec}θ}$

can be expressed in the form

`\left(\text{sec} \; \theta - 2\right) \left(\text{sec} \; \theta - 1\right) = 0`
parts.solutionMd:
Multiply every term by $\text{sec}  θ$ to clear the fraction

$3 \text{sec}  θ - \text{sec}^{2} θ = 2$

Collect everything on one side to form a quadratic in $\text{sec}  θ$

$\text{sec}^{2} θ - 3 \text{sec}  θ + 2 = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise, looking for two numbers with product $2$ and sum $- 3$

**Final answer:** `\left(\text{sec} \; \theta - 2\right) \left(\text{sec} \; \theta - 1\right) = 0`** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Both sides multiplied by $\text{sec}  θ$ and the terms collected to give a three term quadratic in $\text{sec}  θ$ equal to zero. Working instead in cosine, multiplying by $\text{cos}  θ$ to reach $2 \text{cos}^{2} θ - 3 \text{cos}  θ + 1 = 0$, earns this mark equally provided it is then converted back.
> 
> **A1**: The given factorised form reached. Because the answer is printed, every line must be correct and the $θ$ must be present throughout.

parts.problemMd:
Hence solve the equation

$3 - \text{sec}  θ = \frac{2}{\text{sec}θ}$

for $0 \leq θ \leq 2 π$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the factorised form from part (a), setting each factor to zero

$\text{sec}  θ = 2$* or *$\text{sec}  θ = 1$

Use the definition $\text{sec}  θ = \frac{1}{\text{cos}θ}$

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{1}{2}$* or *$\text{cos}  θ = 1$

**[M1]**
